Core components

Networks

  • A VPC network serves as a container for subnets and routing configurations.
  • Each project starts with a default network, but custom networks can be created.

Subnets

  • Each subnet is associated with a specific region and defined IP range.
  • Subnets can be auto-mode (automatically created) or custom-mode (manually defined).

IP Addressing

  • Internal IPs: For private communication within the network.
  • External IPs: For internet-facing resources.
  • Private IPs: For access to Google APIs via private Google access.


Routes

    • Control traffic direction within the VPC and to external networks.
    • Default routes handle outbound internet traffic for resources with external IPs.

Firewall Rules

    • Allow or deny traffic to and from instances based on configurations.
    • Can be applied to specific instances using tags or service accounts.

Cloud NAT

    • Provides outbound internet access for resources without external IPs.

Best practices

  1. Network Design:

    • Plan IP ranges carefully to avoid overlaps.
    • Use custom-mode VPCs for better control over subnet creation.

  2. Security:

    • Apply the principle of least privilege for firewall rules.
    • Use service accounts and IAM roles for granular access control.

  3. Monitoring and Auditing:

    • Regularly monitor traffic and resource usage using Flow Logs.
    • Audit configurations to ensure compliance with organizational policies.

  4. Scalability and Performance:

    • Design networks with future growth in mind.
    • Use Cloud NAT for scalable and secure internet access.

  5. Cost Management:

    • Regularly review network configurations to identify unused resources.
    • Optimize hybrid connectivity costs by choosing the right option (VPN vs. Interconnect).


Firewall

What it is?

Google Cloud VPC firewalls are a critical component of network security, enabling administrators to control ingress (incoming) and egress (outgoing) traffic for resources deployed in a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Below is an in-depth explanation tailored for aspiring Google Cloud administrators.


Google Cloud firewalls provide managed, distributed, and stateful traffic control for resources in a VPC. The firewalls:

  • Operate globally for VPC networks, which span all regions.
  • Allow or deny traffic at the network level, while decisions to permit or block connections are enforced on a per-instance basis.
  • Protect resources regardless of the underlying operating system.

Each VPC functions as a distributed firewall, and firewall rules can:

  • Control traffic between instances within the same VPC.
  • Regulate traffic between instances and external networks.
  • Apply to individual or all resources in the VPC.

Use cases

  1. Securing Communication Between Instances:

    • Restrict inter-instance communication by creating rules that allow only necessary traffic.

  2. Controlling Internet Access:

    • Deny all ingress from external IPs except for specific trusted IP ranges.
    • Use Cloud NAT for secure outbound internet access without exposing internal IPs.

  3. Hybrid Connectivity:

    • Apply ingress rules to allow traffic from on-premises networks connected via VPN or Interconnect.

  4. Custom Application Rules:

    • Restrict application access by allowing only specific protocols and ports (e.g., TCP 443 for HTTPS).

Key features

Stateful Design

  • Once a connection is initiated and allowed by a rule, return traffic is automatically allowed, enabling bidirectional communication without additional rules.
  • A connection remains active as long as at least one packet is sent every 10 minutes.

Global Applicability

  • Firewall rules are defined at the network level and are inherently global, reflecting the global nature of Google Cloud VPCs.

Flexibility

  • Rules can be applied universally to all instances, to instances with specific tags, or to instances associated with particular service accounts.

Ease of Configuration:

  • Rules are straightforward to define, prioritize, and modify, making it easy to enforce consistent policies.

Parameters


A firewall rule is defined by the following parameters:

  1. Direction:

    • Ingress: Controls incoming traffic to instances.
    • Egress: Controls outgoing traffic from instances.

  2. Source and Destination:

    • Source: Applicable for ingress rules; defines the origin of the traffic.
    • Destination: Applicable for egress rules; defines the target of the traffic.

  3. Targets:

    • Apply rules to:

      • All instances in the network.
      • Instances with specific target tags.
      • Instances associated with particular service accounts.

  4. Protocol and Ports:

    • Define traffic based on protocol (e.g., TCP, UDP, ICMP) and port numbers.
    • If unspecified, the rule applies to all protocols.

  5. Action:

    • Allow: Permits traffic.
    • Deny: Blocks traffic.

  6. Priority:

    • A numerical value between 0 (highest priority) and 65,535 (lowest priority).
    • Rules are evaluated in ascending order of priority, with the first match applied.
    • If priorities conflict, a deny rule overrides an allow rule.

Applying rules

Firewall rules can be applied in multiple ways:

  1. Network-Wide Rules: Apply universally to all instances within the VPC network.
  2. Tagged Instances: Use target tags to apply rules selectively. Instances must be tagged with the specified value to inherit the rule.
  3. Service Accounts: Apply rules to all instances associated with a particular service account. Changing a service account requires stopping and restarting the instance.

Defaults

Implied rules

All VPC networks, whether auto or custom mode, come with implied firewall rules. These rules have the lowest priority (65535) and cannot be removed:

  1. IPv4 Implied Rules:

    • Egress Rule:

      • Action: Allow
      • Destination: 0.0.0.0/0 (any destination)
      • Purpose: Allows outbound traffic unless explicitly blocked.

    • Ingress Rule:

      • Action: Deny
      • Source: 0.0.0.0/0 (any source)
      • Purpose: Denies all incoming traffic by default.

  2. IPv6 Implied Rules (if enabled):

    • Egress Rule:

      • Action: Allow
      • Destination: ::/0 (any IPv6 destination).
      • Purpose: Allows outbound IPv6 traffic unless restricted by a higher-priority rule.

    • Ingress Rule:

      • Action: Deny
      • Source: ::/0 (any IPv6 source).
      • Purpose: Blocks all incoming IPv6 traffic by default.

Implied rules act as a safety net, ensuring that unconfigured traffic is denied (for ingress) or allowed (for egress). Administrators can override these rules by creating higher-priority custom rules.

Default rules

When a project is created, Google Cloud automatically creates a default VPC network that includes additional pre-configured firewall rules with a priority of 65534:

  1. Default-allow-internal:

    • Allows all protocols and ports between instances within the same VPC network.

  2. Default-allow-ssh:

    • Allows SSH (TCP port 22) from any source.

  3. Default-allow-rdp:

    • Allows RDP (TCP port 3389) from any source.

  4. Default-allow-icmp:

    • Allows ICMP traffic (e.g., ping) from any source.

These rules are convenient for initial testing but may pose security risks in production environments. Administrators should delete or modify them as needed.

Always allowed traffic

Certain types of traffic bypass firewall rules and are always allowed:

  1. Google Cloud Metadata Server:

    • Traffic to/from the metadata server is always allowed for instance management.

  2. Loopback Addresses and NIC Traffic:

    • Traffic sent to an instance's own IPs, including alias IP ranges and internal/external IPv4/IPv6 addresses.

  3. Load Balancer and Protocol Forwarding:

    • Traffic associated with forwarding rules for load balancing or protocol forwarding is permitted.

  4. Networking Overlay Software:

    • Addresses configured within the instance's networking overlay.

Always blocked traffic

Some types of traffic are inherently blocked by Google Cloud for security and compliance:

  1. Unsolicited DHCP Traffic:

    • Only DHCP packets from the metadata server are allowed.

  2. Unsupported Protocols:

    • External IPs only accept specific protocols (e.g., TCP, UDP, ICMP).

  3. Email (Port 25):

    • Outbound traffic to TCP port 25 (SMTP) is blocked by default, except for select customers.

Hierarchy

Google Cloud VPC firewall rules operate within a structured hierarchy, ensuring centralized and granular control over network traffic.

Firewall rules in Google Cloud are applied at different levels to provide flexibility and scalability in managing traffic:

  1. Hierarchical Firewall Policies:

    • These policies are created at the organization or folder level and cascade down to projects and VPC networks.
    • They ensure consistent security policies across the organization.
    • Administrators can define allow or deny rules that override or complement VPC-level rules.

  2. Global and Regional Network Firewall Policies:

    • Global Network Firewall Policies:

      • Apply firewall rules globally across all regions in a VPC network.
      • Suitable for resources deployed in multiple regions.

    • Regional Network Firewall Policies:

      • Limit rules to a specific region within a VPC network.
      • Ideal for localized control over resources in specific regions.

  3. VPC Firewall Rules:

    • These are defined within a specific VPC network.
    • Operate on individual instances or groups of instances using tags or service accounts.
    • Provide finer-grained control within the scope of a single VPC.

  4. Instance-Level Configuration:

    • Connections are allowed or denied on a per-instance basis based on applied firewall rules.

Interaction between levels

  • Rules at higher levels (e.g., hierarchical policies) are evaluated first.
  • VPC firewall rules are applied only after hierarchical policies have been processed.
  • This layered approach ensures that organizational security policies can enforce broad controls, while project-level or instance-level rules provide customization.

Key characteristics

  1. Priority:

    • Rules have a priority value (0–65,535). Lower numbers indicate higher priority.
    • Rules with the same priority are evaluated based on their action: deny rules override allow rules.

  2. Default Behavior:

    • If no rule explicitly allows traffic, it is denied by the implied ingress deny rule.

  3. IAM-Governed Tags:

    • Both global and regional network policies support IAM-governed tags for more secure and structured rule application.

  4. Propagation:

    • Hierarchical policies and global rules propagate automatically to all relevant resources.
    • Regional policies affect only the specified region.

Benefits

  1. Centralized Management:

    • Hierarchical policies simplify the enforcement of security standards across an organization.
    • Policies can be applied universally or targeted to specific folders, projects, or regions.

  2. Consistency:

    • Ensures uniform security configurations while allowing flexibility at lower levels for project-specific needs.

  3. Batch Updates:

    • Network firewall policies allow simultaneous updates to multiple rules in a single policy, reducing configuration errors.

Best practices

  1. Adopt the Principle of Least Privilege:

    • Define rules to explicitly allow only the traffic necessary for your applications to communicate.
    • Avoid overly permissive rules.

  2. Minimize Direct Internet Exposure:

    • Avoid “allow” rules with 0.0.0.0/0 as the source or destination range unless absolutely necessary.
    • Use specific IP ranges to limit access.

  3. Create a Deny-All Outbound Rule:

    • Set a firewall rule with the lowest priority to block all outbound traffic for all protocols and ports.
    • Define higher-priority rules for specific instances and required traffic.

  4. Standardize Naming Conventions:

    • Use consistent and descriptive names for firewall rules, e.g., ingress-allow-ssh-from-onprem or egress-allow-http-to-internet.
    • Include details like direction, action, protocol, and source/destination in the naming format.

  5. Use Service Account-Based Rules:

    • Prefer service account-based rules over tag-based rules for better control and security.
    • Service accounts require explicit IAM permissions, while tags can be applied by any user with the appropriate role.

  6. Leverage Hierarchical Firewall Policies:

    • Create consistent firewall policies at the organizational or folder level to enforce uniform security controls.
    • Use these policies to allow or deny connections across multiple VPC networks.

  7. Use Global and Regional Network Firewall Policies:

    • Global policies provide a unified firewall configuration across all regions in a VPC network.
    • Regional policies apply rules to workloads in a specific region, offering localized control.

  8. Monitor and Optimize Rules with Firewall Insights:

    • Use Firewall Insights (part of the Network Intelligence Center) to analyze rule usage, detect misconfigurations, and identify opportunities to tighten rules.
    • Integrate with Cloud Monitoring and Recommender to gain actionable insights.

  9. Audit and Refine Regularly:

    • Periodically review and update firewall rules to ensure they remain aligned with security and operational requirements.

  10. Test Changes Before Deployment:

    • Test new or modified rules in a controlled environment to confirm their behavior before applying them in production.

  11. Use Metrics and Insights for Continuous Improvement:

    • Leverage Cloud Monitoring metrics to track performance and identify bottlenecks.
    • Use Recommender to receive heuristic or machine-learning-based recommendations for improving firewall configurations.



VPC peering

What it is?

VPC Network Peering enables private and secure communication between two non-overlapping VPC networks, even if they are in separate projects or organizations. It is a cost-effective and secure method for connecting networks without exposing resources to the public internet.


Key features

  1. Private Communication:

    • Uses private RFC1918 IP addresses for communication, reducing exposure to external attacks.

  2. Independence:

    • Network firewall rules and routes are managed independently by each VPC.
    • No automatic sharing of firewall rules; administrators must configure rules in each VPC to manage cross-VPC traffic.

  3. Compatibility:

    • VPCs do not need to be in the same project or organization to establish peering.

  4. Scalability:

    • A single VPC can directly peer with up to 25 other VPCs.
    • Peered networks can use hub-and-spoke or series connectivity models, provided subnet IP ranges do not overlap.

  5. Performance:

    • Provides lower latency compared to public IP networking.
    • Does not require external IPs or VPNs, reducing security risks and operational complexity.

  6. Cost-Efficiency:

    • Avoids egress bandwidth charges for using external IPs by utilizing internal IPs for communication.
    • Regular network pricing applies to all peering traffic.

  7. Limitations:

    • No granular route control for subnet CIDRs; firewall rules must filter traffic if needed.

Advantages

  1. Decreased Network Latency: Traffic flows over Google’s private network infrastructure rather than the public internet.
  2. Enhanced Security: Services remain private, avoiding exposure to public internet-related risks.
  3. Reduced Costs: Internal IP communication through peering eliminates additional egress bandwidth costs.

Shared VPC Comparison

Shared VPC is another networking option in Google Cloud, allowing resources in multiple projects within the same organization to share a common VPC network:

  1. Structure:

    • A host project contains the shared VPC network.
    • One or more service projects are attached to the shared network, using specific subnets.

  2. Security and Administration:

    • Centralizes network management and delegates administrative tasks to Network and Security Admins in the host project.
    • Service Project Admins cannot make network-impacting changes, enforcing least privilege access.

  3. Scope:

    • Shared VPC is limited to projects within the same organization and cannot connect projects across different organizations.

Key Differences: VPC Peering vs. Shared VPC

Feature

VPC Peering

Shared VPC

Scope

Across projects/organizations.

Within the same organization only.

Management

Independent network management.

Centralized in the host project.

Subnet Sharing

No sharing; connects two separate VPCs.

Shares subnets among service projects.

Firewall Rules

Managed separately in each VPC.

Managed centrally in the host project.

Best practices

  1. Avoid Overlapping Subnets: Ensure subnet IP ranges do not conflict across peered networks.
  2. Configure Firewall Rules: Explicitly define rules in both VPCs to control cross-VPC traffic.
  3. Optimize for Hub-and-Spoke: Use a hub-and-spoke architecture for better scalability and manageability.
  4. Monitor Traffic: Regularly audit peered networks and associated rules to ensure optimal performance and security.
  5. Evaluate Needs for Shared VPC: Use Shared VPC for centralized network administration within the same organization, especially when managing multiple projects.




VPC Service Controls

What it is?

VPC Service Controls enhance the security of Google-managed services like Cloud Storage and BigQuery by creating security perimeters around these resources. These perimeters limit data movement, control access, and reduce the risk of data exfiltration. Below is a detailed look at their features, functionality, and configuration.


VPC Service Controls add an extra layer of defense for securing Google-managed services by restricting data movement, enhancing context-aware access, and supporting hybrid environments with private connectivity. They are a critical tool for organizations requiring advanced security and compliance in Google Cloud.

Key features

  1. Security Perimeters:

    • Protect Google-managed resources by creating a boundary that controls how data moves across the perimeter.
    • Resources within a perimeter can only be accessed from authorized VPC networks using Private Google Access.

  2. Context-Based Security:

    • Provides perimeter-level security that is independent of IAM.
    • While IAM offers granular identity-based access control, VPC Service Controls manage broader context-based security.

  3. Ingress and Egress Rules:

    • Ingress Rules: Allow API clients outside the perimeter to access resources within it.
    • Egress Rules: Permit resources or API clients inside the perimeter to access services outside of it.
    • These rules enable fine-grained control over data exchange and communication across perimeter boundaries.

  4. Private Connectivity:

    • Supports Private Google Access for hybrid environments, ensuring that private communication is maintained between VPC networks spanning on-premises and Google Cloud.

  5. Context-Aware Access:

    • Enables access based on client attributes, such as:

      • Identity (e.g., user or service account).
      • Device data.
      • Network origin (e.g., IP address or VPC network).

  6. Data Movement Controls:

    • Restricts operations like copying data to unauthorized resources or transferring data to public endpoints.

  7. Hybrid Cloud Support:

    • Perimeter Bridges: Allow secure communication between projects in different service perimeters.
    • Recommended to use ingress and egress rules instead for more granular control.


Benefits

  1. Reduced Data Exfiltration Risks: Prevents unauthorized access to managed resources and data leakage to external locations.
  2. Broader Security Controls: Works alongside IAM to provide multi-layered defense by combining identity-based and context-aware security.
  3. Seamless Hybrid Cloud Integration: Ensures secure access to resources in hybrid setups by combining service perimeters with private connectivity options.
  4. Granular Data Access Management: Control resource access based on detailed attributes such as IP ranges, identity types, or device characteristics.
  5. Internet Isolation: By default, access from the internet to resources within a service perimeter is denied unless explicitly allowlisted.

Configuration steps

  1. Create an Access Policy: Access policies define and group service perimeters and access levels for the organization.
  2. Define Service Perimeters: Identify projects and Google-managed services to be included in each perimeter.
  3. Enable VPC Accessible Services (Optional): Limit access to a subset of services within a perimeter for stricter control.
  4. Set Up Private Connectivity (Optional): Use Private Google Access to securely connect on-premises networks to resources within a service perimeter.
  5. Allow Context-Aware Access (Optional): Create access levels that restrict or allow access based on client attributes.
  6. Configure Ingress and Egress Rules (Optional): Allow controlled communication across perimeter boundaries.

Key considerations

  1. Single Perimeter Membership: A project can belong to only one service perimeter but can be part of multiple perimeter bridges for communication.
  2. No Blocking of Third-Party APIs: Service perimeters do not block access to third-party APIs or external internet services.
  3. Access Levels: Requests from outside the perimeter must meet specific criteria defined in access levels, such as IP ranges or user identities.

Best practices

  1. Combine with IAM: Use IAM for fine-grained access control and VPC Service Controls for broader, context-aware security.
  2. Leverage Private Google Access: Ensure secure, private communication for hybrid setups and reduce dependency on public internet connections.
  3. Use Ingress and Egress Rules: Replace perimeter bridges with ingress/egress rules for better granularity and control over data exchange.
  4. Regularly Audit Configurations: Monitor and refine service perimeters, ingress/egress rules, and access levels to align with security and operational requirements.





Private Google API access

What it is?

Private Google API Access enables Compute Engine instances in a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) subnet to securely access Google APIs and services using an internal IP address, without requiring public IPs or NAT gateways. This approach enhances security by avoiding unnecessary exposure to the internet.


Private Google API Access is a powerful feature for organizations seeking secure, internal communication with Google APIs and services. By leveraging this feature, businesses can enhance security, reduce reliance on public internet routes, and streamline their VPC architecture.

Key features

  1. Internal API Access:

    • Compute Engine instances in a subnet with Private Google Access enabled can reach Google APIs and services using internal IPs, even though the API resolves to a public IP.

  2. Transparent Network Address Translation (NAT):

    • API traffic is routed through Google’s infrastructure and NATed internally, ensuring that the communication remains private and secure.
    • This process is invisible to the user, maintaining simplicity.

  3. Enhanced Security:

    • Eliminates the need for external IP addresses or NAT gateways to access Google APIs.
    • Reduces the risk of exposing your VPC network to the public internet, even though the API calls are encrypted.

  4. Supported APIs and Services:

    • Accessible services include:

      • BigQuery
      • Cloud Bigtable
      • Container Registry
      • Dataproc
      • Datastore
      • Pub/Sub
      • Cloud Spanner
      • Cloud Storage
    • These services (and more) are securely accessible without public internet routes.

How it works

  1. DNS and Routing Requirements:

    • The VPC must be configured with the appropriate DNS, routing, and firewall rules to enable communication with Google APIs and services.

  2. Subnet Configuration:

    • Private Google Access is enabled at the subnet level.
    • Compute Engine instances within a subnet inherit the access settings of that subnet.

  3. Behavior Based on Subnet Settings and IP Types:

    • Instances in a subnet with Private Google Access enabled and internal IP addresses can access Google APIs.
    • Instances with external IP addresses can always access Google APIs, regardless of whether Private Google Access is enabled.
    • Instances in subnets without Private Google Access enabled and only internal IP addresses cannot access Google APIs.

Example scenarios

  1. Subnet with Private Google Access Enabled:

    • VM A1: Located in subnet-a (Private Google Access enabled), with only an internal IP.

      • Can access Google APIs and services.

    • VM A2: Located in subnet-a, with an external IP.

      • Can access Google APIs regardless of Private Google Access settings.

  2. Subnet without Private Google Access:

    • VM B1: Located in subnet-b (Private Google Access disabled), with only an internal IP.

      • Cannot access Google APIs.

    • VM B2: Located in subnet-b, with an external IP.

      • Can access Google APIs despite Private Google Access being disabled.


Benefits

  1. Improved Security: Avoids reliance on external IPs, minimizing the attack surface for API access.
  2. Simplified Network Architecture: Eliminates the need for NAT gateways or public paths to access Google-managed APIs and services.
  3. Cost Efficiency: Reduces costs associated with NAT gateway configurations and public IP address management.
  4. Seamless Integration: Provides secure and private communication with Google APIs and services while ensuring minimal configuration.

Best practices

  1. Enable Private Google Access for All Sensitive Subnets: Ensure that subnets hosting critical workloads are configured with Private Google Access to protect API communication.
  2. Review Subnet Configurations Regularly: Audit subnets to verify the correct enablement of Private Google Access based on security and connectivity requirements.
  3. Minimize External IP Usage: Avoid assigning external IP addresses to instances when not necessary, relying on Private Google Access instead.
  4. Secure DNS and Routing: Validate that DNS and routing configurations meet the requirements for API connectivity to prevent misconfigurations.



Access Context Manager

What it is?

Access Context Manager is a Google Cloud tool that allows organization administrators to define fine-grained, attribute-based access control for projects and resources. It enables secure and flexible access policies tailored to organizational needs, enhancing the overall security posture.

Key features

  1. Access Policy:

    • Acts as an organization-wide container for access levels and service perimeters.

    • Specifies the requirements for requests to be allowed, such as:

      • Device type and operating system.
      • IP address.
      • User identity.

  2. Access Levels:

    • Define the set of attributes that control access to resources.
    • Examples: High_Trust, Medium_Trust, and Low_Trust.
    • Multiple access levels can be included in a single access policy.

  3. Attribute-Based Access:

    • IP Address:

      • Define access levels based on IP ranges specified using CIDR blocks.
      • Supports single or multiple IP ranges for fine-grained control.

    • Device Attributes:

      • Uses Endpoint Verification to gather device details (e.g., operating system and version).
      • Access can be customized for devices meeting specific requirements, such as running the latest OS.

    • User Identity:

      • Grants access based on the identity of the requester, such as a user account or service account.
      • Often used with VPC Service Controls for secure data access.

  4. Integration with VPC Service Controls:

    • Access policies can define requirements for service perimeter requests.
    • Ensures consistent security across organizational boundaries.

  5. Identity-Only Access Levels:

    • Enables access based solely on user or service account identity.
    • Managed via the gcloud command-line tool (not available in the Google Cloud Console).

How it works

  1. Defining Access Policies:

    • Administrators create access policies as containers for multiple access levels.
    • These policies can be attached to projects for quota management or used across the organization.

  2. Customizing Access Levels:

    • Access levels specify attributes like IP ranges, device information, or user identity.

    • For example:

      • High_Trust: Allows access only from company-owned devices running the latest OS.
      • Low_Trust: Grants limited access from less secure devices or public networks.

  3. Policy Enforcement:

    • Access Context Manager describes desired rules but does not enforce them directly.
    • Enforcement occurs through other tools, such as IAM or VPC Service Controls.

Key benefits

  1. Enhanced Security: Provides an additional layer of attribute-based access control, reducing reliance solely on IAM roles.
  2. Granular Access Control: Tailors access permissions based on multiple criteria, such as device type, user identity, and network location.
  3. Integration with Other Google Cloud Services: Seamlessly integrates with VPC Service Controls to enforce perimeter security.
  4. Customizable Policies: Flexible access level configurations allow organizations to align policies with specific security needs.

Best practices

  1. Define Comprehensive Access Policies: Create access policies that incorporate a variety of attributes (e.g., IP ranges, device types) to ensure robust access control.
  2. Regularly Audit and Update Policies: Review access levels and policies periodically to adapt to organizational changes or security updates.
  3. Use Endpoint Verification: Leverage endpoint verification to enforce device-specific access rules, ensuring compliance with security standards.
  4. Combine with IAM and VPC Service Controls: Use Access Context Manager in conjunction with IAM for identity-based controls and VPC Service Controls for perimeter security.
  5. Minimize Identity-Only Rules: Restrict identity-only access levels to scenarios where they are essential and manage them through the gcloud command-line tool.



Flow Logs

What it is?

VPC Flow Logs provide detailed insights into network traffic to and from Compute Engine VM instances in a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. These logs are an essential tool for network monitoring, security analysis, and cost optimization.

Key features

  1. Traffic Recording:

    • Logs capture network flows sent from or received by VM instances.

    • Include details such as:

      • Source and destination IPs.
      • Geographic details.
      • Connection metadata.

    • Only traffic seen by the VM is logged:

      • Outbound traffic blocked by egress rules is logged.
      • Inbound traffic blocked by ingress rules (not reaching the VM) is not logged.

  2. Real-Time Logging:

    • Logs are aggregated by connection at 5-second intervals and exported in real time.

  3. Integration with Cloud Logging:

    • View flow logs in Cloud Logging (formerly Stackdriver Logging).

    • Logs can be exported to destinations supported by Cloud Logging, such as:

      • Pub/Sub for real-time streaming and custom analysis.
      • BigQuery for querying and advanced analytics.

  4. Subnet-Level Configuration:

    • Enable or disable flow logs per subnet.
    • When enabled, logs apply to all VMs within the subnet.

  5. Native Integration:

    • Built into the VPC network infrastructure with no additional delay or performance impact on routing IP packets.

Use cases

  1. Network Monitoring:

    • Track network traffic patterns to identify abnormal behavior or bottlenecks.

  2. Security Analysis:

    • Conduct real-time or forensic analysis to detect and respond to threats.
    • Identify unauthorized access attempts or unusual data transfers.

  3. Expense Optimization:

    • Analyze traffic patterns to optimize resource usage and reduce costs.
    • Identify unnecessary data transfers or inefficient routing.

  4. Compliance and Auditing:

    • Use logs to meet regulatory requirements and maintain detailed records of network activity.

Benefits

  1. Enhanced Visibility: Provides comprehensive insights into traffic flows, enabling proactive network management.
  2. Real-Time Data: Aggregated at 5-second intervals, flow logs allow near-instantaneous analysis and alerting.
  3. Flexibility in Data Handling: Export logs to various destinations (e.g., Pub/Sub or BigQuery) for tailored analytics.
  4. Minimal Performance Impact: Native integration ensures no performance penalties for logging-enabled networks.

Considerations

  1. Cost Implications:

    • Logs can generate significant data, especially in high-traffic networks, potentially increasing Cloud Logging costs.
    • Regularly review log retention and export configurations to optimize costs.

  2. Traffic Scope:

    • Logs capture only traffic seen by VMs, which may not fully represent all network activity (e.g., blocked inbound traffic).

  3. Granularity:

    • Flow logs are enabled at the subnet level, applying to all VMs in the subnet. Individual VM-specific configurations are not supported.

Best practices

  1. Enable Logs Selectively: Only enable flow logs for subnets or workloads requiring detailed traffic analysis to avoid unnecessary costs.
  2. Export Logs Efficiently: Use destinations like BigQuery for advanced analytics or Pub/Sub for real-time streaming to optimize storage and query costs.
  3. Integrate with Security Tools: Pair flow logs with security systems or monitoring tools for automated threat detection and incident response.
  4. Monitor Logging Costs: Analyze usage patterns and adjust logging configurations to minimize costs while retaining essential insights.
  5. Use Real-Time Analysis: Leverage Pub/Sub APIs to monitor traffic anomalies and respond quickly to potential issues.



Load balancing

What it is?

Google Cloud load balancers distribute traffic across backend instances to ensure scalability, availability, and reliability for applications. They provide key features such as a global anycast IP address and built-in DDoS protection. There are multiple types of load balancers, and each supports specific use cases, including handling HTTPS and non-HTTPS traffic.

Key features

HTTPS Load Balancing

  • Terminates user HTTPS connections at the load balancing layer.
  • Balances traffic across backend instances using the HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP protocols.
  • Requires at least one signed SSL certificate installed on the target HTTPS proxy.

SSL Proxy Load Balancing

  • Designed for non-HTTPS SSL/TLS traffic.
  • Terminates SSL connections at the load balancer before forwarding traffic to backends using TCP.

Key benefits

  • Offloads SSL termination from backend servers, improving performance.
  • Provides centralized management of SSL certificates and policies.
  • Enhances security by isolating backend instances from direct public traffic.

How it works

Types


Application Load Balancers

What it is?

Application Load Balancer (ALB) in Google Cloud is a Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) proxy-based load balancing system designed to:

  • Distribute traffic across application backends
  • Perform intelligent routing based on application-level data
  • Act as a secure, programmable entry point (edge) for services
  • Integrate with security, observability, and traffic control mechanisms

Key Concept

Unlike traditional load balancers:

  • It is not just traffic distribution
  • It is a policy enforcement + routing + security + edge control layer

You should think of it as:

“Application-aware edge gateway with built-in load balancing”

Architectural Position

In modern GCP architectures, ALB typically acts as:

  • Public Entry Point (North-South traffic)
  • Internal Service Router (East-West traffic)
  • Multi-environment traffic orchestrator

Typical Placement

  • Internet → ALB → API / Web / Microservices
  • Internal services → Internal ALB → Microservices
  • Hybrid → ALB → on-prem / multi-cloud services

Types of Application Load Balancers

External (Public)

Global External Application Load Balancer

  • Global Anycast IP
  • Traffic enters closest Google edge location
  • Routed over Google backbone

Regional External Application Load Balancer

  • Region-scoped
  • Lower latency for localized apps
  • Supports Standard Tier

Internal (Private)

Regional Internal Application Load Balancer

  • Internal IP (RFC1918)
  • Used inside VPC
  • Ideal for microservices

Cross-region Internal Application Load Balancer

  • Multi-region internal routing
  • Internal failover across regions

Core Components

Understanding this is essential to mastery.

Frontend Layer

    • Forwarding Rule Defines:

      • IP address (external/internal)
      • Port (80/443)
    • Entry point for traffic

Target Proxy

  • Terminates connections

  • Types:

    • HTTP Proxy
    • HTTPS Proxy

Responsibilities:

  • TLS termination
  • Forwarding to URL map

URL Map (Brain of ALB)

This is where routing decisions happen.

Supports:

  • Host-based routing
  • Path-based routing

  • Advanced routing:

    • Header matching
    • Query parameter matching

Example:

api.example.com → backend-api
example.com/images → backend-static

Backend Service

Defines how traffic is handled after routing.

Key configurations:

  • Health checks
  • Timeout settings
  • Session affinity
  • Load balancing policy
  • Connection draining

Also integrates with:

  • Cloud CDN
  • Cloud Armor

Backends

Multiple supported backend types:

  • Compute Engine (Instance Groups)
  • GKE (Pods via NEGs)
  • Cloud Run (serverless NEGs)
  • App Engine
  • Hybrid (on-prem via NEGs)

Request Flow (End-to-End)

Understanding packet/request flow is critical.

Step-by-step:

  1. Client sends request to ALB IP
  2. Traffic reaches Google Front End (GFE) or Envoy
  3. TLS is terminated (if HTTPS)
  4. Request passed to URL Map
  5. Routing decision made
  6. Backend service selected
  7. Healthy backend instance chosen
  8. Request forwarded to backend
  9. Response returned via same path

Key Capabilities

Advanced Routing

  • Path-based routing
  • Host-based routing
  • Header-based routing
  • Query-based routing

Traffic Engineering

  • Canary deployments (traffic splitting)
  • Blue-green deployments
  • Request mirroring (shadow traffic)

Serverless Integration

  • Direct integration with:

    • Cloud Run
    • App Engine

No need for:

  • VM management
  • Kubernetes

Hybrid & Multi-cloud Support

Via NEGs:

  • On-prem services
  • Other cloud providers

Security Capabilities

TLS Termination

  • Centralized certificate management

  • Supports:

    • Google-managed certs
    • Custom certs

Cloud Armor (WAF)

Protection against:

  • OWASP Top 10
  • DDoS attacks
  • IP reputation filtering
  • Geo-blocking

Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)

  • Enforces authentication before access
  • Enables Zero Trust access

Header Manipulation

  • Add/remove headers

  • Enforce security headers:

    • HSTS
    • CSP
    • X-Frame-Options

Performance & Scalability

Global Anycast (Global ALB)

  • Single IP worldwide
  • Traffic routed to nearest edge
  • Uses Google backbone (low latency)

Autoscaling

  • No manual scaling required

  • Handles:

    • Millions of RPS
    • Sudden traffic spikes

Connection Optimization

  • HTTP/2 support
  • Keep-alive
  • Efficient connection reuse

Observability & Monitoring

Built-in capabilities:

  • Cloud Logging
  • Cloud Monitoring

  • Metrics:

    • Request count
    • Latency
    • Backend errors
    • Health check status

Advanced Observability

  • Integration with OpenTelemetry

  • Tracing via:

    • request headers
    • correlation IDs

Advanced Topics

Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs)

Critical abstraction layer.

Types:

  • Zonal NEGs (VMs)
  • Serverless NEGs
  • Hybrid NEGs
  • PSC NEGs

Use cases:

  • Multi-environment routing
  • Service mesh integration
  • Gradual migrations

Traffic Director Integration

  • Service mesh control plane
  • Envoy-based routing
  • Fine-grained traffic control

Cloud CDN Integration

  • Edge caching
  • Reduces latency
  • Offloads backend

Request Mirroring

  • Send copy of traffic to another backend

  • Use cases:

    • Testing
    • ML inference validation

Failover & Resiliency

  • Health checks determine backend health
  • Automatic failover
  • Multi-region resilience (global ALB)

Practical Use Cases

Public API Gateway

  • ALB + Cloud Armor + IAP

  • Backend:

    • GKE or Cloud Run

Microservices Architecture

  • Internal ALB
  • Service-to-service routing

Hybrid Migration

  • ALB routes:

    • legacy (on-prem)
    • new (cloud)

SaaS Platform

  • Multi-tenant routing
  • Domain-based routing per customer

Common pitfalls

Wrong LB Type Selection

  • Using L4 instead of L7 → no routing flexibility

Misconfigured Health Checks

  • Causes:

    • false negatives
    • traffic blackholes

Ignoring Security Layer

  • No Cloud Armor → exposed to attacks

Improper Backend Timeouts

  • Leads to:

    • 502/504 errors

Best Practices

Architecture

  • Use global ALB for internet-facing apps
  • Use internal ALB for microservices

Security

  • Always enable:

    • Cloud Armor
    • TLS (HTTPS only)
    • IAP where applicable

Traffic Management

  • Use:

    • Canary deployments
    • Traffic splitting

Observability

  • Enable:

    • Access logs
    • Metrics
    • Distributed tracing

Performance

  • Use Cloud CDN for static content
  • Optimize backend latency

Summary

To operate at expert level, think of ALB as:

  • Edge gateway
  • Security enforcement layer
  • Traffic control plane
  • Integration hub for backends

Network Load Balancers

What it is?

Network Load Balancer (NLB) in Google Cloud is a Layer 4 (transport layer) load balancing system designed to:

  • Distribute traffic based on:

    • IP address
    • Port
    • Protocol (TCP/UDP)
  • Handle non-HTTP workloads
  • Provide high-performance, low-latency traffic distribution

Key Concept

Network Load Balancer is protocol-agnostic at application level — it does NOT understand HTTP semantics.

This means:

  • No path-based routing
  • No header inspection
  • No content-aware decisions

Purpose

You choose NLB when:

  • You are not using HTTP/HTTPS

  • You need:

    • raw TCP/UDP handling
    • ultra-low latency
    • high throughput

  • You need to:

    • preserve client IP (passthrough)
    • avoid proxy overhead

Typical Workloads

  • Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL)
  • Gaming servers (UDP-heavy)
  • VoIP / real-time communication
  • Custom protocols
  • TCP-based APIs (non-HTTP)
  • High-frequency trading systems

Types of Network Load Balancers

We split them into Proxy vs Passthrough — this is the most important distinction.

Proxy Network Load Balancers

External Proxy Network Load Balancer

  • Type: L4 Proxy (TCP / SSL)

  • Scope: Global

    • Behavior: Terminates client connection
    • Creates new connection to backend

Internal Proxy Network Load Balancer

  • Type: L4 Proxy (TCP)

  • Scope: Regional (VPC internal)

    • Behavior: Internal traffic only
    • Proxy-based routing

Proxy Model — Key Characteristics

  • Load balancer acts as intermediary

  • Enables:

    • TLS termination
    • Connection control
    • Better observability

Passthrough Network Load Balancers

External Passthrough Network Load Balancer

  • Type: L4 Passthrough (TCP / UDP)

  • Scope: Regional

    • Behavior: No connection termination
    • Direct packet forwarding

Internal Passthrough Network Load Balancer

  • Type: L4 Passthrough (TCP / UDP)

  • Scope: Regional

    • Behavior: Internal-only traffic
    • Ultra-low latency

Passthrough Model — Key Characteristics

  • No proxy layer
  • No TLS termination
  • Client connects directly to backend

Architecture & Request Flow

Proxy Load Balancer Flow

  1. Client connects to Load Balancer IP

  2. Load Balancer:

    • terminates TCP/TLS
  3. Load Balancer opens new connection to backend
  4. Backend responds via LB

Result:

  • Client sees LB IP
  • Backend sees LB as client (unless headers passed)

Passthrough Load Balancer Flow

  1. Client sends packet to LB IP
  2. LB selects backend
  3. Packet forwarded directly
  4. Backend responds directly to client

Result:

  • Source IP preserved
  • Minimal overhead

Core Components

Forwarding Rule

  • Defines:

    • IP address
    • Port
    • Protocol

Backend

Depends on type:

  • Instance groups (VMs)
  • Zonal distribution
  • No NEGs (for passthrough classic case)

Health Checks

Critical for:

  • Determining backend availability
  • Removing unhealthy instances

Types:

  • TCP
  • SSL
  • HTTP (in some proxy cases)

Load Distribution Algorithms

Passthrough NLB

  • Hash-based distribution:

    • 5-tuple hash:

      • source IP
      • destination IP
      • source port
      • destination port
      • protocol

Proxy NLB

  • Connection-based balancing
  • More flexible routing

Performance Characteristics

Passthrough NLB

  • Extremely high throughput
  • Near line-rate performance
  • Minimal latency

Proxy NLB

  • Slight overhead due to proxying
  • Better control and features

Security Considerations

Proxy Load Balancer

Pros:

  • TLS termination possible
  • Traffic inspection (limited)
  • Better logging

Cons:

  • Client IP lost unless forwarded

Passthrough Load Balancer

Pros:

  • Preserves client IP
  • Lower attack surface at LB

Cons:

  • No:

    • WAF
    • TLS termination
    • L7 filtering

Firewall Dependency

With NLB:

  • Security shifts to:

    • VPC firewall rules
    • Host-based security
    • Application-level security

Observability

Proxy NLB

  • Better logging capabilities
  • Connection-level metrics

Passthrough NLB

  • Limited visibility

  • Must rely on:

    • backend logging
    • network monitoring

Advanced Topics

Connection Tracking

  • Proxy:

    • tracks connections

  • Passthrough:

    • stateless forwarding logic

Session Affinity

  • Limited support
  • Typically hash-based (passthrough)

Failover Behavior

  • Based on health checks
  • Automatic removal of unhealthy nodes

DDoS Considerations

  • No Cloud Armor support

  • Must rely on:

    • Google infrastructure protections
    • network-level defenses

Integration with GKE

  • Used for:

    • exposing services via TCP/UDP

  • Common in:

    • Stateful workloads
    • Game servers

Practical Use Cases

Database Layer

  • Internal passthrough LB

  • Example:

    • PostgreSQL cluster

Gaming Infrastructure

  • External passthrough LB
  • UDP traffic
  • Low latency critical

Internal Microservices (Non-HTTP)

  • Internal proxy or passthrough LB

High-performance APIs

  • TCP-based services
  • Financial systems

Common pitfalls

Using NLB for HTTP

  • You lose:

    • routing capabilities
    • security features

No TLS Strategy

  • Passthrough requires:

    • TLS at backend

Misconfigured Firewalls

  • NLB relies heavily on firewall rules

Ignoring Health Checks

  • Leads to traffic sent to dead instances

Best Practices

Architecture

  • Use:

    • Passthrough → for performance-critical
    • Proxy → for control

Security

  • Always:

    • enforce TLS (backend if passthrough)
    • restrict firewall rules

Observability

  • Implement:

    • backend logging
    • metrics collection

Reliability

  • Use:

    • multiple zones
    • health checks

Summary

Think of Network Load Balancer as:

  • Packet distributor (passthrough)
  • OR
  • Connection broker (proxy)

NOT as:

  • Application-aware system

TLS termination

WAF

Classic Load Balancers


SSL

What it is?

SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and its successor TLS (Transport Layer Security) ensure encryption in transit for secure communication between clients and servers. Google Cloud integrates SSL/TLS with its load balancers to protect data in transit and provide flexible SSL management.

Key features

  1. SSL Certificate Options:

    • Google-managed certificates: Automatically renewed and managed by Google.
    • Self-managed certificates: Uploaded and maintained by the user.

  2. SSL Policies:

    • Allow control over SSL/TLS features negotiated between clients and the load balancer.
    • Define a minimum TLS version (e.g., TLS 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3) and a profile.

  3. SSL Profiles:

    • COMPATIBLE: Supports the broadest range of clients, including older systems with outdated SSL features.
    • MODERN: Offers compatibility with most modern SSL/TLS features.
    • RESTRICTED: Focused on compliance, supporting a reduced set of SSL features.
    • Custom: Allows users to define specific SSL/TLS features manually.

  4. Default SSL Policy:

    • If no SSL policy is set, the default "COMPATIBLE" profile is applied, ensuring maximum client compatibility.

Use cases

  • HTTPS Load Balancers for secure web traffic.
  • SSL Proxy for secure non-HTTP applications.

Profiles

  • COMPATIBLE: Supports the broadest range of clients, including older systems with outdated SSL features.
  • MODERN: Offers compatibility with most modern SSL/TLS features.
  • RESTRICTED: Focused on compliance, supporting a reduced set of SSL features.


Cloud VPN

What it is?

Google Cloud VPN provides secure and encrypted connections between your on-premises network, data center, or other cloud service providers and your Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. It uses the industry-standard IPsec protocol for end-to-end encryption and supports both static and dynamic routing, making it a versatile choice for hybrid cloud setups.

Use cases

  1. Hybrid Cloud Architectures:Securely extend on-premises networks to Google Cloud VPC for hybrid workloads.
  2. Multi-Cloud Connectivity: Link different cloud providers securely.
  3. Secure Data Center Extensions: Create encrypted connections for critical data center workloads.

Key features

  1. Secure Connections:

    • Uses IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) for encrypting data in transit.
    • Supports IKEv1 and IKEv2 protocols with a shared secret (pre-shared key).

  2. Traffic Handling:

    • Traffic can traverse the public internet or use a direct peering link to Google’s network for enhanced performance.

    • Bandwidth limits:

      • Up to 3 Gbps for direct peering links.
      • Up to 1.5 Gbps when traversing the public internet.

  3. Managed Solution:

    • Fully managed by Google Cloud, ensuring reliability and reducing administrative overhead.

  4. Routing Support:

    • Offers both static routing and dynamic routing through Cloud Router.

Static vs. dynamic routing

  1. Static Routing:

    • Requires manual configuration of routes.
    • Network changes, such as adding new subnets, necessitate manual updates and reboots.
    • Suitable for simple and static network environments.

  2. Dynamic Routing (via Cloud Router):

    • Automatically exchanges routes using Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).
    • Learns and announces new subnets in your VPC or on-premises network dynamically.
    • Ideal for environments with frequent topology changes, ensuring continuous connectivity without disruptions.

    • Required for:

      • Dedicated Interconnect
      • Partner Interconnect
      • High-availability VPN tunnels
      • Classic VPN tunnels using dynamic routing.

How it works

  1. Establishing a Tunnel:

    • A VPN tunnel connects your on-premises network to the Google Cloud VPC.
    • Traffic is encrypted and securely transmitted through the tunnel.

  2. Routes and Traffic Flow:

    • Google Cloud routes define paths for traffic from VM instances to destinations (inside or outside the VPC network).

    • A route specifies:

      • A destination prefix in CIDR format.
      • A next hop, determining where packets are sent.

  3. Dynamic Route Discovery:

    • With Cloud Router, topology changes are automatically detected, and routes are adjusted, ensuring seamless connectivity.
    • Users experience no disruptions during these updates.


Advantages

  1. Enhanced Security: Encrypted IPsec connections protect sensitive data during transit.
  2. High Availability: Supports high-availability configurations, ensuring minimal downtime.
  3. Cost-Effective: Eliminates the need for expensive dedicated connections in certain scenarios. Reduces administrative efforts with dynamic routing.
  4. Scalability: Supports various bandwidth requirements and hybrid connectivity options.
  5. Versatility: Compatible with on-premises networks, other cloud providers, and Google Cloud resources.

Best practices

  1. Choose Routing Type Wisely:

    • Use dynamic routing for environments with frequent changes and complex topologies.
    • Opt for static routing in simpler, fixed setups.

  2. Leverage Cloud Router:

    • Automate route management and enable seamless network updates without manual intervention.

  3. Monitor Traffic:

    • Regularly audit VPN configurations and monitor performance to ensure optimal usage.

  4. Optimize Bandwidth:

    • Use direct peering links when higher bandwidth and lower latency are critical.

  5. Secure Configuration:

    • Use strong pre-shared keys and restrict access to the VPN endpoints.


Cloud Interconnect

What it is?

Google Cloud Interconnect provides low-latency, highly available, and private connections to link your on-premises network with Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks. It enables reliable data transfer and direct access to private IP addresses (RFC 1918 communication) without using the public internet.

Use cases

  1. High-Performance Workloads: Data-intensive applications like machine learning, data warehousing, or real-time analytics benefit from the high bandwidth and low latency of Dedicated Interconnect.
  2. Flexible Connectivity: Small to medium-sized enterprises or those without colocation facilities can use Partner Interconnect for secure and cost-effective connections.
  3. Hybrid Cloud Architectures: Securely extend on-premises environments to Google Cloud for hybrid cloud operations.

Types

Dedicated Interconnect

Establishes a direct physical connection between your on-premises network and Google Cloud VPCs.

Key Features:

  • Minimum bandwidth: 10 Gbps per connection.
  • Supports multiple interconnects for bandwidth scaling beyond 10 Gbps.
  • Requires routing equipment in a Google-supported colocation facility near the desired Google Cloud region.
  • Traffic flows exclusively on a private network, avoiding the public internet.
  • End-to-End SLA: Google guarantees availability and performance for the entire connection.

Partner Interconnect

Provides connectivity via a Google Cloud-supported service provider, making it accessible for users without direct access to a colocation facility.

Key Features:

  • Bandwidth starts at 50 Mbps and offers multiple capacity options.
  • Suitable for scenarios where 10 Gbps isn’t required or physical access to a colocation facility isn’t feasible.
  • Traffic flows through the service provider’s private network, bypassing the public internet.

SLA Coverage:

  • Google guarantees the connection between Google and the service provider.
  • End-to-end SLA depends on the service provider's terms.

Dedicated vs. Partner Interconnect

Feature

Dedicated Interconnect

Partner Interconnect

Connection Type

Direct physical connection

Via service provider

Minimum Bandwidth

10 Gbps

50 Mbps

Maximum Bandwidth

Scalable with multiple interconnects

Scalable per service provider offering

Traffic Path

Private, bypasses public internet

Through service provider’s private network

SLA Coverage

End-to-end by Google

Partial (Google-to-service provider); service provider handles the rest

Colocation Facility

Required

Not required

Key benefits

  1. Low Latency and High Availability:

    • Ideal for workloads requiring consistent, high-performance connectivity.

  2. Private IP Communication:

    • Ensures secure access between on-premises and VPC networks using internal IP addresses.

  3. Scalability:

    • Dedicated Interconnect supports large-scale data transfers with multiple 10 Gbps connections.
    • Partner Interconnect offers flexibility with lower bandwidth requirements and varied capacity options.

  4. Avoids Public Internet:

    • All traffic remains on private networks, improving security and reducing exposure to public internet risks.


Apigee

What it is?

Apigee is a full-lifecycle API management platform: you place an Apigee proxy (also called an API proxy) in front of your services so you can secure, mediate, observe, monetize, and govern API traffic without changing the backends. Think of it as a policy-driven control layer for APIs—distinct from the API implementation itself. On Google Cloud it comes as Apigee X (fully managed) and Apigee hybrid (Google-hosted control plane, customer-managed runtime on Kubernetes). Google Cloud+2Apigee Docs+2

Architectural overview

Planes and topology

  • Management (control) plane – hosted by Google (both X and hybrid). You design and manage API proxies, policies, products, developers, analytics, and CI/CD here.

  • Runtime (data) plane – executes your API proxies.

    • In Apigee X, Google hosts and scales the runtime in Google-managed VPCs that you interconnect with your VPC(s).
    • In Apigee hybrid, you install the runtime on a supported Kubernetes platform (typically GKE), giving you more control over placement, upgrades, and data locality.

Networking pattern (Apigee X)

Provisioning creates a Google-managed Apigee VPC and your customer VPC; you set up private connectivity between them (VPC peering/Private Service Connect depending on pattern). External access typically uses Google Cloud HTTPS Load Balancing in front of the Apigee runtime.

Data residency

Apigee supports regionalized orgs (control plane/runtime/analytics) to help with residency constraints; hybrid gives additional control because the runtime runs where you deploy it.

Core building blocks (runtime model)

  • API Proxy – the programmable façade (request/response flow + policies + target(s)).
  • Policies – plug-in building blocks for auth, quota, spike arrest, caching, transformation, mediation, content-based security, etc.
  • Shared Flows – reusable policy sequences across proxies.
  • Products – bundles of proxies + rate plans used for access control and monetization.
  • Developers & Apps – identities and API keys used by consumers/partners.
  • Developer Portal – self-service onboarding and documentation (integrated portal on Apigee X).

Flow

An Apigee X organization requires two Google Cloud projects: one managed by the customer, and one managed by Google for the Apigee X runtime. Each project uses its own Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. By default, VPC networks in two separate projects cannot communicate with each other.

To enable communication between these VPCs, Apigee uses VPC network peering. Network peering allows internal IP address connectivity between the two networks.


The Apigee runtime runs your API proxies, and is provisioned in the Google-managed project. Incoming requests to the runtime are sent to an internal TCP load balancer which is accessible by using a private IP address in the peered network.

To route traffic from clients on the internet to the Apigee runtime, you can use a global external HTTPS load balancer (XLB). However, an XLB cannot communicate directly with an internal IP address in another project, even if the networks are peered. To solve this problem, a managed instance group (MIG) of virtual machines (VMs) serves as a network bridge.

The VMs in the MIG can communicate bidirectionally across the peered networks. A request coming from the internet would flow through the XLB to a bridge VM in the MIG. The VM can call the private IP of the Apigee runtime's internal load balancer.

The runtime can also directly call internal IP addresses in the peered network in the customer project, or call external IPs through the Google-managed project's Cloud NAT (network address translation) gateway.

API proxy call lifecycle

The following illustration shows the lifecycle of an API proxy call for a paid Apigee X org.

  1. A client calls an Apigee API proxy.
  2. The request lands on a global external HTTPS load balancer (XLB). The XLB is configured with an external public IP address and a TLS certificate.
  3. The XLB forwards the request to a VM in the MIG.
  4. The VM forwards the request to the internal load balancer private IP address which is routed to the Apigee runtime.
  5. After processing the request, the Apigee runtime sends the request to the backend service. The response returns along the same path.

Features

Security & governance capabilities

  • Authentication & authorization: API keys, OAuth 2.0 (authorization code, client credentials, refresh tokens), JWT issuance/validation, mTLS to backends.
  • Threat protection / content-based security: schema validation, size limits, header/payload controls; integrate with Cloud Armor for L7 DDoS/WAF when exposing publicly.
  • Traffic governance: spike arrest, quotas, concurrent rate limits, flow-control, fault handling, circuit-breaking patterns via policies/shared flows.
  • Secrets & identity: integrates with Google Cloud IAM and KMS in X; in hybrid you manage K8s secrets and cluster posture. (Conceptually derived from platform docs.)
  • Auditability: change history via revisions; org-level audit via Cloud Logging on X; hybrid ties into cluster logging/monitoring. (Conceptually derived from platform docs.)

Traffic management & performance features

  • Edge caching & response caching to reduce backend load.
  • Load-balancing to targets and failover via target servers; smart routing and mediation for legacy backends (HTTP/REST/GraphQL).
  • Protocol & payload mediation: JSON↔XML mappings, headers, path/query re-writes; conditional flows for blue/green or canary routing.

Observability & analytics

  • Built-in API analytics (latency, hit/miss, developer/app usage, product adoption).
  • Export/pipe analytics to BigQuery / Cloud Storage for long-term analysis and ML; integrate with Cloud Monitoring/Logging/Trace for SRE workflows.

Monetization & portals

  • Define API products, plans (rate/quotas), and optionally charge for access; expose documentation and keys through the integrated developer portal for self-service onboarding.

Delivery models

  • Apigee X: best when you want fully managed runtime, tight integration with Google networking, Cloud Armor, Cloud Ops, and SLA up to 99.99% on enterprise SKUs.
  • Apigee hybrid: best when you need strict data locality, outbound-only connectivity to on-prem systems, or existing K8s ops processes. You manage scaling/patching/availability of the runtime plane.

Pricing

Apigee offers Evaluation (trial), Pay-as-you-go, and Subscription models. With Pay-as-you-go you’re billed per proxy call tier and optional features; Google provides a pricing calculator and example scenarios. Note that networking (e.g., external load balancer/egress) can add cost even in evaluation mode. For large enterprises, Enterprise Plus subscriptions provide higher quotas, more environments, longer analytics retention, and higher SLAs.

Key use cases

  • Externalization of core services to partners/developers with productized APIs and SLAs.
  • Security front door for heterogeneous backends (legacy and modern) needing unified OAuth/JWT, quotas, WAF, DDoS protection.
  • Modernization & mediation—wrap SOAP/legacy with RESTful façades; gradual decompositions of monoliths.
  • Analytics-driven API programs—export to BigQuery for adoption and business KPI tracking.
  • Regulatory & residency constraints—hybrid runtime placement and regionalized orgs.

Limitations & trade-offs

  • Cost & complexity: Enterprise-grade feature set comes with non-trivial cost and governance overhead; overkill for small internal-only APIs.
  • Cold-start/latency considerations: You’re adding a hop; architectural tuning (caching, connection reuse, routing) mitigates most cases. (Architectural inference.)
  • Hybrid operational burden: You own cluster operations (capacity, upgrades, patching, HA/DR).
  • Feature parity differences: Apigee X vs former Apigee Edge vs hybrid vary; check the comparison & migration notes when planning upgrades/portability.

Reference architecture patterns

  1. Public API front door (internet-facing)

    • External HTTPS LB → Apigee X → backend on Cloud Run/GKE/Compute Engine.
    • Add Cloud Armor policies (WAF, reCAPTCHA Enterprise if needed), OAuth2/JWT at proxy, quota/spike arrest policies, and per-product API keys.

  2. Private-to-private service mediation (east-west)

    • Internal LB or PSC → Apigee X private service → VPC-peered backends; or hybrid runtime inside a restricted GKE. Useful for zero-egress compliance and on-prem systems.

  3. Partner API w/ monetization and portal

    • Products & plans on Apigee, managed app keys, integrated portal for onboarding, BigQuery export for reporting.

  4. Legacy SOAP to REST bridge

    • Transform using policies (XML<→JSON, XPath/JS, JSONPath), cache idempotent responses, enforce quotas.

Security blueprint

  • Identity: Prefer OAuth2/OIDC with short-lived JWT access tokens; rotate keys via KMS.
  • Transport: TLS everywhere; mTLS from Apigee→backend for service identity. (Platform capability within security policies.)
  • Edge protection: Cloud Armor rulesets (OWASP CRS, IP allow/deny, geo, bot management) for public entry points.
  • Abuse controls: Spike Arrest + Quotas per API Product; per-consumer analytics for anomaly detection.
  • Content validation: size limits, schema validation, and threat-mitigation policies.

Operations & SRE considerations

  • Environments & revisions: Use separate environments (dev/test/stage/prod). Every proxy change is a revision—safe rollbacks are instant by switching the revision. (Standard Apigee behavior.)
  • CI/CD: Keep proxies and shared flows in source control; use gcloud/Apigee APIs to automate deploys; lint policies and run contract/perf tests in pipelines.
  • Observability: Forward logs/metrics to Cloud Logging/Monitoring; export analytics to BigQuery for long retention and business KPIs.

  • Capacity & HA:

    • X: Google manages runtime scaling and HA; select multi-region for resilience where available.
    • Hybrid: design GKE for zonal/regional HA, set pod disruption budgets, autoscaling, and regular upgrades; follow Apigee hybrid service tuning guides.

Choosing between Apigee X, hybrid, and alternatives

  • Pick Apigee X for fully managed, internet-scale programs, tight Google Cloud integration, and minimal ops.
  • Pick hybrid for data residency/sovereignty, on-prem reach, or when you already run regulated K8s platforms and want runtime control.
  • Simpler/internal-only APIs may fit API Gateway/Cloud Endpoints or OSS gateways (Kong, Tyk), but you’ll miss enterprise features (monetization, advanced analytics/portal). (Comparative inference from official positioning.)


Network Intelligence Center (NIC)

What it is?

Google Cloud Network Intelligence Center (NIC) is a suite of integrated network monitoring, visibility, and troubleshooting tools in Google Cloud Platform (GCP).

Its main goal is to give you a unified, intelligent view of your network, enabling you to monitor performance, verify connectivity, detect configuration errors, and ensure compliance across hybrid and multi-cloud environments.

Key objectives:

  • Prevent network outages by detecting misconfigurations early.
  • Improve security and compliance through continuous analysis of firewall rules, routes, and traffic.
  • Provide operational visibility across VPCs, hybrid connections, and managed services.

Core modules


Module

Purpose

Practical Use Cases

Security / Limitations

Network Topology

Provides a visual map of your entire network — including VPCs, subnets, interconnects, and managed services.

Visualize dependencies and network paths across hybrid environments. Essential during migration or audits.

Limited visibility into Google-managed services; requires appropriate IAM permissions.

Connectivity Tests

Simulates and analyzes end-to-end packet flow between two network endpoints (VMs, load balancers, on-premises).

Diagnose routing or firewall issues, validate hybrid connectivity, and verify reachability pre-deployment.

Free for up to 20 tests per month; paid beyond that. IAM permissions required for network diagnostics.

Performance Dashboard

Displays latency, packet loss, and throughput metrics between regions or zones.

Monitor SLA adherence, detect latency bottlenecks, and proactively identify degradation.

Requires VPC Flow Logs and Monitoring metrics; interpretation of results must consider app-level delays.

Firewall Insights

Analyzes firewall rule usage and efficiency — detects unused, shadowed, or redundant rules.

Reduce attack surface and simplify policies through periodic cleanup and audits.

Data is limited to GCP-managed firewalls only.

Network Analyzer

Automatically identifies configuration errors, overlapping routes, and connectivity issues across projects.

Detect root causes of connectivity problems and enforce best practices in large environments.

Needs proper data access and IAM roles; might not capture external (non-GCP) links.

Key technical

Path Tracing and Connectivity Simulation

The Connectivity Tests module performs simulated or live (data-plane) packet tracing between endpoints. It analyzes routes, firewall rules, and VPC peering configurations to detect reachability issues.

It can pinpoint where traffic is dropped (e.g., misconfigured firewall or routing).

Security relevance: helps verify segmentation, validate isolation between environments, and detect potential lateral movement paths.

Network Visualization and Metrics

Network Topology combines configuration and telemetry data, showing real-time and historical traffic between resources.

You can view past states — essential for post-incident analysis and change validation.

From a DevSecOps standpoint, it’s an excellent way to confirm that your segmentation, routing, and access boundaries match the intended architecture.

Latency, Packet Loss, and Health Monitoring

Performance Dashboard tracks latency, packet loss, and throughput over time, helping distinguish between network-level and application-level issues.

It’s particularly valuable for mission-critical workloads that require low latency or high availability.

Firewall and Configuration Analysis

Firewall Insights and Network Analyzer identify redundant, conflicting, or unused firewall rules — reducing operational overhead and risk.

Simplifying your rule set improves both security posture and audit readiness.

Network Intent Verification

NIC supports proactive verification of network intent — ensuring that the deployed configuration matches your intended design.

You can simulate changes and validate expected connectivity before applying them.

This is key for shift-left network security and automated verification in CI/CD pipelines.

Implementation and integration

Requirements

  • Enable required APIs (e.g., networkmanagement.googleapis.com).
  • Assign IAM roles for network viewing, firewall inspection, and connectivity testing.
  • Enable VPC Flow Logs and Firewall Logs to collect metrics.
  • Integrate through Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools like Terraform or Deployment Manager to automate setup.

Integration Workflow

  1. Inventory – Identify all VPCs, subnets, interconnects, and hybrid links.
  2. Visualize – Use Network Topology to confirm actual architecture and dependencies.
  3. Test Connectivity – Create Connectivity Tests for critical paths (e.g., app → DB, client → API, VPN → GCP).
  4. Monitor Performance – Set up Performance Dashboard to track latency and packet loss against defined SLAs.
  5. Audit Firewalls – Run Firewall Insights and Network Analyzer to detect risky or unused rules.
  6. Automate – Integrate tests and analysis into CI/CD pipelines for continuous validation.

Security and Compliance

NIC supports compliance with frameworks like ISO 27001, CIS Benchmarks, and NIST SP 800-53 by providing visibility and configuration validation.

It enhances:

  • Audit readiness through traceable connectivity validation.
  • Incident response via traffic path analysis.
  • Zero-Trust enforcement by validating per-connection isolation.

Best practices

  • Establish a baseline network snapshot before major changes.
  • Automate Connectivity Tests as part of CI/CD deployments.
  • Configure alerts for latency, packet loss, or routing changes.
  • Periodically review Firewall Insights for stale rules.
  • Integrate NIC data with Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring, or external SIEMs.
  • Enforce least privilege IAM for viewing or modifying network topology data.
  • Use NIC as part of a broader network observability and incident management strategy.

Common pitfalls and limitations

  • Cost: beyond free test quotas, Connectivity Tests are billable.
  • Visibility gaps: managed services (e.g., Cloud SQL) may not fully appear in the topology view.
  • IAM restrictions: missing permissions can result in partial data.
  • Large-scale complexity: cross-project analysis requires Shared VPC or hub-and-spoke design.
  • False positives: excessive automated testing without validation may create noise.
  • Metric misinterpretation: latency doesn’t always indicate network issues — it may be application-related.

Use cases

  • Pre-deployment validation: test reachability between services automatically after Terraform apply.
  • Change verification: ensure new routes or firewall rules don’t break critical paths.
  • Continuous compliance: run weekly firewall audits and export reports for security teams.
  • Operational monitoring: integrate latency/packet-loss metrics into dashboards and alerting systems.
  • Post-incident analysis: use topology and connectivity data to trace the origin of network failures or security incidents.

Security and standards alignment


Standard

NIC Contribution

NIST SP 800-53 (SI-4, CA-7, CM-6)

Continuous monitoring, configuration validation.

CIS Benchmarks

Firewall and routing audits.

ISO 27001 (A.12, A.13)

Network security and system monitoring.

MITRE ATT&CK

Detection of lateral movement and network traversal paths.

NIC promotes a “shift-left” security mindset in infrastructure management — validating configurations early and automatically, rather than reacting to production issues.

Recommendations

Given your DevOps and DevSecOps background:

  • Enable NIC APIs via Terraform as part of infrastructure provisioning.
  • Create automated Connectivity Tests between critical services (frontend → backend, backend → database).
  • Configure CI/CD pipelines to fail deployments if tests return UNREACHABLE.
  • Integrate Firewall Insights audits into monthly compliance checks.
  • Use Performance Dashboard to define and enforce SLA thresholds.
  • Export NIC data to Cloud Monitoring or Grafana for observability.
  • Restrict IAM roles — only authorized personnel should access topology data.
  • If using hybrid or multi-cloud, combine NIC with SASE/SD-WAN or third-party visibility tools.

Summary

Google Cloud Network Intelligence Center is a central observability and diagnostic platform that transforms how you manage and secure your GCP networks.

It bridges the gap between operations, security, and compliance, allowing proactive management instead of reactive troubleshooting.

When properly integrated into DevSecOps workflows and IaC pipelines, NIC provides:

  • End-to-end visibility
  • Automated validation
  • Continuous assurance of security and performance


Private Service Connect

What it is?

Private Service Connect (PSC) is a Google Cloud networking capability that enables:

Private, secure, and controlled connectivity to services across VPC boundaries using internal IP addresses.

It allows consumers to:

  • Access services without exposing them publicly
  • Use private IP instead of public endpoints
  • Maintain network isolation and control

Core Purpose

PSC solves a fundamental problem:

How to securely expose and consume services across projects, organizations, or networks without using public internet.

Key Use Cases

Access Google APIs Privately

  • Access services like:

    • Cloud Storage
    • BigQuery
    • Pub/Sub

without public internet

Service Producer / Consumer Model

  • One team exposes a service (producer)
  • Other teams consume it privately

SaaS / Multi-Tenant Platforms

  • Securely expose backend services to customers
  • Each customer connects via private endpoint

Hybrid Connectivity

  • On-prem → GCP services (via PSC + VPN/Interconnect)

Architecture

4.1 Core Model

PSC introduces a Producer–Consumer architecture:

[Consumer VPC] → PSC Endpoint → PSC Service Attachment → [Producer VPC Service]

Components

Service Producer

  • Owns the backend service

  • Exposes it via:

    • Internal Load Balancer
    • Service Attachment

Service Attachment

  • Defines how the service is exposed

  • Controls:

    • Who can connect
    • Connection limits
    • Acceptance policies

PSC Endpoint (Consumer Side)

  • Created in consumer VPC
  • Assigned private IP
  • Connects to producer service

Types of PSC

PSC for Google APIs

  • Private access to Google services
  • Replaces public API endpoints

PSC for Published Services

  • Internal services exposed across projects/orgs

PSC for Third-Party Services

  • SaaS providers expose services via PSC

Traffic Flow

Client → Private IP (PSC Endpoint)
        ↓
Forwarding Rule
        ↓
Google Internal Network
        ↓
Service Attachment
        ↓
Producer Load Balancer
        ↓
Backend Service

Security Model

No Public Exposure

  • No public IP required
  • Traffic stays within Google’s network

Access Control

Producer defines:

  • Allowed consumers (projects/orgs)

  • Connection approval model:

    • Automatic
    • Manual approval

Network Isolation

  • Consumer cannot see producer network
  • Only specific service is exposed

IAM + Network-Level Control

  • Combine:

    • IAM policies
    • VPC firewall rules
    • PSC attachment policies

Zero Trust Alignment

PSC supports Zero Trust by:

  • Eliminating public endpoints
  • Enforcing explicit access policies
  • Restricting lateral movement
  • Enabling service-level isolation
