Compute


Cloud Run

Introduction

Google Cloud Run is a fully managed compute platform that enables you to run containerized applications in a serverless environment. It automatically handles infrastructure management, scaling, and provisioning, allowing developers and DevOps engineers to focus on application logic without worrying about server setup or orchestration.

Key features

  • Serverless: No need to manage servers or clusters.
  • Container-based: Deploy any application packaged as a container image.
  • Automatic Scaling: Scales down to zero and up to thousands of instances based on traffic.
  • Pay-per-use: You only pay for the resources your container consumes while it's handling requests.
  • Stateless HTTP services: Ideal for REST APIs, webhooks, and backend services.

Use Cases

  • APIs and Web Services: Deploy microservices or monolithic APIs quickly.
  • Event-driven Processing: Integrate with Pub/Sub, Cloud Tasks, or Cloud Scheduler to process asynchronous workloads.
  • Webhooks and Lightweight Backends: Perfect for CI/CD triggers or third-party integrations.
  • CI/CD Pipelines: Cloud Run can serve as a build artifact deployment target.

Scaling

Automatic and granular horizontal scaling

Cloud Run automatically scales horizontally by increasing or decreasing the number of container instances in response to HTTP request load:

  • If no requests are incoming, all instances can scale down to zero.
  • When demand increases, Cloud Run creates new instances instantly to handle the load.

This makes it ideal for unpredictable, spiky traffic patterns and event-driven workloads.

Concurrency

Each container instance in Cloud Run handles only one request at a time by default. This guarantees isolation and avoids concurrency issues.

However, Cloud Run supports configurable concurrency, allowing a single instance to process multiple requests simultaneously if the app is designed to handle concurrent processing. This allows better resource utilization and cost-efficiency.

Cold starts

A cold start occurs when Cloud Run spins up a new instance to handle an incoming request. This involves:

  • Allocating resources.
  • Pulling the container image (if not cached).
  • Running startup logic.

Cold starts introduce latency, especially in low-traffic services that frequently scale down to zero. They can be mitigated by keeping minimum active instances always warm.

Minimum and maximum instance settings

  • Minimum instances: You can reserve a fixed number of warm instances to reduce cold start latency. These are billed even if idle.
  • Maximum instances: You can cap the number of instances to avoid resource exhaustion, backend overload, or uncontrolled cost during traffic spikes.

This control allows Cloud Run to support burst traffic while respecting system or cost limitations.

CPU allocation modes

  • Default behavior: CPU is allocated only while the request is being processed. During idle time (between requests), CPU is throttled to zero.
  • This is efficient, but unsuitable for workloads that need background processing or long startup times.
  • Always-on CPU can be enabled to support background tasks or pre-initialization, improving latency but increasing cost.

Stateless design requirement

All instances must be stateless:

  • No shared memory or session state between requests or instances.
  • Persistent state must be stored externally (e.g., in Cloud Storage, Firestore, or a database).
  • This constraint ensures safe scaling and allows ephemeral instances to be terminated or recreated at any time.

Scaling granularity and speed

Cloud Run scales quickly but not instantaneously. The scaling speed depends on:

  • Container startup time.
  • Image size and caching.
  • Regional capacity availability.

Cloud Run is designed for fine-grained scaling, which helps control costs while adapting to real-time load changes.

Limitations

Aspect

Limit

Max container instances

Default 1000 (soft limit, can be increased)

Max concurrency per instance

1000

CPU per instance

Up to 4 vCPU

Memory per instance

Up to 16 GiB

No vertical autoscaling

CPU/RAM per instance is fixed per revision

No GPU support

Cloud Run does not support GPUs (as of now)

Cost model

  • Cloud Run charges per request, per CPU-second, and per memory used only during active request processing.
  • This incentivizes efficient concurrency and lightweight startup logic.
  • Overprovisioning instances (e.g., by setting high min-instances or low concurrency) increases cost without performance benefits.

IAM & Access Control

Two layers of access control

Cloud Run uses two distinct access control layers:

  • Service-level IAM: Controls who can deploy, update, delete, or invoke a Cloud Run service.
  • Runtime authentication: Controls how end users or services access the deployed application (via HTTPS).

IAM roles

Key predefined roles:

Role

Purpose

roles/run.admin

Full control over Cloud Run services

roles/run.developer

Can deploy/update services, but not delete

roles/run.invoker

Permission to invoke (call) a Cloud Run app

roles/viewer

Read-only access to resources

Public vs. Private access

  • By default, services deployed in Cloud Run require authentication (only identities with roles/run.invoker can call them).
  • To make a service public (accessible to unauthenticated users), bind the role roles/run.invoker to allUsers.

Making a service public:

  • Easy for APIs or web apps
  • Risky for internal tools—should be avoided unless behind an API Gateway or firewall

Service-to-Service Authentication (Internal Access)

  • Cloud Run supports identity-based invocation using OAuth 2.0 ID tokens.

  • When one service needs to call another securely:

    • It uses its own service account identity.
    • Cloud Run validates the token and IAM permissions.
  • This enables zero-trust architecture and fine-grained control over internal communications.

Service Accounts

  • Each Cloud Run service runs under a service account identity.
  • This identity determines what other GCP resources the service can access (e.g., Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage).
  • Best practice: Use a custom, least-privilege service account per service.
  • A Cloud Run service has access to a default service account.
  • Google client libraries use the default service account to call Google Cloud APIs.
  • The default service account has the Editor basic role, which has broad permissions across all services.
  • In production environments, you must replace the default service account with a user-managed per-service account with predefined roles.

Container lifecycle

The relevant states of a container are:

  • Starting The starting state is when Cloud Run materializes the container image and starts your application.
  • Serving requests This is when your container is handling web requests.
  • Idle The container is idle when it is not handling web requests.
  • Shutting down If you handle the shutdown hook, Cloud Run lets you stop your application gracefully.
  • Stopped The final state in the lifecycle is when the container is stopped

Development, testing and integration

Execution environments

Revisions

A revision is an immutable, versioned snapshot of a Cloud Run service at a specific point in time.

Each deployment (code change, config change, or env change) creates a new revision.

  • Think of revisions as read-only deployments.

  • They contain:

    • Container image
    • Environment variables
    • CPU/memory allocation
    • Concurrency settings
    • Service account and IAM bindings

Key characteristics

Property

Description

Immutable

Once created, a revision cannot be modified. A new deploy = new revision

Versioned History

Old revisions are retained (until deleted) and can be rolled back

Stateless

No persistent storage—revision stores config only, not runtime state

Shared URL

All revisions of a service share the same base URL, but can be routed differently

Revision lifecycle

  1. Created: When a service is deployed or updated.
  2. Active: If it receives traffic (manual or automatic).
  3. Idle: If it receives no traffic (can still be invoked manually).
  4. Deleted: Manually removed or garbage collected after long inactivity.

Traffic management and routing

Default behavior

  • When a new revision is deployed, 100% of traffic is routed to it by default.
  • Old revisions remain accessible via direct invocation (by full URL).

Traffic splitting

  • Cloud Run allows splitting traffic between multiple revisions:

    • Use percentages (e.g., 90% to v2, 10% to v1).
    • Useful for canary releases, A/B testing, or gradual rollouts.

Tag-Based routing

  • Revisions can be assigned tags for direct invocation (e.g., /v1, /canary, /stable).
  • Enables calling specific versions without affecting live traffic.

Rolling updates

Mechanism

  • Cloud Run performs gradual rollouts to reduce deployment risk:

    • Starts new instances from the new revision.
    • Retires old revision instances as traffic shifts.
    • Avoids downtime and maintains SLAs.

Manual rollbacks

  • You can roll back by re-allocating 100% traffic to a previous revision.
  • No need to redeploy—just reconfigure routing.

Pinning

Pinning refers to manually routing traffic to a specific revision of a Cloud Run service, ensuring that a particular revision continues receiving traffic even as new revisions are deployed.

  • To freeze traffic on a known-good revision.
  • To avoid automatic traffic shift to new deployments.
  • To implement progressive rollout by maintaining traffic on multiple revisions.
  • To support blue/green or canary deployments.

Key concepts

Aspect

Description

Pinned Revision

A revision that continues receiving a defined percentage of traffic.

Unpinned Revisions

Newly deployed revisions that, by default, receive 100% traffic unless overridden.

Manual Traffic Control

Pinning disables automatic traffic shifting—you manually control routing.

Persistence

A pinned revision remains active as long as it has traffic assigned.

Pinning vs Rolling Update

Feature

Rolling Update

Pinning

Traffic Distribution

Automatically shifts to latest revision

Manually assigned to specific revisions

Default Behavior

100% to new revision

Keeps traffic on chosen revisions

Control

Less granular (default)

Full manual control over traffic routing

Best practices

  • Use small, atomic changes to control revision behavior.
  • Tag revisions for manual QA or staging.
  • Monitor logs and metrics during rollout using Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging.
  • Always validate new revisions before sending full production traffic.


Security

Introduction

Google Cloud security operates on a robust multi-layered architecture designed to protect infrastructure, data, applications, and users from diverse cybersecurity threats. This approach addresses both security-by-design principles and continuous innovation to help organizations protect assets while remaining compliant with global standards. Here’s an in-depth look at Google Cloud security, detailing each layer and its functions, alongside key features and aspects that contribute to a secure cloud environment.

Infrastructure security

The foundation of Google Cloud’s security architecture is its global infrastructure, which encompasses physical, operational, and network layers to deliver high reliability and security.

  • Physical Security: Google data centers are protected by advanced physical security controls, including 24/7 surveillance, biometric identification, and multi-factor access controls. Google restricts access based on strict job requirements and continuously monitors its facilities to detect and respond to potential breaches.
  • Hardware Security: Google designs its servers and network hardware to run a custom version of Linux, reinforcing the security of its stack. Hardware-level security measures include using custom security chips (Titan) to verify hardware integrity and help prevent firmware and boot-level attacks.
  • Global Network Security: Google operates its own private global fiber network, ensuring that data in transit between data centers remains secure and isolated from public internet traffic. Network protections include encryption, Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) protection, firewalls, and advanced intrusion detection/prevention mechanisms.

Identity and Access Management (IAM)

IAM ensures that only authorized users and services have access to cloud resources, which is crucial for controlling and securing Google Cloud.

  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Google Cloud IAM allows administrators to grant granular access permissions to resources by assigning roles to users, groups, or service accounts. Roles can be predefined or customized to match specific security requirements, allowing for the principle of least privilege.
  • Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP): IAP provides secure application access by verifying user identity and access context before granting access to web applications and VMs. It enforces authentication and authorization without relying on a VPN.
  • Service Accounts and OAuth: Google Cloud uses service accounts for machine-to-machine authentication and permissions, using OAuth 2.0 tokens to control and grant application access. These accounts allow applications to authenticate and access specific resources securely.
  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Google Cloud mandates MFA for privileged accounts, adding an extra layer of security by requiring additional verification factors, such as Google Authenticator or Titan Security Keys.

Data security

Google Cloud emphasizes encryption, control, and protection of data both at rest and in transit, with compliance support and data management capabilities.

  • Encryption at Rest: Google Cloud automatically encrypts data at rest using AES-256 bit encryption and manages encryption keys using Google’s internal key management system. Data encryption applies to storage solutions like Cloud Storage, Bigtable, and Persistent Disk.
  • Encryption in Transit: Data traveling between Google’s servers and user devices or between data centers is encrypted using Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Google’s proprietary encryption protocols. This ensures confidentiality and integrity, protecting data from interception.
  • Key Management and BYOK: Google Cloud offers Cloud Key Management (KMS), allowing users to manage cryptographic keys for their applications. With Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), customers retain control over encryption keys, enabling integration with third-party key management systems.
  • Confidential Computing: Google Cloud supports Confidential Computing for protecting data during processing by using Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs). This feature isolates workloads within secure environments, protecting them from unauthorized access, even from Google administrators.

Application security

Google Cloud provides tools to secure applications and APIs, from scanning for vulnerabilities to protecting against malicious traffic.

  • Web Application Firewall (WAF): Google Cloud Armor is Google’s WAF, designed to protect applications from DDoS attacks, SQL injection, and cross-site scripting (XSS). It offers fine-grained rules to control access and mitigate threats from unauthorized traffic.
  • API Security: Apigee, Google’s API management platform, includes built-in security policies like OAuth, rate limiting, and IP whitelisting. It enables API developers to control access, enforce quotas, and monitor API usage to prevent abuse.
  • Vulnerability Scanning: Google Cloud Security Command Center includes Container Analysis and Web Security Scanner to help detect vulnerabilities in container images, web applications, and VMs. These scanners help maintain compliance by identifying issues before they become risks.
  • ReCAPTCHA Enterprise: Google offers ReCAPTCHA Enterprise for automated bot detection and mitigation, enhancing security by distinguishing between genuine user traffic and bot activity.

Threat Detection and Incident Response

Google Cloud employs advanced threat intelligence and automated response capabilities to detect and respond to security incidents swiftly.

  • Security Command Center: This centralized security management tool provides a comprehensive view of security and risk across Google Cloud. It continuously monitors resources, detects vulnerabilities, and generates alerts for misconfigurations, compliance issues, and security threats.
  • Cloud Logging and Monitoring: Google Cloud’s monitoring tools provide visibility into system performance and user activities, including Cloud Audit Logs and Cloud Monitoring. These tools enable security teams to analyze and respond to suspicious activity in real time.
  • Threat Intelligence: Google’s Threat Intelligence provides up-to-date insights into emerging threats, and Google Cloud benefits from Google’s experience in security research and incident response. This intelligence powers tools like Chronicle, which uses machine learning to analyze large data volumes for potential threats.
  • Chronicle Security Operations: Chronicle, Google’s cybersecurity analytics platform, assists organizations in detecting, investigating, and mitigating security threats by analyzing large datasets and applying threat intelligence. It helps detect advanced threats that traditional security tools might miss.

Compliance and Data Governance

Google Cloud’s compliance certifications and data governance tools ensure that organizations remain compliant with industry regulations while keeping their data secure.

  • Compliance Certifications: Google Cloud meets a wide range of international and industry-specific security standards and regulations, such as GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, and FedRAMP. These certifications are designed to give businesses confidence that their data will remain protected in the cloud.
  • Resource Manager: Google Cloud Resource Manager helps users organize resources hierarchically for governance and compliance, such as assigning policies and permissions at different levels (organization, folder, project, and resource).
  • Data Loss Prevention (DLP): Cloud DLP is a tool that detects and anonymizes sensitive data, including personally identifiable information (PII). By identifying and managing sensitive information, organizations can mitigate the risks of data exposure and comply with data privacy regulations.

User Protection and Endpoint Security

Protecting users and their devices is essential for preventing unauthorized access and maintaining the integrity of applications and data.

  • Advanced Protection Program: This program provides the highest level of Google Account security by requiring two-factor authentication, protecting users from phishing, and enforcing strict account recovery policies.
  • Endpoint Management: Google Cloud provides endpoint management to enforce policies on devices accessing resources, including requiring device encryption and screen locks. This capability ensures that only compliant devices can access Google Cloud resources.
  • BeyondCorp Zero Trust Security: Google’s BeyondCorp architecture enables Zero Trust security by enforcing continuous authentication and authorization, regardless of network location. This approach minimizes reliance on VPNs and enforces strict access policies, verifying identity and context with each access request.

Continuous Improvement and Innovation

Google Cloud is continuously evolving to counter emerging threats and improve security features. Some of the aspects of this ongoing improvement include:

  • Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence: Google Cloud uses machine learning algorithms to detect patterns and identify threats in real time. These algorithms analyze massive amounts of data, looking for anomalies that could indicate potential security incidents.
  • Bug Bounty Programs: Google’s Vulnerability Reward Program incentivizes security researchers to find vulnerabilities in Google products. This proactive approach helps identify and address security weaknesses before they can be exploited.
  • Security Best Practices and Resources: Google Cloud provides security blueprints, best practice guides, and access to community forums. These resources educate and support organizations in implementing strong security practices and addressing unique security requirements.

Securing access


Cloud Identity

What it is?

Google Cloud Identity is an Identity as a Service (IDaaS) solution designed to help organizations manage user identities, authentication, and access across their cloud resources. The service offers:

  • Identity and Access Management: Securely manage access permissions for users and groups.
  • Device and Application Management: Enforce policies across devices and apps.
  • Scalability: Support for enterprises of all sizes with domain-wide management capabilities.

Tiers

  1. Free Edition:

    • Core identity and endpoint management services.
    • Ideal for users not requiring Google Workspace services.
    • Includes basic user provisioning and security settings.

  2. Premium Edition:

    • Advanced enterprise features such as:

      • Automated user provisioning.
      • Application allowlisting.
      • Advanced mobile device management.
    • Additional cost for enhanced functionality.

Core features

  1. Cloud-Based Directory: Acts as a central directory for user accounts.

  2. Authentication & Authorization:

    • Secure access with multi-factor authentication (MFA).
    • OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect support.

  3. User Lifecycle Management:

    • Easy user provisioning and deprovisioning.
    • Synchronization with Active Directory or LDAP.

  4. Endpoint Management:

    • Device-level security policies for mobile and desktop devices.
    • Automatic enrollment for managed devices.
  5. Multi-Tenant Support: Manage identities across SaaS apps, APIs, and web platforms.

Integration tools

Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS):

  • Synchronizes user data between Google Accounts and Microsoft Active Directory/LDAP servers.
  • Synchronizable elements: users, aliases, groups, and more.

Managed Microsoft Active Directory:

  • Automates maintenance and security configurations for Active Directory-dependent applications.

Identity Platform (CIAM):

  • Adds identity and access management functionality to apps.
  • Use cases: SaaS applications, mobile apps, APIs, and gaming platforms.

How it works

  1. Domain Verification: Organizations must verify ownership of their domain names.

  2. User Provisioning:

    • Manual account creation.
    • Batch enrollments via spreadsheets or automated tools.

  3. Centralized Management:

    • Admin Console (admin.google.com) provides a single pane of glass for managing users, groups, and settings.
    • Enforce security roles and policies organization-wide.

  4. Scalable Domain Management:

    • Support for up to 600 domains per organization.
    • Multiple domains can be managed from the same console.

Advantages & disadvantages

Advantages

  1. Centralized Identity Management: Single console for user, group, and domain management.
  2. Integration with Google Services: Seamless integration with Google Workspace and third-party tools.
  3. Scalability: Supports large organizations with multiple domains and millions of users.
  4. Strong Security: Built-in MFA and advanced security settings.
  5. Device Management: Policy enforcement for both corporate and personal devices (BYOD).
  6. Cost-Efficiency: Free accounts available for non-Google Workspace users.

Disadvantages

  1. Limited Customization: Less flexibility compared to on-premises identity solutions.
  2. Dependency on Google Ecosystem: Optimal usage is tied to Google Workspace and related tools.
  3. Learning Curve: Initial setup and domain verification require administrative expertise.

Practical tips

  1. Plan Your Domain Structure: Define primary and secondary domains based on organizational needs.
  2. Leverage GCDS: Use Google Cloud Directory Sync to ensure consistent user data across systems.
  3. Implement MFA: Enforce multi-factor authentication for all users to enhance security.
  4. Utilize Device Management: Set up endpoint management to protect devices accessing your network.
  5. Regularly Audit Access: Periodically review user permissions and remove unnecessary access.

Best Practices

  1. Enable Single Sign-On (SSO): Reduce password fatigue and enhance security by integrating SSO.
  2. Configure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Assign permissions based on roles to minimize access risks.
  3. Train Administrators: Ensure IT admins are familiar with the Admin Console and security policies.
  4. Monitor Security Alerts: Use the Google Admin Console to track security-related events and anomalies.
  5. Automate User Provisioning: Streamline user account management with automated tools.




Cloud Directory Sync

What it is?

Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) is a tool designed to synchronize user, group, and shared contact information from an existing Microsoft Active Directory or LDAP server to Google Workspace or Cloud Identity accounts. This synchronization helps streamline account management, ensuring data consistency and reducing administrative overhead.

Use cases

  1. Organizations with Existing Directory Services: Companies using Microsoft Active Directory or LDAP for internal user management can easily integrate with Google Workspace or Cloud Identity.
  2. Onboarding and Offboarding Employees: Automates user provisioning and deprovisioning, reducing administrative delays and ensuring security.
  3. Hybrid IT Environments: Ensures data consistency across on-premises and cloud-based systems.

Key features

  1. One-Way Synchronization:

    • Data is synchronized from the directory server to Google Workspace or Cloud Identity.
    • The original directory server remains unaltered.

  2. Automated Provisioning and Deprovisioning:

    • Automatically adds or removes user accounts in Google Workspace based on changes in Active Directory or LDAP.
    • Enhances security by deprovisioning access promptly when a user is removed from the directory.

  3. Customizable Rules:

    • Administrators can set specific rules for how and when data is synchronized.

  4. Detailed Reporting:

    • Provides a report after each synchronization cycle, detailing the changes made.

How it works

The synchronization process occurs in four steps:

  1. Data Export: GCDS exports a list of users, groups, and shared contacts from your Active Directory or LDAP server based on predefined rules.
  2. Google Domain Data Collection: GCDS connects to your Google domain and generates a list of existing Google users, groups, and shared contacts.
  3. Comparison and Updates: GCDS compares the exported data from the directory server with the Google domain data and updates Google Workspace accounts to reflect the changes.
  4. Report Generation: Once synchronization is complete, GCDS sends a detailed report to specified email addresses.

Advantages & disadvantages

Advantages of Using GCDS

  1. Simplified User Management: Centralized management of users across Active Directory/LDAP and Google Workspace.
  2. Operational Efficiency: Automates provisioning and deprovisioning, reducing manual administrative tasks.
  3. Enhanced Security: Ensures timely deprovisioning of users, minimizing potential security risks.
  4. No External Access Required: GCDS runs locally on your server and does not require external access to your directory.
  5. Consistency Across Systems: Ensures that Google Workspace or Cloud Identity accounts mirror the data in your Active Directory or LDAP server.

Disadvantages

  1. One-Way Synchronization: Changes made in Google Workspace or Cloud Identity are not synchronized back to Active Directory or LDAP.
  2. Complexity for Beginners: Initial setup and configuration can be challenging for administrators unfamiliar with directory systems.
  3. Dependency on Directory Server: GCDS relies entirely on the directory server for data; any errors or inconsistencies in the directory will propagate to Google Workspace.

Security considerations

  • No Cloud Dependency: GCDS operates within your local IT environment, ensuring that no external parties access your directory data.
  • Role-Based Access Control: Assign permissions to specific administrators to manage synchronization securely.
  • Audit Logs: Keep track of synchronization activities and changes for accountability and compliance.

Best practices

  1. Define Clear Rules: Establish synchronization rules to specify which users, groups, and shared contacts are synchronized.
  2. Test Before Full Deployment: Run synchronization in a test environment to ensure the configuration is correct before implementing it organization-wide.
  3. Regularly Review Reports: Monitor synchronization reports to identify and resolve any discrepancies or errors.
  4. Schedule Synchronization: Set up regular synchronization intervals to keep data up-to-date without overloading the system.
  5. Secure the Environment: Ensure the server running GCDS is protected within your organization’s IT perimeter.

Practical tips

  1. Verify Directory Data Accuracy: Ensure user and group information in Active Directory or LDAP is clean and accurate before synchronization.
  2. Back Up Data: Perform backups of both the directory server and Google Workspace data as a precautionary measure.
  3. Use Incremental Synchronization: Synchronize changes incrementally to avoid excessive resource usage during large updates.
  4. Leverage Email Notifications: Configure GCDS to send synchronization reports to administrators for easy monitoring.




Managed Microsoft Active Directory

What it is?

Google’s Managed Microsoft Active Directory is a fully managed service for deploying Microsoft AD on Google Cloud. It extends the capabilities of on-premises Active Directory to cloud deployments, ensuring compatibility and seamless integration between environments.

GCDS vs. Managed Microsoft AD

Feature

GCDS

Managed Microsoft AD

Purpose

Synchronizes Google accounts with on-premises AD or LDAP.

Fully managed service running actual Microsoft AD.

Data Flow

One-way sync from AD/LDAP to Google.

Provides bi-directional interaction with AD domains.

Hosting

GCDS runs locally on your servers.

Managed service hosted on Google Cloud.

Maintenance

Admins handle on-premises AD maintenance.

Google manages maintenance and updates.

Use cases

  1. Hybrid Environments: Extend on-premises Active Directory functionality to Google Cloud.
  2. Enterprise Applications: Support enterprise apps that rely on Active Directory for authentication and authorization.
  3. Disaster Recovery: Use snapshots and high availability to ensure business continuity.
  4. Cloud-Native Workloads: Enable low-latency domain access for VMs and apps hosted in Google Cloud.

Key features

  1. Full Compatibility:

    • Uses actual Microsoft Active Directory controllers, ensuring no application incompatibility issues.
    • Integrates with existing Microsoft tools like Group Policies and Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT).

  2. Managed Service:

    • Google handles routine maintenance tasks, including:

      • System patching.
      • Firewall rule management.
      • High availability configuration.

  3. Flexible Deployment:

    • Supports different architectures for on-premises and cloud interaction:

      • Standalone domains: Cloud and on-premises domains run independently.
      • Connected domains: Cloud domains integrate with on-premises domains.

  4. High Availability:

    • Built on hardened servers with snapshot capabilities for disaster recovery.
    • Multi-regional infrastructure for low-latency access and scalability.

  5. Cloud Integration:

    • Compatible with Cloud DNS for domain discovery within Virtual Machines (VMs).
    • Provides low-latency domain access through Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).

  6. Scalability:

    • Easily add additional regions to increase workload capacity as your organization grows.

How it works

  1. Service Setup: Google provides the managed AD infrastructure, including domain controllers and DNS.
  2. Integration Options: Choose between standalone or connected domains based on workload and deployment needs.
  3. Maintenance Automation: Patching, monitoring, and scaling are handled by Google to ensure optimal performance and security.
  4. Domain Connectivity: Apps and VMs access the Active Directory domain over low-latency VPC connections.

Advantages & disadvantages

Advantages

  1. Simplified Management: Google handles updates, patching, and firewall rules, reducing administrative burden.
  2. Seamless Integration: Leverages actual Microsoft AD controllers, ensuring compatibility with existing applications and tools.
  3. High Availability and Disaster Recovery: Built-in snapshots and hardened infrastructure provide enhanced reliability and recovery options.
  4. Scalability: Add regions on demand to support growing workloads.
  5. Cloud-Native Features: Integration with Cloud DNS and VPC for enhanced network performance.

Disadvantages

  1. Cost: Higher operational costs compared to self-managed AD setups due to the fully managed nature.
  2. Limited Customization: Google manages much of the infrastructure, limiting customization options.
  3. Dependency on Google Cloud: May lead to vendor lock-in for organizations heavily reliant on Google Cloud infrastructure.

Best practices

  1. Plan Integration: Decide whether to deploy standalone domains or connected domains based on your organization's structure.
  2. Monitor Domain Health: Use Google Cloud monitoring tools to ensure domain performance and identify potential issues.
  3. Leverage Familiar Tools: Continue using tools like RSAT and Group Policies for management.
  4. Configure Snapshots: Regularly schedule snapshots for recovery in case of unexpected failures.
  5. Optimize DNS: Use Cloud DNS to enable efficient domain discovery and streamline network operations.

Security considerations

  1. Hardened Infrastructure: Managed AD runs on Google’s secure servers with built-in redundancy.
  2. Firewall Management: Automated rule updates ensure secure network access.
  3. Role-Based Access Control: Use Google Cloud IAM to restrict administrative access to Managed AD resources.
  4. Encryption: Ensure data is encrypted in transit and at rest for added security.


Identity Platform


Identity and Access Management (IAM)

What it is?

Google Cloud’s Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a central tool for managing access to Google Cloud resources. It provides granular control over permissions and policies, enabling organizations to enforce the principle of least privilege and secure their cloud environments effectively.

Use cases

  1. Team Collaboration: Assign roles to team members based on their responsibilities (e.g., developers, admins).
  2. Service-to-Service Communication: Use service accounts to securely enable applications to interact with Google Cloud resources.
  3. Compliance and Auditing: Use audit logs to track resource access and ensure compliance with regulations.
  4. Conditional Access: Restrict access based on contextual factors, such as location or time.

Key features

  1. Granular Permissions:

    • Control access at the project, folder, and resource levels.
    • Assign permissions tailored to specific actions (e.g., read-only, write access).

  2. IAM Policies:

    • Policies are structured using principals (users, groups, or services), roles, and resources.
    • Policies determine "who can do what on which resource."

  3. Predefined and Custom Roles:

    • Predefined roles for common use cases (e.g., Viewer, Editor, Owner).
    • Custom roles for tailored access control based on organizational needs.

  4. Service Accounts:

    • Special accounts for applications and workloads to authenticate and interact with Google Cloud resources securely.

  5. Audit Logs:

    • Provide detailed activity logs for resource access and IAM policy changes.

  6. IAM Conditions:

    • Introduce context-based access control by applying conditions (e.g., time, location, or request attributes).

How it works

  1. Policy Hierarchy:

    • IAM operates at different levels: Organization > Folder > Project > Resource.
    • Policies applied at higher levels are inherited by lower levels unless explicitly overridden.

  2. Principal Assignment:

    • Principals (users, groups, or service accounts) are granted roles in policies.

  3. Permissions via Roles:

    • Permissions are grouped into roles, and roles are assigned to principals.

  4. Resource-Based Access Control:

    • Policies are applied to specific resources, enabling fine-grained access control.

  5. Condition-Based Policies:

    • Access can be granted or denied based on specific conditions, enhancing flexibility.


Hierarchy

Advantages & disadvantages

Advantages

  1. Fine-Grained Access Control: Enables precise control over who can perform specific actions on specific resources.
  2. Ease of Use: Predefined roles simplify setup for common use cases, while custom roles provide flexibility.
  3. Improved Security: Supports the principle of least privilege by allowing users only the permissions necessary for their tasks.
  4. Scalability: Designed to handle complex environments with thousands of users and resources.
  5. Comprehensive Auditing: Logs all access and policy changes, helping with compliance and troubleshooting.

Disadvantages

  1. Learning Curve: Understanding the hierarchical policies and permissions can be challenging for beginners.
  2. Complexity in Large Organizations: Managing IAM for multiple teams and projects can become complex without clear governance.
  3. Risk of Misconfiguration: Incorrect policy settings can lead to unauthorized access or overly restrictive environments.

IAM roles

In Google Cloud, IAM roles are a central mechanism for granting permissions to users, groups, and service accounts. They define "who can do what on which resources," ensuring access is managed in a secure and efficient manner.

IAM roles allow administrators to:

  • Assign predefined or custom access levels to users or services.
  • Maintain granular or broad control over resource permissions.
  • Manage resource access at various levels in the Google Cloud resource hierarchy.

Types


There are three main types of IAM roles:


Basic roles (Legacy Roles)

Overview:

  • Coarse-grained roles that existed prior to IAM's introduction.
  • Provide broad access to all resources within a project.

Types:

  • Viewer: Read-only access to all project resources.
  • Editor: Read and write access to all project resources, including the ability to modify them.
  • Owner: Full control over the project, including resource management, permissions, and billing.
  • Billing Administrator: Manages billing accounts, payment instruments, and cost-related configurations.

Scope:

  • Applied at the project or service resource level.

Drawbacks:

  • Excessive access can lead to security risks.
  • Not suitable for modern, granular access needs.


Predefined Roles

Overview:

  • Fine-grained roles curated by Google Cloud to provide access tailored to specific job functions or services.
  • Examples: Compute Network Admin, Security Reviewer, Storage Admin, Instance Admin.

Key Features:

  • Managed and updated by Google Cloud.
  • Automatically include permissions for new features or services as they are released.

Granularity:

  • Predefined roles are service-specific, minimizing unnecessary access.
  • Example: The Browser role allows users to view the project hierarchy (folders, organizations, IAM policies) but does not provide access to project resources.

Example Permissions:

  • Instance Admin (Compute Engine): Permissions to create, delete, and manage virtual machine instances.
  • Storage Admin: Permissions to manage Cloud Storage buckets and objects.


Custom Roles

Overview:

  • User-defined roles that allow administrators to map specific permissions to unique job functions.
  • Tailored to an organization's needs for even finer-grained control.

Use Case:

  • Example: Create a Privacy Reviewer role to audit data in storage services like Cloud Storage, Bigtable, and Spanner.

Management:

  • Administrators must manually update custom roles to include permissions for new features or services.

Granularity:

  • Permissions are defined at a very specific level, ensuring the role aligns precisely with a job's requirements.

Caveats:

  • Greater management overhead compared to predefined roles.
  • Requires ongoing updates as Google Cloud services evolve.


Role scope and inheritance

Hierarchy Levels:

  • IAM roles can be assigned at different levels:

    • Organization: Apply to all resources within the organization.
    • Folder: Apply to all resources within the folder.
    • Project: Apply to all resources within the project.
    • Resource: Apply to specific resources, such as a Cloud Storage bucket or Compute Engine instance.

Inheritance:

  • Roles granted at higher levels in the hierarchy are inherited by lower levels.
  • Example: A Viewer role at the organization level allows read-only access to all projects and resources within the organization.

Examples of IAM roles

Role Type

Example Role

Scope

Use Case

Basic Role

Owner

Project

Full project management, including billing.


Viewer

Project

Read-only access to all resources in a project.

Predefined Role

Specific service (Compute Engine)

Manage VPC networks and firewall rules.

Best practices

  1. Use Predefined Roles: Where possible, rely on predefined roles to minimize administrative overhead and ensure up-to-date permissions.
  2. Follow the Principle of Least Privilege: Grant only the permissions necessary for a user or service to perform their tasks.
  3. Be Cautious with Basic Roles: Avoid using basic roles like Owner or Editor unless absolutely necessary.
  4. Leverage Custom Roles Judiciously: Create custom roles only when predefined roles cannot meet specific access requirements. Regularly review and update custom roles as Google Cloud services evolve.
  5. Audit Roles and Permissions Regularly: Periodically review IAM policies to identify and remove unnecessary or excessive permissions.
  6. Use Conditional Policies: Apply IAM Conditions for additional granularity, such as time-bound or IP-restricted access.

IAM policies

  1. Policy Components:

    • Principal: The entity requesting access (e.g., user, group, service account).
    • Role: A collection of permissions.
    • Resource: The object being accessed (e.g., a project or bucket).

  2. Inheritance and Overrides:

    • Policies set at higher levels (e.g., Organization) are inherited by lower levels (e.g., Projects).
    • Lower-level policies can override inherited settings where necessary.

  3. IAM Conditions:

    • Allow you to define more granular access controls, such as:

      • Time-based access: Grant access only during specified hours.
      • IP restrictions: Allow access from specific IP ranges.

Deny policies

IAM deny policies in Google Cloud offer an additional layer of control over access to resources by explicitly denying certain permissions to specified principals (users, groups, or service accounts). This mechanism overrides any permissions granted through roles, enforcing strict guardrails that cannot be bypassed. Here are the key aspects:

  1. Components of Deny Policies:

    • Deny Rules: A deny policy consists of deny rules that define:

      • Principals: Who is denied access.
      • Permissions: What permissions are denied.
      • Conditions (optional): Under what circumstances the deny rules apply.

  2. Behavior:

    • Deny policies are checked before allow policies, ensuring that any explicitly denied permission cannot be used, even if it is granted through an IAM role.
    • This hierarchy ensures robust access control and serves as a safeguard against misconfigurations.

  3. Applications:

    • Guardrails for sensitive resources.
    • Preventing accidental or unauthorized actions, such as deleting critical infrastructure.

IAM Conditions

IAM Conditions enable conditional, attribute-based access control, refining access permissions based on specific conditions. This feature is used in role bindings within IAM policies.

  1. Condition Attributes:

    • Resource Attributes: Evaluate attributes of the resource in the access request, such as resource name or type.
    • Request Attributes: Evaluate attributes of the request, such as timestamp, requester's IP address, or other metadata.

  2. Examples:

    • Restricting access to Cloud Storage buckets whose names start with a specific prefix.
    • Allowing access to resources only during certain hours or from specific IP ranges.

  3. Use Cases:

    • Enforcing access restrictions based on the context of the request.
    • Implementing fine-grained control over resource access.

Organization Policies and Constraints

While IAM policies control who can access resources, organization policies focus on what actions or configurations are allowed across resources, services, or groups of services.

  1. Types of Constraints:

    • List Constraints: Allow or deny specific values (e.g., external IP usage for VMs).
    • Boolean Constraints: Turn specific behaviors or features on or off (e.g., disabling serial port access).

  2. Inheritance:

    • Organization policies set at a higher level in the resource hierarchy (e.g., root organization node) are inherited by all descendant nodes unless explicitly overridden.

  3. Complementary Roles:

    • Organization policies define what actions are restricted.
    • IAM policies define who can take actions, ensuring cohesive resource control.

By combining IAM Deny Policies, IAM Conditions, and Organization Policies, administrators can implement a robust, fine-grained access control system tailored to the needs of their Google Cloud environment.

Service accounts

Service accounts in Google Cloud are special types of accounts used for server-to-server communication and application authentication. They play a crucial role in controlling what actions an application or service can perform within the Google Cloud environment.

  1. Purpose:

    • Authenticate applications and services with other Google Cloud services.
    • Control permissions for actions performed by applications or services.

  2. Usage Example:

    • If an application running on a Compute Engine instance needs to access a Cloud Storage bucket, you can assign a service account with the Cloud Storage Object Viewer role to that instance. This allows the application to read files in the bucket securely.

  3. Identification:

    • Service accounts are identified using email addresses in the gserviceaccount.com domain.


Types

Google-Managed Service Accounts:

  • Created and managed automatically by Google for Google Cloud services.
  • Used when Google services need access to your resources to perform actions on your behalf (e.g., triggering a Cloud Run container with Pub/Sub).
  • Not visible in your project’s service accounts list but may appear in IAM policies, audit logs, or the IAM page.

  • Key Features:

    • Google manages the private key securely and rotates it regularly.
    • You cannot directly manage these accounts.

User-Managed Service Accounts:

  • Created, managed, and controlled by users within their projects.
  • Fully customizable: users can update, disable, enable, or delete them.
  • Permissions can be assigned to other principals for these accounts.

  • Creation Methods:

    • Google Cloud Console
    • Google Cloud CLI
    • IAM API
  • Limits: By default, up to 100 user-managed service accounts can be created per project.

Google API service accounts:

  • An example of a Google-managed service account is a Google API service account identifiable using the email: PROJECT_NUMBER@cloudservices.gserviceaccount.com.
  • This service account is designed specifically to run internal Google processes on your behalf and is not listed in the Service Accounts section of the Cloud Console. By default, the account is automatically granted the project editor role on the project and is listed in the IAM section of the Cloud Console.
  • This service account is deleted only when the project is deleted. Google services rely on the account having access to your project, so you should not remove or change the service account’s role on your project.

Authentication mechanism

  1. Key Pairs:

    • Service accounts use RSA key pairs for authentication instead of passwords.
    • Key pairs are used to generate JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), which can then request access tokens.

  2. Types of Key Pairs:

    • Google-Managed Keys:

      • Google securely stores both public and private keys.
      • Keys are rotated regularly.
      • Public keys are valid for signing for a maximum of two weeks.

    • User-Managed Keys (External Keys):

      • Google stores only the public portion of the key.
      • Users manage the private key, including security and rotation.
      • Up to 10 user-managed keys can be created per service account for rotation purposes.

  3. Security Considerations:

    • The private key is as sensitive as a password; it should be protected rigorously.
    • Google cannot recover lost private keys, so users are responsible for managing backups and secure storage.

Best practices

  1. Key Management:

    • Rotate user-managed keys regularly to reduce the risk of exposure.
    • Limit the number of keys created to simplify management.

  2. Minimize Permissions:

    • Follow the principle of least privilege by granting only the permissions required for a specific task or service.

  3. Audit and Monitor:

    • Regularly review service account usage and audit logs for suspicious activity.
    • Use the Google Cloud CLI (gcloud) to list all keys and monitor their usage.

  4. Secure Key Storage:

    • Use secure methods to store and handle private keys, such as a secrets manager or a secure filesystem.

Best practices

  1. Use the Principle of Least Privilege: Grant only the permissions necessary for users and applications to perform their roles.
  2. Regularly Audit Permissions: Periodically review and revoke unnecessary permissions to reduce security risks.
  3. Leverage Predefined Roles: Use predefined roles for common tasks to reduce the risk of errors in custom role creation.
  4. Implement IAM Conditions: Use conditions to enforce additional security, such as allowing access only during specific times or from specific IP ranges.
  5. Use Service Accounts for Applications: Assign service accounts to applications instead of individual users to manage resource access securely.
  6. Enable Audit Logging: Ensure all resource and policy activities are logged for compliance and forensic purposes.

Practical tips

  1. Define Organizational Roles Early: Establish clear roles and responsibilities to simplify IAM policy design.
  2. Document Policies: Maintain detailed documentation of IAM policies for clarity and ease of troubleshooting.
  3. Automate Policy Management: Use tools like Terraform to manage and version-control IAM policies.
  4. Restrict Broad Roles: Avoid assigning broad roles (e.g., Owner) unless absolutely necessary.
  5. Segment Projects: Use separate projects for different teams or environments (e.g., dev, test, prod) to simplify IAM policy enforcement.


IAM vs Other Identity Services

Managed Microsoft AD

Control access to Google Cloud resources.

Granularity
