Firestore

Google Cloud Firestore is a fully managed, serverless, NoSQL document database that enables real-time synchronization and offline capabilities. Designed for modern application development, it is particularly suitable for mobile, web, and server-side applications requiring flexible, scalable, and responsive data storage solutions.

1. Key Features

a. Document-Oriented Database

  • Stores data in documents, organized into collections.
  • Documents are JSON-like structures with key-value pairs.
  • Schema-less design allows flexible data modeling.

b. Real-Time Data Synchronization

  • Automatically syncs data across client devices in real-time.
  • Ideal for collaborative applications and dynamic user experiences.

c. Offline Support

  • Clients can read and write data locally even without internet connectivity.
  • Data syncs automatically when the connection is restored.

d. Fully Managed and Serverless

  • No server management required; Google handles scaling, updates, and maintenance.
  • Automatically scales to accommodate workload demands.

e. Global Scalability

  • Designed for horizontal scaling.
  • Supports regional or multi-regional configurations for high availability.

f. ACID Transactions

  • Ensures data consistency with support for multi-document transactions.
  • Useful for complex operations requiring atomic updates.

g. Security and Access Control

  • Fine-grained access control using Firestore Security Rules.
  • Fully integrated with Firebase Authentication and Google Identity.

2. Data Model

Firestore organizes data hierarchically for flexibility and scalability:

  1. Collections and Documents:

    • Collections: Containers for documents; cannot directly store data.
    • Documents: JSON-like data structures stored in collections.

  2. Subcollections:

    • Documents can contain subcollections, enabling nested data structures.
    • Useful for organizing related data hierarchically.

  3. Fields:

    • Documents have fields storing key-value pairs.
    • Supported data types: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, maps, timestamps, and more.

3. Querying Capabilities

Firestore supports powerful querying with a variety of options:

a. Indexed Queries

  • Automatically indexes data for efficient querying.
  • Supports complex compound queries.

b. Range Queries

  • Perform range-based operations, such as greater than, less than, and between.

c. Compound Queries

  • Combine multiple conditions using logical operators.

d. Order and Limit

  • Order results by field and limit the number of returned documents.

e. Realtime Listeners

  • Subscribes to changes in data and updates applications in real-time.

4. Integration with Google Cloud and Firebase

Firestore is integrated deeply within the Google Cloud and Firebase ecosystems:

a. Firebase SDKs

  • Enables seamless integration with mobile and web applications.
  • Real-time data synchronization with minimal code.

b. Google Cloud Services

  • Connects to Google Cloud functions, BigQuery, and Dataflow for advanced workflows.
  • Supports Google Cloud Pub/Sub for event-driven architectures.

c. BigQuery

  • Export Firestore data to BigQuery for analytics and reporting.

5. Use Cases

a. Mobile and Web Applications

  • Real-time synchronization for chat applications, collaborative tools, and dynamic content updates.

b. E-Commerce Platforms

  • Manage inventory, user profiles, and real-time order tracking.

c. IoT Applications

  • Store and analyze data from IoT devices.
  • Use offline capabilities for intermittent connectivity.

d. Gaming

  • Real-time leaderboards, multiplayer state synchronization, and player profiles.

e. Analytics and Reporting

  • Combine Firestore with BigQuery for data-driven decision-making.

6. Pricing Structure

Firestore pricing is based on usage, with separate charges for the following:

a. Operations

  • Read, write, and delete operations are billed individually.

b. Storage

  • Charged based on the amount of data stored (per GB per month).

c. Network Usage

  • Data transfer charges for outbound network traffic.

d. Free Tier

  • Offers free quotas for reads, writes, deletes, and storage.

Example Cost Calculation:

  • High read/write workloads can increase operational costs.
  • Efficient data modeling reduces unnecessary reads and writes.

7. Security and Access Control

a. Firestore Security Rules

  • Define rules to restrict access based on request properties, user authentication, and more.
  • Example: Allow a user to access only their data.

b. Firebase Authentication

  • Seamless integration with Firestore to manage user authentication.

c. IAM Integration

  • Fine-grained role-based access control for managing permissions.

8. High Availability and Scalability

a. Regional and Multi-Regional Configurations

  • Regional: Low-latency access within a specific region.
  • Multi-Regional: High availability with automatic replication across regions.

b. Automatic Scaling

  • Handles workload spikes without manual intervention.
  • Designed to accommodate millions of concurrent connections.

c. Backup and Restore

  • Automated backups for disaster recovery.

9. Offline Support

Firestore’s offline capabilities allow applications to function without an internet connection:

  • Client-Side Persistence: Data is cached locally on the device.
  • Conflict Resolution: Firestore handles conflicts automatically when syncing data.

11. Best Practices

a. Efficient Data Modeling

  • Structure collections and subcollections to minimize the number of operations.
  • Denormalize data for read-heavy workloads.

b. Security Rules

  • Regularly audit and update Firestore Security Rules.
  • Test rules in Firebase’s built-in emulator.

c. Optimize Reads and Writes

  • Use queries to fetch only necessary data.
  • Avoid unnecessary writes and excessive document size.

d. Monitor Costs

  • Track usage patterns using Firebase Console or Google Cloud Monitoring.
  • Leverage caching and pagination to reduce read operations.

e. Testing and Debugging

  • Use Firebase Emulator Suite for local testing.
  • Simulate different network conditions for robust offline support.

12. Advantages

  • Real-time synchronization simplifies dynamic applications.
  • Offline support improves user experience.
  • Fully managed and serverless, eliminating operational overhead.
  • Deep integration with Firebase for mobile and web applications.

13. Limitations

  • Higher costs for read/write-heavy applications compared to batch-oriented databases.
  • No support for complex transactional workloads.
  • Not suitable for analytical workloads (use BigQuery instead).

Conclusion

Google Cloud Firestore is a versatile, scalable, and real-time database solution for modern application development. Its serverless nature, real-time sync, and offline capabilities make it an excellent choice for building dynamic mobile, web, and IoT applications. By leveraging Firestore’s features, developers can create robust, responsive, and user-friendly applications with minimal operational overhead.


AI & ML


Services

AutoML

What it is?

AutoML, short for Automated Machine Learning, is an innovative approach that automates the entire machine learning (ML) pipeline. It allows users with little or no ML expertise to develop, train, and deploy powerful machine learning models with minimal effort.


Google Cloud integrates AutoML within Vertex AI, its unified AI/ML platform, enabling no-code and low-code ML development. AutoML allows users to:

  • Automate data preprocessing, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning.
  • Leverage transfer learning to enhance models without extensive training data.
  • Use pre-built, high-accuracy ML models while maintaining flexibility for custom training.

Key phases

AutoML consists of four primary phases that automate the ML pipeline from data processing to model deployment.

Phase 1: Data Processing

  • The first step involves preparing the dataset for ML.

  • AutoML can automatically clean and structure data, converting:

    • Text → Tokenized and vectorized for NLP models.
    • Numbers & Datetime → Normalized for tabular models.
    • Images → Augmented and preprocessed for vision models.
  • Feature Engineering is automated, helping users avoid manual preprocessing.

Phase 2: Model Selection and Hyperparameter Tuning

AutoML leverages two powerful techniques to find the best model architecture:

  1. Neural Architecture Search (NAS):

    • Explores multiple ML architectures and automatically selects the best-performing model.
    • Optimizes model structure and hyperparameters for higher accuracy.
    • Eliminates the need for manual trial-and-error model tuning.

  2. Transfer Learning:

    • Uses pre-trained models as a foundation, requiring less training data.
    • Enables rapid adaptation of models to new datasets without starting from scratch.
    • Example: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on general text can be fine-tuned for finance, healthcare, or retail applications.

Phase 3: Model Assembly

  • Instead of using one model, AutoML selects and combines multiple top models (typically around 10).

  • Ensemble Learning techniques:

    • Aggregates predictions from top models for higher accuracy.
    • Reduces overfitting by combining multiple perspectives.

Phase 4: Model Deployment and Prediction

  • After training, AutoML optimizes the best-performing models for deployment.

  • Users can:

    • Deploy the model in Vertex AI for online predictions.
    • Export the trained model for edge computing.
    • Integrate predictions with other Google Cloud services.

How it works

AutoML incorporates state-of-the-art ML techniques to automate model development.

Transfer learning

  • Speeds up training by leveraging knowledge from pre-trained models.
  • Enables high-accuracy results with smaller datasets.

  • Used in:

    • Text classification (Google’s NLP models pre-trained on large datasets).
    • Image recognition (Models trained on ImageNet used for new tasks).
    • Speech-to-text applications.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS)

  • Automates the search for the best model architecture.
  • Evaluates multiple ML architectures and fine-tunes hyperparameters.
  • Eliminates manual tuning, reducing human effort and error.

Ensemble learning

  • Uses multiple models instead of one to enhance accuracy.
  • Voting or averaging techniques combine predictions for robust results.
  • Improves generalization and resilience against overfitting.

How to use

AutoML is accessible via Google Cloud Console (UI), SDKs, and APIs. Below is the step-by-step workflow for training an AutoML model.

Steps to train model

  1. Upload and Prepare Data:

    • Use Google Cloud Storage (GCS) or BigQuery.
    • AutoML automatically preprocesses and structures the data.

  2. Select ML Task Type:

    • AutoML Tables (for structured/tabular data).
    • AutoML Vision (for image classification).
    • AutoML NLP (for text-based models).
    • AutoML Video Intelligence (for video analysis).

  3. Train Model:

    • AutoML automatically selects, trains, and tunes models.
    • Transfer learning is applied for higher accuracy with less data.

  4. Evaluate Model Performance:

    • AutoML provides accuracy metrics, confusion matrices, and feature importance.
    • Users can fine-tune hyperparameters or retrain with more data.

  5. Deploy Model for Prediction:

    • Deploy on Vertex AI for online inference.
    • Export to Edge Devices for on-device ML.
    • Integrate with Google Cloud APIs for seamless AI applications.

Pricing

Google Cloud AutoML offers flexible pricing models, which vary based on:

  • Training time (charged per hour).
  • Prediction requests (charged per 1,000 predictions).
  • Data storage and compute resources.

For an exact cost estimate, refer to Google Cloud AutoML Pricing.

Limitations

While AutoML is a powerful tool, it has some limitations:

  • Limited Model Customization: Cannot modify model architecture like custom ML training.
  • Training Costs: AutoML can be costly for large-scale datasets.
  • Less Control Over Interpretability: Difficult to understand inner workings of automated models.

Conclusion

AutoML democratizes AI development, making ML accessible to non-experts while delivering high-accuracy models with minimal effort. By leveraging transfer learning, neural architecture search, and ensemble learning, AutoML reduces model development time and enables businesses to deploy AI-powered applications faster.

For organizations seeking to implement AI without deep ML expertise, AutoML on Vertex AI is an ideal solution. Whether for image recognition, text analysis, or predictive analytics, AutoML provides an efficient and scalable approach to leveraging AI for business growth.


Development

Introduction

Developing AI and machine learning (ML) models in Google Cloud can follow different approaches depending on expertise, data availability, and customization needs. Google Cloud provides four main options for building and deploying ML models: pre-trained APIs, BigQuery ML, AutoML, and custom training. Each of these approaches caters to different levels of expertise, business needs, and computational complexity.

Options


Google Cloud provides a spectrum of AI solutions that range from fully managed APIs to custom training solutions, allowing organizations to balance ease of use with flexibility.

Pre-trained APIs

Best for: Developers and businesses with little or no ML experience who want to integrate AI quickly.

Google Cloud offers a set of pre-trained APIs that allow users to perform common AI tasks without training their own models. These APIs include:

  • Vision API (image classification, object detection)
  • Natural Language API (text analysis, entity recognition)
  • Speech-to-Text API and Text-to-Speech API
  • Translation API
  • Video Intelligence API

Advantages:

  • No need for ML expertise.
  • No training data required.
  • Instant results with minimal configuration.

Limitations:

  • Limited to predefined AI functionalities.
  • No control over model tuning or training data.

BigQuery ML

Best for: Data analysts or engineers familiar with SQL who need to build ML models on tabular data.

BigQuery ML enables SQL-based ML model training directly within BigQuery. It removes the need for coding in Python or TensorFlow, allowing analysts to run ML models using SQL queries.

Advantages:

  • Works well with structured data (tabular data).
  • Supports automated feature engineering.
  • Fast model training with minimal computational overhead.

Limitations:

  • Limited to tabular data.
  • Less flexibility in custom model architectures.
  • Requires knowledge of SQL queries.

AutoML

Best for: Business users, analysts, or developers who need custom models but lack deep ML knowledge.

AutoML (hosted on Vertex AI) provides an easy-to-use interface for custom AI model training without extensive coding.

  • Allows users to upload training data and automatically build ML models.
  • Supports image, text, video, and structured data.
  • Provides automatic hyperparameter tuning and model selection.

Advantages:

  • No coding required (point-and-click interface).
  • Ideal for custom models without complex ML knowledge.
  • Supports transfer learning for better model accuracy.

Limitations:

  • Less flexible than custom training.
  • Hyperparameters cannot be fine-tuned manually.
  • Training data is required (unlike pre-trained APIs).

Custom training

Best for: ML engineers, data scientists, or AI specialists who require full control over model development.

This option allows users to train fully customized ML models using TensorFlow, PyTorch, or scikit-learn on Vertex AI Workbench.

  • Offers full control over model architecture, training parameters, and deployment.
  • Supports distributed training for large-scale AI models.

Advantages:

  • Maximum flexibility for AI development.
  • Ability to fine-tune hyperparameters.
  • Custom model architectures (CNNs, RNNs, transformers, etc.).

Limitations:

  • Requires high ML expertise.
  • Longer development time and computational costs.
  • Needs infrastructure management for GPUs/TPUs.

Infrastructure

Introduction

Google Cloud Platform AI/ML infrastructure is not a single product. It is a layered ecosystem composed of accelerator hardware, distributed compute platforms, storage systems, networking, managed machine learning services, data platforms, security controls, and operational tooling. The central architectural decision is not “which GPU should I use?”, but rather: which workload pattern am I running, what level of control do I need, what latency or throughput target must I meet, and how much infrastructure responsibility am I willing to own?

At a high level, Google Cloud AI/ML infrastructure consists of the following layers:


Layer

Main Google Cloud capabilities

Purpose

AI Hypercomputer, GPU superclusters, Cloud TPU, high-performance networking, scheduling, storage

Large-scale model training, fine-tuning, serving, high-performance computing

Compute layer

Compute Engine, accelerator-optimized virtual machines, Cloud TPU, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run GPU

Raw execution environment for training, inference, preprocessing, distributed workloads

Managed ML layer

Vertex AI, Vertex AI Training, Vertex AI Prediction, Vertex AI Pipelines, Model Garden, Vector Search

Managed model development, deployment, MLOps, generative AI, model registry, pipelines

Google Kubernetes Engine, GKE Autopilot, GKE Standard, Kueue, Ray on GKE, Inference Gateway

Custom AI platforms, multi-tenant ML platforms, large-scale training and inference

Serverless inference layer

Containerized inference with serverless scaling, including scale-to-zero

Data and storage layer

Cloud Storage, Cloud Storage FUSE, Hyperdisk ML, Managed Lustre, Parallelstore, BigQuery, Dataflow, Managed Service for Apache Spark

Training data, model artifacts, checkpoints, feature data, analytics, distributed data processing

Security and governance layer

Identity and Access Management, VPC Service Controls, Private Service Connect, encryption, audit logging, Model Armor, Artifact Registry, Binary Authorization

Protect data, models, pipelines, APIs, supply chain, and runtime environments

Operations layer

Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Logging, Vertex AI Experiments, Vertex AI TensorBoard, GPU metrics, cost labels, reservations, Dynamic Workload Scheduler

Observability, capacity planning, reliability, cost control


Google describes AI Hypercomputer as a supercomputing system that combines performance-optimized hardware, open software, machine learning frameworks, and flexible consumption models for AI training, tuning, and serving. This is the umbrella concept for Google’s highest-performance AI infrastructure, especially when workloads require dense accelerator clusters and specialized scheduling.

Vertex AI is Google Cloud’s managed platform for training and deploying machine learning models and building AI applications, while GKE provides a managed Kubernetes foundation for custom AI/ML platforms, multi-tenant workloads, scalable training, and production inference.

Vertex AI should usually be the default when you want a managed machine learning platform with lower operational overhead. GKE should be selected when you need Kubernetes-native control, multi-tenancy, custom scheduling, custom networking, advanced inference routing, or deep integration with internal platform engineering. Cloud Run is attractive for serverless inference where container simplicity and scale-to-zero matter. Compute Engine, Slurm, and AI Hypercomputer patterns are appropriate for the largest or most specialized workloads where infrastructure topology, cluster scheduling, and low-level optimization are central concerns. Google’s own model runtime guidance distinguishes Vertex AI, Cloud Run, and GKE according to managed-service depth, custom container control, hardware flexibility, and security/networking requirements.

3. Compute and Accelerator Infrastructure

3.1 CPUs

CPU-only infrastructure is still important in AI/ML. Not every workload requires accelerators. CPUs are commonly used for data preprocessing, feature engineering, orchestration, lightweight classical machine learning, batch data transformation, model evaluation, pipeline execution, and serving small models.

In Google Cloud, CPU workloads can run on Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, Dataflow, BigQuery, Managed Service for Apache Spark, and Vertex AI custom training. For many production systems, the correct design is hybrid: CPUs handle preprocessing, orchestration, and post-processing, while GPUs or TPUs handle dense tensor computation.

CPU-based infrastructure is often underestimated. A specialist should understand that expensive accelerators are frequently idle because input pipelines, storage throughput, tokenizer performance, checkpointing, network placement, or CPU preprocessing are poorly designed.

3.2 GPUs on Google Cloud

Google Cloud provides GPU infrastructure through accelerator-optimized Compute Engine machine families, GKE GPU node pools, Vertex AI training and prediction, and Cloud Run GPU for serverless inference. Google’s GPU machine type documentation covers NVIDIA GPU models for machine learning, data processing, and graphics workloads, including accelerator-optimized A-series and G-series machines as well as older GPU attachments to N1 machine types.

The main GPU families relevant to AI/ML are:


GPU family

Typical role

Notes

Based on NVIDIA GB300 / GB200 class systems; positioned for compute-, memory-, and network-intensive AI workloads

A4

Uses NVIDIA B200 GPUs; designed for high-end AI workloads

A3 Ultra / A3 Mega / A3 High / A3 Edge

Large-scale training and serving

A3 Ultra uses NVIDIA H200; A3 Mega/High/Edge use NVIDIA H100 variants, with Edge oriented more toward serving regions

A2 Ultra / A2 Standard

A100-based training, fine-tuning, inference, smaller distributed workloads

N1 attached GPUs

Legacy or compatibility scenarios

Supports older attachable GPUs such as T4, P4, V100, and P100


Google’s documentation classifies the A-series as designed for high-performance computing, artificial intelligence, and machine learning, with newer A-series machines positioned for foundation model pre-training and fine-tuning. G-series machines are more commonly aligned with graphics, video, smaller models, and single-host inference.

A specialist should evaluate GPUs across several dimensions:

Why it matters

Google explicitly warns that GPU availability depends on region and quota, and new projects may need both regional GPU quota and global GPU quota planning.

3.3 Cloud TPU

Cloud TPU is Google’s custom accelerator family for machine learning workloads. Google describes TPUs as custom-developed application-specific integrated circuits designed to accelerate machine learning workloads, accessible from Compute Engine, GKE, and Vertex AI.

TPUs are especially relevant when your workload is well-supported by TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch/XLA, or Google’s TPU-optimized training and inference stacks. TPUs are not simply “Google GPUs.” They have different programming, topology, memory, compilation, and scaling characteristics. A good GCP AI infrastructure specialist must understand when TPUs are the better architectural choice and when GPUs are more practical.

Current TPU generations relevant to modern AI/ML include:


TPU generation

Main role

Specialist notes

TPU7x / Ironwood

Latest large-scale TPU generation for training and inference

Google identifies TPU7x as a seventh-generation TPU designed for large-scale AI training and inference; TPU7x usage requires GKE according to Google’s TPU software version documentation

TPU v6e / Trillium

Training, fine-tuning, and serving for transformer, text-to-image, and convolutional workloads

Supports JAX and PyTorch/XLA; Google positions it for modern AI models including transformer and diffusion-style workloads

TPU v5p

Very large-scale training

Google documents TPU v5p pods with thousands of chips and large-job support

TPU v5e

Cost-efficient training and inference

Suitable for many training, fine-tuning, and inference scenarios, including single-host and multi-host configurations



TPU selection depends on model architecture, framework, model size, batch size, required precision, topology, availability, quota, and whether the workload can tolerate TPU-specific compilation and runtime constraints. Google’s TPU planning documentation emphasizes choosing the TPU version based on workload requirements, quota, and resource planning.

3.4 GPU vs TPU: Practical Selection Logic

A simplified decision model:


Choose GPUs when…

Choose TPUs when…

You need maximum framework flexibility, broad CUDA ecosystem support, or custom kernels

Your workload maps well to TPU-supported frameworks and TPU-optimized execution

You rely on PyTorch/CUDA-native libraries, custom inference engines, or NVIDIA-specific tooling

You use JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch/XLA, or Google-provided TPU training patterns

You need compatibility with popular open-source serving stacks such as vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Triton, or Hugging Face runtimes

You want large-scale Google TPU pod-style training or TPU-optimized serving

You need broad model ecosystem portability

You are optimizing for Google’s TPU architecture, scaling, and cost/performance profile

You need Cloud Run GPU or GKE GPU-based serving

You are building on GKE TPU, Vertex AI TPU training, or Cloud TPU patterns


The best expert-level answer is rarely “GPU is better” or “TPU is better.” The correct answer is workload-specific and depends on model type, framework, scaling pattern, precision, memory pressure, serving latency, developer skill set, capacity availability, and cost model.

4. Main AI/ML Runtime Platforms

4.1 Vertex AI

Vertex AI is Google Cloud’s managed machine learning and AI platform. It supports model training, deployment, generative AI development, model discovery through Model Garden, pipelines, and managed inference. Google’s documentation describes Vertex AI as a platform for training and deploying machine learning models and AI applications, combining workflows for data engineering, data science, and ML engineering.

Google’s Vertex AI training documentation describes a spectrum from AutoML to custom training, serverless training, training clusters, and Ray on Vertex AI. Google distinguishes online inference, where a model is deployed to an endpoint with associated compute resources, from batch inference, where requests are processed asynchronously when immediate responses are not required. Vertex AI endpoints support autoscaling, with minimum and maximum replica configuration and usage-based scaling behavior.

When Vertex AI is the right default

Use Vertex AI when you want:

  • Managed training jobs without operating clusters manually.
  • Managed endpoints and autoscaling.
  • Model registry, metadata, experiments, and pipeline integration.
  • AutoML or Model Garden workflows.
  • Faster productionization with less platform engineering.
  • Centralized governance for machine learning workflows.
  • Batch prediction at scale.
  • Managed MLOps through Vertex AI Pipelines.

Vertex AI Pipelines provide a serverless way to automate, monitor, and govern machine learning workflows using Kubeflow Pipelines or TensorFlow Extended pipeline definitions. Google describes ML pipelines as portable, extensible MLOps workflow descriptions that can be reused for continuous retraining.

4.2 Google Kubernetes Engine for AI/ML

GKE is Google Cloud’s managed Kubernetes platform. For AI/ML, it is important because many advanced workloads require container orchestration, accelerator node pools, multi-tenant scheduling, custom networking, model-serving frameworks, and platform-level control. Google’s GKE AI/ML documentation explicitly positions GKE for training large foundation models, serving inference at scale, and building AI platforms.

GKE is commonly selected for:


Use case

Why GKE fits

Multi-tenant ML platform

Namespaces, quotas, policies, workload identity, scheduling controls

Large distributed training

GPU/TPU node pools, Kueue, custom schedulers, topology-aware placement

High-throughput inference

Kubernetes services, autoscaling, model-aware routing, custom serving stacks

Platform engineering

Standardized internal ML platform with CI/CD, observability, security controls

Hybrid open-source AI stack

Ray, Kubeflow, KServe, vLLM, Triton, Hugging Face, custom operators

Advanced security/networking

Kubernetes-native policy, private clusters, service mesh, admission controls


Google states that GKE is suitable when you need deeper control, portability, and a high-performance AI platform, while Vertex AI is the more fully managed alternative. Google also positions Cloud Run as an option for smaller serverless model-serving scenarios.

GKE AI/ML features include GPU and TPU support, GKE Inference Gateway for model-aware routing and load balancing, Autopilot support, faster node startup features, Flex-start and Dynamic Workload Scheduler integration, Kueue, TPU multislice support, and Ray on GKE.

GKE Autopilot vs GKE Standard for AI/ML


Mode

Best for

Trade-off

GKE Autopilot

Managed Kubernetes infrastructure, simpler operations, baseline security and autoscaling

Less low-level node control

GKE Standard

Custom node pools, advanced accelerator tuning, specialized scheduling, complex platform requirements

More operational responsibility


Google’s GKE TPU planning documentation states that Autopilot manages infrastructure, node configuration, autoscaling, upgrades, baseline security, networking, and provisioning, while Standard gives you more direct infrastructure control.

4.3 Cloud Run for AI Inference

Cloud Run is Google’s serverless container runtime. It is increasingly relevant for AI inference because it supports GPUs for containerized workloads. Google documents Cloud Run GPU support for AI inference, large language models, video processing, and other GPU-accelerated applications, with NVIDIA L4 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU options, no manual driver installation, on-demand availability, and scale-to-zero behavior.

Cloud Run is a strong fit when:

  • You serve open or custom models in containers.
  • Traffic is variable or intermittent.
  • Scale-to-zero is economically useful.
  • You want to avoid managing Kubernetes.
  • You need simple HTTPS-based inference.
  • One GPU per instance is sufficient.
  • Startup time and model loading are acceptable for your service-level objective.

Cloud Run GPU best practices emphasize fast model loading, concurrent execution optimization, and careful model storage choices. Google recommends loading models from Cloud Storage for many deployments and notes that embedding models into container images can work for smaller models but has trade-offs.

Cloud Run is not a replacement for Vertex AI or GKE in every case. It is best for simpler inference services, prototypes, internal APIs, bursty workloads, and production use cases where serverless behavior aligns with latency and cost requirements.

4.4 Compute Engine, Slurm, and AI Hypercomputer

Compute Engine remains important for AI/ML specialists because it provides direct access to virtual machines, accelerator-optimized machine families, custom images, local SSD, storage mounts, and low-level cluster configuration.

For very large workloads, Google’s AI Hypercomputer model and Slurm-based integrations become relevant. Google documents fully managed Slurm clusters for AI workloads using accelerator families such as A4X, A4, and A3 variants.

This pattern is appropriate when:

  • You are migrating high-performance computing or research workloads.
  • Your organization already uses Slurm.
  • Training jobs require explicit topology and placement control.
  • You need large accelerator reservations.
  • You require low-level control over images, drivers, storage, and network behavior.
  • You want to run framework recipes or distributed training stacks outside a fully managed ML platform.

5. Storage and Data Infrastructure for AI/ML

Storage design is one of the most important parts of AI/ML infrastructure. A poor storage design can waste the value of expensive GPUs and TPUs. Google’s AI/ML storage design guide emphasizes that different phases of the ML lifecycle have different storage requirements: training datasets, tuning, serving, checkpointing, and archiving do not need the same capacity, latency, throughput, consistency, or cost profile.

5.1 Main Storage Options


Storage service

Best for

Key characteristics

Cloud Storage

Durable object storage for datasets, model artifacts, logs, checkpoints, archives

Highly durable object store; common foundation for ML data lakes and model artifact storage

Cloud Storage FUSE

Mounting Cloud Storage buckets into file-system-like paths for training or serving

Useful but requires performance tuning; not identical to a high-performance POSIX file system

Cloud Storage FUSE with Rapid Cache / Rapid Bucket

Faster access patterns for repeated reads and model serving

Designed to improve throughput and latency for AI/ML read workloads

Hyperdisk ML

High-throughput block storage for model weights and immutable datasets

Designed for ML workloads that need high read throughput and faster accelerator utilization

Managed Lustre

High-performance managed parallel file system for AI and high-performance computing

POSIX-compatible, high-throughput, multi-petabyte parallel file system

Parallelstore

Low-latency distributed file system for AI/ML training and HPC scratch workloads

Invitation-only; designed for high metadata performance and low-latency scratch-style workloads

BigQuery

Analytics, feature exploration, SQL-based ML, data warehouse

Supports analytics and BigQuery ML

Dataflow

Batch and streaming preprocessing, feature pipelines, inference pipelines

Managed data processing and machine learning inference workflows

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Spark-based ETL, analytics, and ML preprocessing

Managed open-source Spark environment

Vertex AI Vector Search

Embedding search, retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation, semantic search

Managed vector search service using Google’s ScaNN technology


Google’s storage guidance proposes a three-phase process: define workload requirements, review storage options, and select storage by workflow stage. The same guide explicitly compares Cloud Storage, Cloud Storage FUSE, Managed Lustre, and related options for training, checkpointing, serving, and archiving.

5.2 Cloud Storage and Cloud Storage FUSE

Cloud Storage is commonly the durable source of truth for datasets, model artifacts, checkpoints, and logs. However, object storage is not a normal local file system. When mounted through Cloud Storage FUSE, it can be convenient for ML frameworks, but performance and semantics must be understood.

Google’s Cloud Storage FUSE performance guidance for AI/ML includes workload profiles for training, serving, and checkpointing, and recommends tuning options depending on workload type. Google also recommends hierarchical namespace for some AI/ML workloads because it can improve initial queries per second and provide atomic directory rename behavior useful for checkpointing.

Practical guidance:

  • Use Cloud Storage as durable, regional or multi-regional object storage.
  • Use Cloud Storage FUSE when frameworks expect filesystem paths.
  • Tune FUSE settings for training, serving, or checkpointing.
  • Do not assume object storage behaves like POSIX storage.
  • Use hierarchical namespace where checkpointing and directory operations matter.
  • Use caching strategies when repeated reads occur.

5.3 Hyperdisk ML

Hyperdisk ML is designed for AI/ML workloads needing high read throughput, especially for model weights or immutable datasets. Google positions Hyperdisk ML as the highest-throughput Hyperdisk option and recommends it for machine learning workloads with high read throughput and faster accelerator utilization.

In GKE scenarios, Google describes Hyperdisk ML as a way to accelerate model-weight loading, including read-only-many style access patterns and large node-scale loading architectures.

Use Hyperdisk ML when:

  • You need fast repeated reads of model weights.
  • You serve large models across many nodes.
  • You want to reduce accelerator idle time during model loading.
  • You need block-storage performance rather than object-storage semantics.
  • The data is relatively immutable or read-heavy.

5.4 Managed Lustre

Managed Lustre is Google’s fully managed parallel file system for high-performance computing and AI workloads. Google describes it as a high-performance, POSIX-compatible managed file system optimized for AI and HPC, integrated with Compute Engine and GKE, and capable of transferring data to and from Cloud Storage.

Use Managed Lustre when:

  • You need a real POSIX-style parallel file system.
  • Training requires high-throughput shared file access.
  • You need reliable checkpointing throughput.
  • You are running distributed workloads on Compute Engine or GKE.
  • You need predictable storage performance for large AI/HPC jobs.

Managed Lustre is also relevant from a security perspective because Google documents encryption at rest and in transit for the service.

5.5 Parallelstore

Parallelstore is Google’s low-latency distributed file system for AI/ML and HPC workloads. Google describes it as a managed, low-latency file system with POSIX compatibility, high metadata performance, CSI driver integration, and scaling for high read throughput and IOPS, while noting that it is not intended as long-term storage.

Use Parallelstore when:

  • You need fast scratch storage.
  • Metadata performance is critical.
  • You need a low-latency distributed file system.
  • The workload is temporary, training-oriented, or HPC-style.
  • Long-term durability is handled elsewhere, usually in Cloud Storage.

5.6 BigQuery, Dataflow, Spark, and Vector Search

AI/ML infrastructure is not only accelerators. Data systems are equally important.

BigQuery ML lets users create and run machine learning models using GoogleSQL, with models stored in BigQuery datasets. BigQuery can also access Vertex AI models and Cloud AI APIs for tasks such as text generation and translation.

Dataflow ML supports complete ML pipelines for batch and streaming use cases, including local and remote inference, data preparation for training, and processing inference results.

Managed Service for Apache Spark provides managed open-source Spark capabilities for batch processing, querying, streaming, and machine learning.

Vertex AI Vector Search is Google’s managed vector search service using ScaNN, relevant for semantic search, recommendations, and retrieval-augmented generation systems.

6. Training Infrastructure Patterns

6.1 Pattern 1: AutoML on Vertex AI

Use AutoML when you want to build models without writing training code and the problem type is supported. This is useful for teams that need production ML quickly but do not need custom model architecture or framework-level control.

Best for:

  • Tabular, image, text, or other supported AutoML tasks.
  • Teams with limited ML engineering capacity.
  • Rapid baselines.
  • Business-facing ML prototypes.
  • Cases where explainability, lifecycle management, and managed deployment matter more than architecture customization.

Risk:

  • Less flexibility.
  • Less control over architecture and training internals.
  • May be insufficient for advanced deep learning or foundation model workflows.

Vertex AI documentation explicitly positions AutoML as a code-free way to build models for supported tasks.

6.2 Pattern 2: Custom Training on Vertex AI

Custom training on Vertex AI is one of the most common production patterns. You bring your own training code, usually packaged in a container. Vertex AI provisions the training infrastructure, runs the job, and deletes the resources afterward.

Best for:

  • PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, XGBoost, JAX, or custom containers.
  • Managed training without operating clusters.
  • Single-node or distributed training.
  • Jobs needing GPUs or TPUs.
  • Integration with Vertex AI Experiments, Model Registry, Pipelines, and endpoints.

Security considerations:

  • Use dedicated service accounts with least privilege.
  • Store images in Artifact Registry.
  • Avoid embedding secrets in containers.
  • Use Secret Manager or workload identity patterns.
  • Restrict data access to required buckets, BigQuery datasets, and model artifacts.
  • Use customer-managed encryption keys where required.
  • Use private networking and service perimeters for sensitive environments.

6.3 Pattern 3: Distributed Training on GKE

Use GKE when distributed training requires Kubernetes-native scheduling, custom operators, multi-tenant control, GPU or TPU node pools, framework-specific launchers, or platform engineering standardization.

Best for:

  • Internal ML platforms.
  • Ray, Kubeflow, Kueue, custom operators.
  • Multi-team accelerator sharing.
  • Distributed PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow, or custom training.
  • Fine control over node pools, topology, and autoscaling.
  • CI/CD-controlled ML workloads.

Google documents GKE support for both GPUs and TPUs, including lifecycle management, autoscaling, upgrades, load balancing, Kueue resource management, and sandboxing-related capabilities for TPU workloads.

6.4 Pattern 4: AI Hypercomputer and Slurm-Based Training

For very large jobs, especially foundation model training or HPC-like AI workloads, AI Hypercomputer and Slurm-based clusters become relevant. This pattern emphasizes placement, topology, high-performance networking, high-throughput storage, fault tolerance, and scheduler-aware capacity allocation.

Best for:

  • Foundation model pre-training.
  • Massive distributed training.
  • Research and high-performance computing teams.
  • Slurm users migrating to cloud.
  • Large accelerator reservations.
  • Jobs sensitive to topology and collective communication performance.

Google documents Topology Aware Scheduling for GKE workloads to reduce communication overhead and improve performance for large AI/ML workloads.

7. Inference Infrastructure Patterns

7.1 Vertex AI Online Prediction

Use Vertex AI online prediction when you want managed endpoints, autoscaling, model deployment lifecycle, and integration with Vertex AI’s model management capabilities. Vertex AI online inference requires deploying a model to an endpoint with compute resources, and endpoints can autoscale based on configured replica settings and utilization.

Best for:

  • Production ML APIs.
  • Managed model deployment.
  • Model registry integration.
  • Standardized deployment workflows.
  • Teams that want less infrastructure ownership.
  • Batch and online inference under one managed ML platform.

7.2 Vertex AI Batch Prediction

Use batch prediction when latency is not interactive and you need to score large datasets asynchronously. This is common for recommendation refreshes, fraud scoring, churn prediction, offline evaluation, document processing, and bulk embedding generation.

Vertex AI documentation distinguishes batch inference from online inference by the absence of an immediate response requirement.

7.3 GKE Model Serving

Use GKE for inference when you need advanced control:

  • Custom model servers.
  • vLLM, Triton, KServe, Hugging Face Text Generation Inference, JetStream, or custom runtimes.
  • Multi-model routing.
  • Kubernetes-native autoscaling.
  • Model-aware load balancing.
  • Advanced security/networking.
  • Shared platform across many teams.
  • GPU or TPU serving infrastructure.

Google’s GKE AI/ML documentation includes Inference Gateway for model-aware routing and load balancing, GPU and TPU support, Kueue, Ray on GKE, and other AI workload capabilities.

7.4 Cloud Run GPU Inference

Use Cloud Run GPU when you want a simpler serverless inference model with containerized deployment, managed GPU support, and scale-to-zero economics. Google documents Cloud Run GPU support with NVIDIA L4 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell options, one GPU per instance, and no manual driver installation requirement.

Best for:

  • Bursty inference.
  • Internal AI APIs.
  • Small to medium open models.
  • Embedding services.
  • Vision or video processing.
  • Stateless model-serving containers.
  • Teams avoiding Kubernetes operational complexity.

Primary risks:

  • Cold-start and model-loading latency.
  • One-GPU-per-instance constraint.
  • Model size versus startup time.
  • Limited control compared with GKE.
  • Cost impact if minimum instances are configured.
  • Need for careful concurrency tuning.

Google’s Cloud Run GPU best practices emphasize model-loading strategy and concurrent execution optimization.

8. Capacity, Quotas, and Cost Models

Capacity planning is a first-class discipline in AI infrastructure. For high-end GPUs and TPUs, the question is often not only “what is the best accelerator?”, but “can I obtain the required capacity in the right region, with the right topology, for the right duration?”

Google Cloud offers several consumption and capacity models for AI workloads, including on-demand usage, reservations, committed use discounts, Spot, Flex-start, and Dynamic Workload Scheduler-based patterns. Google’s AI Hypercomputer consumption documentation frames these options around workload duration, cost, and access to capacity.

8.1 Common Capacity Models


Model

Best for

Risk

On-demand

Development, experiments, unpredictable usage

Capacity may not be available; higher unit cost

Reservations

Production, guaranteed access, planned training runs

Commitment and planning overhead

Committed use discounts

Predictable long-term usage

Less flexible if workload changes

Spot VMs

Fault-tolerant jobs, batch workloads, non-critical training

Can be preempted

Flex-start / Dynamic Workload Scheduler

Discounted access to high-demand resources for suitable workloads

Allocation is not immediate and runtime is limited

Future/calendar reservations

Planned large training events

Requires forecasting and coordination


Google describes Flex-start VMs as using Dynamic Workload Scheduler to provision discounted high-demand resources such as GPUs, with allocation attempted in a requested timeframe and workloads running for a limited duration. Google’s capacity documentation also distinguishes Flex-start and Spot from reservation-backed models.

Expert-level capacity planning requires:

  • Region and zone selection.
  • GPU or TPU quota planning.
  • Reservation strategy.
  • Storage locality.
  • Network topology.
  • Training duration and checkpointing strategy.
  • Failure tolerance.
  • Cost attribution.
  • Preemption handling.
  • Business service-level objectives.

9. Networking and Locality

Networking is a major performance factor in distributed AI workloads. Large training jobs depend on communication patterns such as all-reduce, parameter synchronization, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and checkpoint transfer. Poor placement can reduce accelerator utilization even when each individual GPU or TPU is powerful.

Key principles:


Principle

Explanation

Co-locate compute and storage

Keep training data, checkpoints, and model artifacts close to accelerator clusters

Choose regions early

Accelerator availability, quota, storage, and compliance requirements are regional decisions

Minimize cross-region data movement

Cross-region movement can increase latency, cost, and operational complexity

Design for topology

Multi-node training benefits from placement and topology-aware scheduling

Treat networking as part of model performance

Network bottlenecks can directly reduce tokens/sec, images/sec, or samples/sec

Use private connectivity for sensitive workloads

Avoid unnecessary public exposure of data, model endpoints, and control planes


Google’s GKE AI/ML documentation includes topology-aware scheduling for large workloads to minimize communication overhead and improve performance.

10. Security and Governance Foundation

Security for AI/ML infrastructure must cover more than the model endpoint. It includes data ingestion, training data, feature stores, containers, model artifacts, checkpoints, pipelines, service accounts, deployment automation, inference requests, generated outputs, audit logs, and supply-chain dependencies.

Google’s AI/ML security guidance emphasizes a holistic approach across conceptualization, development, deployment, and operations.

10.1 Security Domains for GCP AI/ML


Domain

What to secure

Identity

Users, service accounts, workload identities, pipeline identities, runtime identities

Data

Training data, validation data, prompts, inference outputs, embeddings, checkpoints

Models

Model artifacts, weights, adapters, fine-tuned models, evaluation results

Pipelines

CI/CD, Vertex AI Pipelines, Kubeflow workflows, Dataflow jobs, build systems

Containers

Base images, dependencies, vulnerabilities, signatures, runtime permissions

Networks

Private endpoints, VPC boundaries, service perimeters, ingress/egress rules

Secrets

API keys, database credentials, tokens, model provider keys

Runtime

GKE pods, Cloud Run services, Vertex AI endpoints, Compute Engine VMs

Observability

Logs, traces, metrics, audit trails, sensitive output redaction

Governance

Policy enforcement, lineage, approvals, model risk, compliance evidence


10.2 VPC Service Controls and Data Exfiltration Defense

For sensitive AI/ML workloads, VPC Service Controls are especially important. Google documents VPC Service Controls for Vertex AI as a way to mitigate data exfiltration risks by creating service perimeters around resources such as training data, models, prediction requests, and prediction results. The same documentation notes that Google Cloud APIs are generally reachable from the internet by default but require Identity and Access Management authorization, and that VPC Service Controls can add perimeter-based restrictions.

Security-first baseline:

  • Use least-privilege Identity and Access Management roles.
  • Use dedicated service accounts per workload or pipeline stage.
  • Avoid broad project-level permissions.
  • Use VPC Service Controls for sensitive ML projects.
  • Use private access patterns where possible.
  • Store secrets in Secret Manager, not in code, images, or notebooks.
  • Use Artifact Registry for container images.
  • Scan and harden containers.
  • Use customer-managed encryption keys where required.
  • Enable audit logging and monitoring.
  • Restrict public endpoints.
  • Apply organization policies for guardrails.
  • Use model and prompt protection controls where appropriate.
  • Separate development, staging, and production ML environments.

Google’s model runtime security guidance also references different security capabilities across Vertex AI, Cloud Run, and GKE, including managed isolation, private networking options, Kubernetes policies, and Model Armor integration patterns.

11. Observability and Operations

AI/ML observability has several layers:


Layer

What to monitor

Infrastructure

GPU utilization, GPU memory, TPU utilization, CPU, RAM, disk, network, node health

Training

Loss, accuracy, throughput, step time, checkpoint duration, data loading time

Inference

Latency, throughput, queue depth, error rate, cold starts, model load time, token throughput

Data

Drift, schema changes, missing values, data freshness, feature distribution

Model

Quality metrics, bias/fairness metrics, hallucination rate, evaluation scores

Cost

Accelerator hours, idle time, storage egress, endpoint replicas, pipeline costs

Security

Audit logs, denied requests, unusual access, data exfiltration attempts, container vulnerabilities


Google documents GPU monitoring through the Ops Agent, NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager, and NVIDIA Management Library metrics integrated with Cloud Monitoring.

For MLOps cost attribution, Google Cloud Pipeline Components include support for Vertex AI Pipelines and billing labels that can connect pipeline usage to billing export analysis in BigQuery.

Operational maturity means you can answer:

  • Are accelerators fully utilized?
  • Is the bottleneck compute, memory, storage, network, or preprocessing?
  • How long does checkpointing take?
  • What happens when a Spot VM is preempted?
  • Can the job resume safely?
  • Which team owns the cost?
  • Which model version is deployed?
  • Which data version trained the model?
  • Which service account accessed the training data?
  • Are inference logs leaking sensitive prompts or outputs?
  • Can the deployment be rolled back?

13. Reference Architecture Patterns You Should Master

13.1 Managed ML Platform Pattern

Use when the organization wants standard ML workflows with minimal infrastructure management.

Architecture:

  1. Data in BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
  2. Feature preparation through BigQuery, Dataflow, or Spark.
  3. Training through Vertex AI custom training.
  4. Model registration in Vertex AI Model Registry.
  5. Deployment to Vertex AI Endpoint.
  6. Monitoring through Cloud Monitoring and Vertex AI tooling.
  7. Pipelines through Vertex AI Pipelines.
  8. Security with IAM, VPC Service Controls, private access, encryption, and audit logs.

Best for:

  • Enterprise ML teams.
  • Regulated workloads.
  • Teams prioritizing governance and repeatability.
  • Standard classification, regression, forecasting, ranking, and managed deep learning.

13.2 Kubernetes AI Platform Pattern

Use when the organization wants a custom internal platform for many teams.

Architecture:

  1. GKE private cluster.
  2. Separate namespaces per team or project.
  3. GPU and/or TPU node pools.
  4. Kueue or custom scheduling.
  5. Workload Identity for service account isolation.
  6. Artifact Registry for images.
  7. Cloud Storage, Hyperdisk ML, Managed Lustre, or Parallelstore for data/model storage.
  8. Inference Gateway, KServe, vLLM, Triton, or custom serving stack.
  9. Cloud Monitoring and Logging.
  10. Policy controls, admission controls, network policies, and service mesh where needed.

Best for:

  • Platform engineering teams.
  • Advanced AI product organizations.
  • Multi-tenant GPU/TPU sharing.
  • Custom inference platforms.
  • Teams needing open-source ML infrastructure.

Google’s GKE documentation positions GKE for multi-tenant AI platforms, low-latency online inference, large-scale training, and high-performance AI platforms.

13.3 Serverless Inference Pattern

Use when inference is containerized, traffic is variable, and Kubernetes is unnecessary.

Architecture:

  1. Model artifacts in Cloud Storage or embedded in container image for smaller models.
  2. Container image in Artifact Registry.
  3. Cloud Run service with GPU.
  4. Identity-restricted HTTPS endpoint.
  5. Optional minimum instances for latency control.
  6. Cloud Logging and Monitoring.
  7. Secret Manager for configuration.
  8. VPC connector or private access for backend resources.

Best for:

  • Internal tools.
  • Embedding APIs.
  • Lightweight LLM serving.
  • Computer vision inference.
  • Batch-like request processing.
  • Bursty traffic.

Google documents Cloud Run GPU as fully managed, with scale-to-zero behavior, no manual GPU driver installation, and service-level deployment across zones by default.

13.4 Large-Scale Training Pattern

Use for foundation models, very large fine-tuning, or research-scale distributed training.

Architecture:

  1. AI Hypercomputer or accelerator-optimized Compute Engine/GKE infrastructure.
  2. High-end GPUs or TPUs.
  3. Capacity reservations or scheduler-managed capacity.
  4. Topology-aware scheduling.
  5. High-throughput storage such as Managed Lustre, Hyperdisk ML, Cloud Storage FUSE tuning, or Parallelstore.
  6. Distributed framework stack: PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow, XLA, Ray, Slurm, or Kubernetes-native operators.
  7. Frequent checkpointing.
  8. Failure recovery and preemption handling.
  9. Deep observability for accelerator utilization, communication overhead, storage throughput, and training metrics.

Best for:

  • Foundation model pre-training.
  • Large model fine-tuning.
  • Research labs.
  • HPC-style AI workloads.
  • Organizations with specialized ML infrastructure teams.

13.5 Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pattern

Use for enterprise generative AI applications that require grounding model responses in private or domain-specific data.

Architecture:

  1. Source documents in Cloud Storage, BigQuery, databases, or enterprise systems.
  2. Data processing through Dataflow, Spark, Cloud Run jobs, or custom pipelines.
  3. Embedding generation through Vertex AI or custom models.
  4. Vector index in Vertex AI Vector Search.
  5. Retrieval service on Cloud Run, GKE, or Vertex AI-based application stack.
  6. LLM invocation through Vertex AI generative AI APIs or deployed open models.
  7. Security with IAM, VPC Service Controls, data classification, logging controls, and prompt/output protection.

Vertex AI Vector Search is directly relevant here because it supports embedding-based search for generative AI, recommendation, and semantic retrieval workloads.

14. Common Pitfalls

Pitfall 1: Starting with hardware instead of workload requirements

Bad question: “Which GPU should I use?”

Better question: “What model, batch size, precision, latency target, throughput target, framework, storage pattern, and scaling model do I need?”

Pitfall 2: Ignoring quota and regional availability

Accelerator availability and quota can dominate project timelines. GPU and TPU planning must happen early, not after the architecture is designed. Google’s GPU and TPU documentation both emphasize quota and resource planning.

Pitfall 3: Treating Cloud Storage FUSE as a universal POSIX file system

Cloud Storage FUSE is useful, but it needs workload-specific tuning and has object-storage semantics underneath. Google provides separate performance guidance for training, serving, and checkpointing profiles.

Pitfall 4: Underestimating model loading

For inference, model loading can dominate cold-start time and affect autoscaling. This is especially important for Cloud Run GPU and multi-replica GKE inference. Google’s Cloud Run GPU best practices explicitly focus on fast model loading and concurrency optimization.

Pitfall 5: No checkpointing strategy

Large training jobs must assume interruption, failure, or preemption. Storage, checkpoint frequency, checkpoint write throughput, and resume logic should be designed before production training starts.

Pitfall 6: Weak service account design

Many ML platforms accidentally grant broad permissions to notebooks, training jobs, pipelines, and endpoints. A secure design uses dedicated identities per workload stage.

Pitfall 7: Leaking sensitive data through logs

Inference prompts, generated outputs, labels, features, and training examples can contain sensitive data. Logging must be intentionally designed.

Pitfall 8: Overusing managed platforms or overengineering Kubernetes

Vertex AI is often best for managed ML workflows. GKE is often best for platform control. Cloud Run is often best for simple serverless inference. Expert architecture means choosing the lowest operational complexity that still satisfies the workload requirements.

You are becoming competent in GCP AI/ML infrastructure when you can answer these questions without guessing:

  18. What is the rollback strategy?
  19. What is the disaster recovery strategy?

17. Summary

Google Cloud’s AI/ML infrastructure can be understood as a stack:

  • AI Hypercomputer for the highest-performance AI supercomputing patterns.
  • GPUs and TPUs as the main accelerator choices.
  • Vertex AI for managed ML development, training, deployment, inference, and MLOps.
  • GKE for custom AI platforms, multi-tenant ML, advanced scheduling, and high-control inference.
  • Cloud Run for serverless containerized inference with GPU support.
  • Cloud Storage, Hyperdisk ML, Managed Lustre, Parallelstore, BigQuery, Dataflow, Spark, and Vector Search as the data and storage foundation.

  • Monitoring, cost attribution, reservations, Flex-start, Spot, and scheduling as the operational layer.


CI/CD


Artifact Registry

Introduction

Google Cloud Artifact Registry is a fully managed service designed to securely store, manage, and deploy artifacts such as container images, packages, and binaries used in CI/CD pipelines. It supports various artifact formats and integrates seamlessly with Google Cloud services and third-party tools.

1. Key Features

a. Support for Multiple Artifact Formats

  • Container Images: Compatible with Docker and Kubernetes.

  • Language Packages:

    • Java (Maven): Store and manage .jar files.
    • Node.js (npm): Store JavaScript packages.
    • Python (PyPI): Store .whl and .tar.gz files.
    • Go Modules: Manage Go dependencies.
  • Generic Artifacts: Store any custom or unsupported artifacts.

b. Fine-Grained Access Control

  • Integrated with Google Cloud IAM for role-based access.
  • Supports granular permissions at the repository or artifact level.

c. Secure Storage

  • Artifacts are encrypted at rest by default.
  • Scans container images for vulnerabilities using Container Analysis.

d. Regional and Multi-Regional Repositories

  • Store artifacts in specific regions to optimize performance and compliance.
  • Multi-regional setups for high availability.

e. Seamless CI/CD Integration

  • Works with CI/CD tools like Cloud Build, Jenkins, and GitHub Actions.
  • Automatic artifact promotion and deployment in pipelines.

f. Unified Artifact Management

  • Centralized platform for managing multiple artifact types.
  • Simplifies artifact management across teams and projects.

g. Scalability and Reliability

  • Designed to handle high-concurrency workloads.
  • Backed by Google Cloud’s global infrastructure.

a. Container Image Storage

  • Improve build efficiency by caching dependencies locally.

c. CI/CD Pipelines

  • Use Artifact Registry as a source and destination in CI/CD pipelines.
  • Automate testing, artifact promotion, and deployments.

d. Custom Artifacts

  • Store non-standard binaries or build outputs as generic artifacts.
  • Centralized storage for internal tooling and frameworks.

4. Repository Types

Artifact Registry supports different types of repositories:

a. Docker Repository

  • Store container images compatible with Docker CLI.
  • Example: gcr.io/my-project/my-repo.

b. Maven Repository

  • Host Java packages for applications built using Maven or Gradle.

c. npm Repository

  • Manage Node.js packages for JavaScript projects.

d. PyPI Repository

  • Store Python packages for machine learning, data science, or general development.

e. Generic Repository

  • Store arbitrary files or binaries.

5. Integration with CI/CD Pipelines

Artifact Registry integrates seamlessly with CI/CD tools to streamline workflows:

a. Cloud Build

  • Automatically push artifacts to Artifact Registry after builds.

b. Jenkins

Artifact Registry’s pricing is based on the following:

b. Network Egress

c. Requests

  • Costs associated with API calls and artifact management operations.

Example:

8. Best Practices

a. Organize Repositories

  • Use separate repositories for different artifact types or environments (e.g., staging, production).

b. Automate Vulnerability Scanning

  • Regularly scan container images and update dependencies to fix vulnerabilities.

c. Optimize Storage

  • Implement lifecycle policies to automatically delete old or unused artifacts.
  • Example: Remove images older than 90 days or untagged images.

d. Secure Access

  • Use IAM roles to enforce least privilege access.
  • Enable Private Google Access to restrict external network access.

e. Use Artifact Promotion

  • Use staged repositories for artifact promotion (e.g., dev, test, prod).

b. Cloud Build

c. Binary Authorization

  • Enforce signed images before deployment to ensure security.

d. Cloud Logging and Monitoring

  • Track access patterns and repository activity for audits and optimization.

10. Advantages

  • Centralized management for multiple artifact types.
  • Seamless integration with Google Cloud services and third-party tools.
  • Granular security controls with IAM and VPC integration.
  • Fully managed service eliminates infrastructure management overhead.

11. Limitations

By following best practices and leveraging its advanced features, teams can streamline their artifact management and deployment processes while maintaining strong security and compliance.


Cloud Build

Introduction

Google Cloud Build is a fully managed continuous integration (CI) and continuous delivery (CD) service provided by Google Cloud. It allows developers to build, test, and deploy applications at scale in a secure and efficient manner. Cloud Build supports a wide range of environments, languages, and tools, making it a versatile choice for modern DevOps workflows.

Key Features

Fully Managed Service

  • No need to manage infrastructure; Google handles scaling, maintenance, and updates.
  • Seamlessly integrates with Google Cloud and third-party tools.

Custom Build Steps

  • Define custom build steps using Docker containers.
  • Execute scripts, commands, or tools required for your build pipeline.

Support for Multiple Artifact Types

  • Build and deploy container images, binaries, packages, and other artifacts.
  • Push artifacts to Artifact Registry, Container Registry, or third-party repositories.

Flexible Build Configurations

  • Use YAML or JSON files to define build pipelines.
  • Configurations support sequential and parallel steps for optimized workflows.

Language and Framework Agnostic

  • Works with any programming language or framework.
  • Pre-built builder images for common tools like Maven, Gradle, npm, and Python.

Multi-Environment Deployment

  • Deploy applications to multiple environments, including:

    • Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
    • Cloud Run
    • App Engine
    • Compute Engine

Scalable and Fast Builds

  • Automatically scales to handle high-concurrency workloads.
  • Parallel execution of build steps reduces build times.

Secure Builds

  • Use Cloud Build's Worker Pools for private, isolated builds.
  • Build artifacts are encrypted at rest and in transit.

Workflow and Architecture

Cloud Build uses a pipeline-oriented approach to execute builds:

  1. Source Code

    • Integrates with repositories like Cloud Source Repositories, GitHub, or Bitbucket.
    • Automatically triggers builds on code changes.

  2. Build Configuration

    • YAML or JSON files define the build process, including steps and environments.

  3. Execution

    • Steps execute in sequence or in parallel on Cloud Build’s infrastructure.
    • Outputs include logs, artifacts, and build status.

  4. Artifact Storage

    • Artifacts can be stored in Artifact Registry, Cloud Storage, or other destinations.

  5. Deployment

    • Deploy artifacts to GKE, Cloud Run, App Engine, or other platforms.

Integration with CI/CD Pipelines

Cloud Build integrates seamlessly with CI/CD workflows:

Trigger-Based Automation

  • Automatically trigger builds on events like:

    • Code commits.
    • Tag or branch creation.
    • Pull request updates.

Integration with Repositories

Direct integration with:

  • Cloud Source Repositories.
  • GitHub and GitHub Enterprise.
  • Bitbucket Cloud.

Artifact Management

  • Push build outputs to Artifact Registry or Container Registry.
  • Manage dependencies using Cloud Build's pre-configured steps.

Deployment Automation

  • Automate deployments to various environments:

    • Kubernetes (using kubectl).
    • Serverless platforms like Cloud Run and App Engine.
    • Compute Engine using scripts or configuration management tools.

Security Features

IAM-Based Access Control

  • Granular permissions for managing builds, triggers, and artifacts.
  • Predefined roles include Viewer, Editor, and Admin.

Private Worker Pools

  • Run builds in isolated environments with access to private resources.
  • Ideal for sensitive builds requiring restricted network access.

Vulnerability Scanning

  • Scan container images for vulnerabilities.
  • Integrates with Google Cloud’s Container Analysis for detailed reports.

Encryption

  • Data encrypted at rest and in transit.
  • Option to use Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK).

Supported Build Steps

Cloud Build supports a variety of pre-built and custom steps:

Pre-Built Builders

  • Docker: Build and push Docker images.
  • npm: Install dependencies and run scripts.
  • Maven and Gradle: Build Java applications.
  • Python: Manage and test Python packages.
  • kubectl: Deploy to Kubernetes clusters.

Custom Builders

  • Define custom steps using Docker images.
  • Example: Use a custom image for proprietary tools or scripts.

Scripts and Commands

  • Run shell scripts directly in a build step.

Use Cases

Containerized Application Development

  • Build, test, and deploy container images to Kubernetes or Cloud Run.

Multi-Language Build Pipelines

  • Combine steps for multiple programming languages in a single pipeline.

Hybrid Deployment Strategies

  • Deploy artifacts to cloud and on-premises environments.

Compliance and Security Audits

  • Automate vulnerability scanning and compliance checks as part of CI/CD workflows.

Mobile Application Builds

  • Use Cloud Build for building, testing, and deploying Android and iOS applications.

Pricing

Cloud Build pricing is based on build minutes and usage:

Free Tier

  • 120 build minutes per day (on default infrastructure).

Build Minutes

  • Charges for additional build minutes vary by machine type.
  • Standard machines: $0.003 per minute.
  • High-memory or high-CPU machines incur higher costs.

Worker Pools

  • Additional charges apply for private worker pools.

8. Best Practices

  • Use parallel steps to reduce build times.
  • Leverage pre-built builder images to simplify configurations.

b. Secure Your Builds

  • Use private worker pools for sensitive builds.
  • Enforce IAM roles to restrict access to triggers and artifacts.

c. Monitor Build Performance

  • Optimize slow build steps using caching or pre-built artifacts.

d. Integrate Testing

Cloud Deploy

Introduction

Google Cloud Deploy is a fully managed continuous delivery (CD) service provided by Google Cloud. It is designed to automate the release of applications to multiple environments, such as Kubernetes clusters or serverless platforms, while ensuring consistency, reliability, and security throughout the deployment process.

Key Features

Managed Continuous Delivery

  • Automates application delivery pipelines, reducing manual effort.
  • Provides a unified platform for managing deployments across environments.

Multi-Environment Support

  • Supports deployment to multiple environments like staging, testing, and production.
  • Automatically promotes releases between environments based on approval workflows.

Kubernetes-Native

  • Designed for deploying workloads to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and other Kubernetes clusters.
  • Simplifies Kubernetes configuration management using kustomize and helm.

Declarative Pipeline Configuration

  • Pipelines are defined using YAML configuration files.

Approval Workflows

  • Integrates manual or automated approval steps before promoting releases.
  • Ensure compliance with organizational policies.

Rollback Capabilities

  • Easy rollback to previous versions in case of failures or issues.
  • Supports version tracking and history.

Seamless Integration

  • Integrates with Cloud Build for CI/CD workflows.
  • Works with tools like Artifact Registry, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Monitoring.

Secure Deployments

  • Role-based access control (RBAC) using IAM.
  • Support for private networking and secure artifact management.

Key Concepts

Delivery Pipeline

  • Represents the overall application release process.
  • Includes multiple stages and targets (e.g., staging, production).

Targets

  • Environments where the application is deployed.
  • Examples: Kubernetes clusters, GKE, or custom environments.

Releases

  • Represent a version of the application to be deployed.
  • Includes configuration files, container images, or other artifacts.

Rollouts

  • Execution of deploying a release to a specific target.
  • Tracks deployment progress, status, and results.

Approval Policies

  • Define manual or automated steps for promoting releases.

Workflow

  1. Define a Delivery Pipeline

    • Create a YAML file describing environments and deployment configurations.

  2. Trigger a Release

    • Create a new release when application code or artifacts are ready for deployment.

  3. Deploy to Targets

    • Deploy to staging, test, or production environments as defined in the pipeline.

  4. Monitor Progress

    • View deployment status and logs in the Google Cloud Console.

  5. Promote or Roll Back

    • Promote releases to the next environment or roll back if necessary.

Supported Deployment Platforms

Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)

  • Native support for Kubernetes clusters.
  • Uses Kubernetes configurations like kustomize and helm.

Anthos

  • Deploy workloads to on-premises or multi-cloud Kubernetes clusters.

Custom Kubernetes Clusters

  • Support for non-Google Kubernetes clusters.

Integration with Google Cloud Services

Cloud Build

  • Automate build, test, and deploy workflows.
  • Build and package artifacts before deploying with Cloud Deploy.

Artifact Registry

  • Store and manage container images and deployment artifacts.

Cloud Monitoring

  • Monitor deployment progress and health.
  • Set up alerts for deployment failures or performance issues.

Cloud Logging

  • Centralized logging for troubleshooting deployment issues.

Use Cases

Application Modernization

  • Automate delivery of containerized applications to Kubernetes clusters.

Multi-Environment Deployments

  • Manage staging, testing, and production environments with approval gates.

Progressive Delivery

  • Implement deployment strategies like canary releases and blue/green deployments.

Disaster Recovery

  • Quickly roll back to previous releases in case of issues.

Compliance and Governance

  • Ensure deployment processes comply with organizational standards using approval workflows.

Cloud Deploy’s pricing is usage-based, with costs determined by:

Active Deployments

  • Charged per active deployment.
  • Free tier includes a certain number of active deployments.

Integrations

  • Charges for related services like Cloud Build and Artifact Registry.

Best Practices

Pipeline Design

  • Use separate pipelines for distinct applications or workflows.
  • Include all necessary environments (e.g., dev, staging, production) in the pipeline.

Secure Deployments

  • Use IAM roles to restrict access to pipelines and deployments.
  • Enable private networking to secure communication between services.

Automate Testing

  • Integrate automated tests into pipelines before promoting releases.

Monitor Rollouts

  • Use Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging to track deployment health.
  • Set alerts for deployment errors or anomalies.

Use Version Control

  • Store pipeline configurations and deployment manifests in version control systems like Git.

Advantages

  • Fully managed service reduces operational overhead.
  • Simplifies multi-environment deployments.
  • Tight integration with Google Cloud services and Kubernetes.
  • Supports progressive delivery strategies like canary and blue/green deployments.
  • Comprehensive logging and monitoring for better visibility and troubleshooting.

Limitations
