Kubernetes


Security


Binary Authorization

What it is?

Architecture

The Binary Authorization and Container Analysis APIs are based upon the open-source projects Grafeas and Kritis.

  • Grafeas defines an API spec for managing metadata about software resources, such as container images, Virtual Machine (VM) images, JAR files, and scripts. You can use Grafeas to define and aggregate information about your project’s components.
  • Kritis defines an API for ensuring a deployment is prevented unless the artifact (container image) is conformant to central policy and optionally has the necessary attestations present.

In a simplified container deployment pipeline such as this:

The container goes through at least 4 steps:

  1. The source code for creating the container is stored in source control.
  2. Upon committing a change to source control, the container is built and tested.
  3. If the build and test steps are completed, the container image artifact is then placed in a central container registry, ready for deployment.
  4. When a deployment of that container version is submitted to the Kubernetes API, the container runtime will pull that container image from the container registry and run it as a pod.


In a container build pipeline, there are opportunities to inject additional processes to signify or "attest" that each step was completed successfully. Examples include running unit tests, source control analysis checks, licensing verification, vulnerability analysis, and more. Each step could be given the power or "attestation authority" to sign for that step being completed. An "attestation authority" is a human or system with the correct PGP key and the ability to register that "attestation" with the Container Analysis API.


By using separate PGP keys for each step, each attestation step could be performed by different humans, systems, or build steps in the pipeline (a). Each PGP key is associated with an "attestation note" which is stored in the Container Analysis API. When a build step "signs" an image, a snippet of JSON metadata about that image is signed via PGP and that signed snippet is submitted to the API as a "note occurrence".

(b).Once the container image has been built and the necessary attestations have been stored centrally, they are available for being queried as a part of a policy decision process. In this case, a Kubernetes Admission Controller, upon receiving an API request to create or update a Pod:

  1. Send a WebHook to the Binary Authorization API for a policy decision.
  2. The Binary Authorization policy is then consulted.
  3. If necessary, the Container Analysis API is also queried for the necessary attestation occurrences.
  4. If the container image conforms to the policy, it is allowed to run.
  5. If the container image fails to meet the policy, an error is presented to the API client with a message describing why it was prevented.


Legacy Compute Engine Metadata API Endpoint

Disabling the Legacy Compute Engine Metadata API Endpoint

The Compute Engine Metadata API is used by Google Cloud instances (VMs and Kubernetes nodes) to retrieve instance-specific information, such as instance metadata, service account tokens, and other sensitive information. By default, this API can be accessed using both http://metadata.google.internal and http://metadata/computeMetadata/v1beta1.

Why Disable the Legacy Metadata API Endpoint?

  • The v1beta1 metadata endpoint does not enforce the required Metadata-Flavor: Google header, which makes it susceptible to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.
  • Attackers can exploit applications that make HTTP calls to untrusted destinations to access sensitive metadata, such as service account credentials.

How to Disable the Legacy Metadata API Endpoint? To mitigate this vulnerability:

  • Specify a custom metadata key and value during the creation of Compute Engine instances or Kubernetes nodes to disable the v1beta1 metadata endpoint.

For example:

bash
Copy code
gcloud compute instances create instance-name \
  --metadata enable-legacy-endpoint=false

When this metadata key is set to false, requests to http://metadata/computeMetadata/v1beta1 will no longer be available, limiting the attack surface for SSRF-based threats.


Metadata Concealment

What is Metadata Concealment? Metadata concealment introduces an additional security layer by installing a lightweight proxy on each node in the Kubernetes cluster. This proxy intercepts requests made to the Metadata API and filters access to sensitive metadata endpoints, such as those used to retrieve:

  • Service account tokens
  • Project metadata
  • Instance metadata

Why Enable Metadata Concealment?

  • Protects against unauthorized access to sensitive metadata by preventing direct access to critical endpoints.
  • Mitigates potential container breakout attacks, where a compromised pod attempts to access the node's metadata server to escalate privileges or steal credentials.

How to Enable Metadata Concealment? During cluster or node pool creation, pass an additional configuration flag:

bash
Copy code
gcloud container clusters create cluster-name \
  --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA_SERVER

Alternatively, for existing clusters, update the node pool:

bash
Copy code
gcloud container node-pools update node-pool-name \
  --cluster=cluster-name \
  --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA_SERVER

This configuration ensures that the metadata server proxy is deployed, providing restricted and secure access to metadata endpoints for pods while protecting sensitive data.



Pod Security Admission (PSA)

What is Pod Security Admission? Pod Security Admission (PSA) is a built-in Kubernetes feature that enforces Pod Security Standards (PSS) at the namespace level. PSS defines three security profiles:

  • Privileged: Allows broad access, suitable only for trusted workloads.
  • Baseline: Offers a minimal set of security settings suitable for most workloads.
  • Restricted: Provides the highest level of security by enforcing strict isolation and minimizing privileges.

Why Enable PSA?

  • It ensures that pods conform to specific security standards, reducing the risk of misconfigurations and vulnerabilities.
  • PSA replaces the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) and integrates seamlessly with Kubernetes admission control.

How to Enable PSA? To enable PSA, modify the PodSecurity admission controller in the API server configuration. This can be done during cluster creation or by updating the cluster settings.

  1. Enable PSA Controller:

    • For GKE, ensure your cluster is running on a version that supports PSA (Kubernetes v1.25+).
    • During cluster creation:
  bash
  Copy code
  gcloud container clusters create cluster-name \
    --enable-pod-security-policy

  1. Apply Namespace Labels for Security Profiles:

    • Add labels to namespaces to enforce specific security profiles.
bash
Copy code
kubectl label namespace <namespace-name> \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<profile>

  1. Examples of valid profiles:

    • privileged
    • baseline
    • restricted
  2. To apply the restricted profile:
bash
Copy code
kubectl label namespace my-namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

Key Benefits of PSA:

  • Ensures all pods in a namespace adhere to a predefined security standard.
  • Helps prevent deployment of insecure or misconfigured workloads.
  • Enforces a consistent security posture across namespaces and workloads.


Optimization

Introduction

Optimizing your GKE clusters is essential to:

  • Ensure reliable application performance under variable workloads.
  • Minimize cloud resource waste and costs.
  • Enhance resilience, elasticity, and scalability.
  • Automatically adapt to usage spikes without manual intervention.

Key areas of GKE optimization include:

  • Workload autoscaling (pods, containers).
  • Cluster and node pool autoscaling.
  • Over-provisioning for burst tolerance.
  • Resource requests and limits tuning.
  • Preemptible nodes and spot instances usage.
  • Monitoring and observability for cost/performance balance.

GKE Autoscaling mechanisms

Google Kubernetes Engine supports three major autoscaling layers:

1. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

What it is: Automatically scales the number of pod replicas in a Deployment, StatefulSet, or ReplicaSet based on observed metrics.

How it works:

  • Scales pods horizontally (adds/removes replicas).
  • Monitors CPU, memory, or custom metrics via the Kubernetes Metrics Server or Cloud Monitoring.
  • You define minReplicas, maxReplicas, and target utilization.

Best Practices:

  • Always set resource requests (cpu, memory) for containers — HPA depends on them.
  • Use custom metrics for better scaling granularity (e.g., QPS, latency).
  • Combine HPA with Cluster Autoscaler for better elasticity.

2. Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)

What it is: Automatically adjusts resource requests (cpu, memory) for containers based on usage patterns.

How it works:

  • Suggests, applies, or enforces optimal resource requests.
  • Can work in recommendation-only, auto, or initial mode.
  • Useful for workloads with stable usage patterns (e.g., batch jobs, ML training).

Limitations:

  • Restart of pods is required for applying changes.
  • Should not be used with HPA (unless using recommendation mode only).

Best Practices:

  • Use recommendation mode in dev to observe suggested values before applying.
  • Use VPA for cron jobs, stateful apps, or background services with predictable workloads.

3. Cluster Autoscaler

What it is: Automatically adds or removes nodes from the entire cluster based on pending pods and underutilized nodes.

How it works:

  • If pods cannot be scheduled due to lack of resources → adds nodes.
  • If nodes are underutilized → removes them (after a grace period).
  • Works with both zonal and regional GKE clusters.

Best Practices:

  • Enable auto-repair and auto-upgrade for resilience.
  • Tag workloads with priorityClasses to influence scheduling decisions.
  • Set taints/tolerations or affinity/anti-affinity to control placement.

4. Node Auto-Provisioning (NAP)

What it is: Allows GKE to automatically create new node pools when existing pools don’t meet pod requirements.

How it works:

  • Works with Cluster Autoscaler.
  • Supports selecting machine types, disk sizes, zones, and GPU if needed.
  • Creates ephemeral node pools for very specific workloads.

Best Practices:

  • Set resource requests correctly to help autoscaler pick the right machine type.
  • Avoid hardcoding too many constraints that limit scheduling flexibility.

5. Node Pool Autoscaling

What it is: Automatically scales the size of a specific node pool within defined limits.

How it works:

  • Scales up/down the number of nodes in that node pool.
  • Configured per node pool, with --enable-autoscaling, --min-nodes, --max-nodes.

Best Practices:

  • Use separate pools for bursty, GPU, or specialized workloads.
  • Customize each pool with different instance types for resource fitting.

Over-provisioning in GKE

Over-provisioning refers to intentionally reserving excess capacity to absorb workload spikes and ensure low-latency responsiveness.

What it is

  • HPA only reacts after utilization rises.
  • Cluster Autoscaler takes 1–2 minutes to provision new nodes.
  • Over-provisioning adds buffer capacity for fast scaling.

Implementation

1. Idle Pods Approach

  • Deploy a low-priority pod that requests CPU/memory, but performs no work.
  • If a real workload comes in, the over-provisioning pod gets evicted.
  • These are often called "pause pods" or "buffer pods".

2. Dedicated Over-Provision Node Pool

  • Create a small node pool for fast provisioning of bursty workloads.
  • Can use spot/preemptible nodes for cost savings.

Cost optimization tips


Technique

Purpose

Use HPA + Cluster Autoscaler

Elastic scaling of workloads and infra

Use preemptible VMs

70-80% cost savings for stateless/batch

Enable VPA (recommendation)

Fine-tune memory/CPU usage

Label and tag workloads

For cost allocation and auditing

Use GKE Autopilot (optional)

Fully managed infra with automatic tuning

Offload heavy jobs to Cloud Run or Cloud Functions

For event-driven or burst workloads

Monitoring and Observability

  • Use Cloud Monitoring (formerly Stackdriver) with Kubernetes Engine Monitoring enabled.

  • Visualize:

    • Pod CPU/memory usage.
    • Node pool utilization.
    • Pending pods.
    • Autoscaler events.

  • Set up alerts:

    • When nodes are saturated.
    • When pods are pending > N seconds.
    • Cost anomalies or budget thresholds.

Best practices

  • Always define resource requests and limits.
  • Use HPA for dynamic horizontal scaling of stateless workloads.
  • Use VPA for memory-bound or predictable apps (non-HPA).
  • Combine HPA + Cluster Autoscaler for workload-infra coordination.
  • Implement over-provisioning to reduce cold start latency.
  • Tag workloads for cost allocation and IAM policies.
  • Monitor everything and use Cloud Monitoring dashboards.
  • Evaluate GKE Autopilot if you prefer a hands-off model with SLA-based optimization.


Networking

Overview

In Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), networking underpins how clusters communicate internally (pods ↔ services), externally (internet ↔ pods), and with hybrid or multi-cloud systems. GKE abstracts much of the complexity, but understanding how it works under the hood is critical for performance, scalability, security, and observability.

Key areas:

  • Pod-to-Pod Communication
  • Service Networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer)
  • Ingress and Traffic Routing
  • Google Cloud Network Integration
  • Firewall Rules and Security
  • IP Management & VPC-native clusters
  • Instance Groups vs. Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs)
  • iptables, kube-proxy, and IP masquerading

Pod networking model

Kubernetes Model

  • Every Pod gets its own unique IP address.
  • Containers inside the Pod share the localhost network (127.0.0.1).
  • No NAT between Pods, even across nodes.

GKE Implementation

  • VPC-native clusters (default): Pods get IPs from VPC subnet ranges using alias IPs.
  • Non-VPC-native (routes-based): Deprecated. Uses custom routes and IP masquerading.

Alias IPs

  • Each node is assigned a secondary IP range for Pods and Services.
  • Better performance and isolation.
  • Enables fine-grained firewall rules, observability, and security.

Pod-to-Pod communication

  • All Pods can communicate with each other (flat network) via their IPs.
  • Communication can span nodes without NAT.
  • Uses Google Cloud's internal SDN instead of traditional overlay networks (e.g., Flannel, Calico).

Services and kube-proxy

kube-proxy

  • Manages networking rules using iptables or IPVS.
  • Redirects traffic from Services to backend Pods (based on label selectors).
  • Manages ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer logic.

Service Types

  • ClusterIP (default):

    • Internal-only IP.
    • Exposes the Service on a virtual IP accessible within the cluster.

  • NodePort:

    • Opens the same port on all nodes.
    • External traffic hits any node’s IP on the NodePort and is forwarded to a Pod.

  • LoadBalancer:

    • Creates a Google Cloud external Load Balancer (L4 TCP/UDP).
    • Forwards to the Service’s NodePort across the cluster.

  • Headless Service (ClusterIP: None):

    • Returns Pod IPs directly.
    • Used with StatefulSets or DNS-based service discovery.

Ingress (HTTP/S L7 Load Balancing)

Ingress Resource

  • Defines rules for routing HTTP(S) traffic to Services.
  • GKE supports Ingress using Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer (L7).

GKE Ingress Controller

  • Deploys:

    • Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer
    • Managed SSL certificates
    • Backend Services → Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs)

Benefits

  • Global load balancing (multi-region)
  • URL/path-based routing
  • SSL termination
  • Autoscaling & health checks

Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs)

  • NEGs register Pods as endpoints to the Load Balancer.

  • Two types:

    • Zonal NEGs: used for GKE Services with Ingress
    • Serverless NEGs: for Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, etc.

Use Case in GKE:

  • When you expose a Pod via Ingress, it uses Container-native Load Balancing with NEGs, giving direct Pod-level routing instead of NodePort → kube-proxy.

Instance Groups vs. NEGs

  • Instance Groups:

    • Used by default in GKE L4 load balancing (NodePort + LoadBalancer).
    • Forward traffic to Node IPs, then kube-proxy routes to Pods.
    • Less efficient due to extra hops.

  • NEGs:

    • Used with L7 load balancing (Ingress).
    • More efficient — direct Pod-level routing.

iptables & IP Masquerading

iptables

  • kube-proxy installs NAT rules.

  • Used for:

    • Service load balancing (ClusterIP).
    • Redirecting traffic to Pod IPs.

IP Masquerading

  • Controls whether Pod traffic to other destinations is SNAT’d (source NAT).
  • GKE supports fine-grained IP masquerade agent for better performance.

Firewall rules

  • GCP uses VPC firewall rules, not iptables, to restrict traffic.
  • In VPC-native mode, each Pod IP can be filtered by firewall rules.
  • Important for Zero Trust, service segmentation, and security audits.

Internal Load Balancer

  • GKE supports internal L4 Load Balancers (ILB) using LoadBalancer type + annotation.
  • ILBs provide internal-only access to services for hybrid/private use cases.
  • Combined with NEGs for Pod-level routing.

Network Policy

  • Implemented using Calico (GKE default) or other CNI plugins.
  • Define Pod-level firewall rules (like iptables on steroids).

  • Policies can:

    • Restrict Pod ↔ Pod communication.
    • Control egress traffic to the internet or internal systems.
  • Required for zero-trust cluster designs.

DNS

  • GKE uses CoreDNS or kube-dns.

  • DNS records are auto-generated for Services and Pods.

    • e.g., myservice.mynamespace.svc.cluster.local
  • Integration with Cloud DNS for hybrid use cases.

Best practices


Practice

Why it Matters

Use VPC-native clusters

Required for Alias IPs, granular firewalling, better scalability

Enable Container-native Load Balancing

Improves efficiency, performance, and reduces hops

Use Network Policies

Enforce security between workloads

Disable Legacy Metadata API

Prevent privilege escalation attacks

Use NEGs with Ingress

Achieve Pod-level load balancing

Monitor with VPC Flow Logs

Gain visibility into network traffic

Use Internal Load Balancers for microservices

Reduces attack surface and secures private service-to-service communication

Traffic flow example

External User → Pod via Ingress

User hits

  1. Example app address
  2. Request routed to Google Global Load Balancer
  3. LB uses URL map → Backend service (NEG).
  4. Traffic sent directly to Pod IP via NEG
  5. Pod handles request and responds via same path

Pod → Internet

  1. Pod makes outbound HTTP request
  2. If masquerading is on, source IP is changed to node IP
  3. Traffic goes through GCP NAT gateway or Cloud NAT if configured

Summary

GKE networking is built on Google Cloud’s scalable SDN, providing a secure, performant, and manageable environment with:

  • Native integration with Cloud Load Balancing
  • Support for Ingress/NEGs for direct routing
  • IP-based and name-based service discovery
  • Advanced network policy control
  • Seamless firewall rule application via alias IPs

Understanding these internals is essential for designing secure, scalable, and high-performing Kubernetes architectures in GKE.


GKE Fleet

What it is?

GKE Fleet is Google Cloud’s centralized, logical management layer for multiple Kubernetes clusters, enabling uniform governance, security, observability, and application lifecycle management across clusters—regardless of where they run.

A Fleet is not a new cluster type.

It is a control abstraction that groups multiple Kubernetes clusters into a single administrative domain.

GKE Fleet is built on Google Kubernetes Engine Hub, which acts as the control plane for fleet-level services.

Primary Goals

  • Enable multi-cluster operations by default
  • Enforce consistent security posture
  • Centralize policy, identity, and observability
  • Reduce operational complexity at scale
  • Support hybrid and multi-cloud architectures

Importance

As Kubernetes usage matures, organizations inevitably move from:

  • single cluster → multiple clusters
  • single environment → multi-environment
  • single region → multi-region
  • cloud-only → hybrid / edge

This introduces challenges:

  • Fragmented security policies
  • Inconsistent configuration drift
  • Difficult identity and access management
  • No unified observability
  • Manual per-cluster operations

GKE Fleet solves this by shifting management “up” from cluster-level to fleet-level.

Core Architecture Overview

High-Level Architecture

A GKE Fleet consists of:

  1. Fleet Host Project
  2. Fleet Member Clusters
  3. GKE Hub
  4. Fleet-level Services
┌───────────────────────────┐
│     Fleet Host Project    │
│                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐ │
│  │      GKE Hub        │ │
│  │  (Fleet Control)   │ │
│  └─────────────────────┘ │
│     ▲        ▲        ▲  │
└─────┼────────┼────────┼──┘
      │        │        │
┌─────┴───┐ ┌──┴────┐ ┌─┴─────┐
│ Cluster │ │Cluster│ │Cluster│
│   A     │ │   B    │ │   C   │
└─────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘

Key Principle

Clusters remain autonomous, but fleet services observe, secure, and govern them centrally.

Fleet Host Project

The Fleet Host Project is a dedicated Google Cloud project that owns:

  • GKE Hub
  • Fleet configuration
  • Fleet-wide services and APIs

Best Practices

  • Do not run workloads in the fleet host project
  • Restrict IAM access strictly
  • Treat it as control-plane infrastructure
  • Enable Audit Logs + Security Command Center

Fleet Membership (Cluster Registration)

Clusters become fleet members by being registered with GKE Hub.

Supported Cluster Types

  • GKE (Standard / Autopilot)
  • GKE on-prem (Anthos)
  • EKS (AWS)
  • AKS (Azure)
  • Any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster

Registration Concept

  • Each cluster installs a GKE Hub agent
  • Secure channel established to GKE Hub
  • Metadata and health are continuously reported

Core Fleet Capabilities

Fleet Identity (Unified IAM)

Fleet enables identity federation across clusters.

Key features:

  • Google IAM ↔ Kubernetes RBAC mapping
  • Centralized access control
  • Workload Identity Federation
  • No static kubeconfig sprawl

Security impact:

  • Strong Zero Trust alignment
  • Reduced credential leakage
  • Central revocation

Fleet Security Posture

Fleet provides policy-driven security enforcement:

Policy Controller (OPA / Gatekeeper)

  • Enforce CIS Benchmarks
  • Block insecure workloads
  • Validate images, namespaces, labels

Security Signals

  • Configuration drift detection
  • Misconfiguration alerts
  • Compliance status visibility

Standards alignment:

  • NIST SP 800-53
  • CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
  • ISO 27001
  • OWASP Kubernetes Top 10

Fleet Observability

Fleet introduces multi-cluster observability:

  • Central metrics aggregation
  • Central logging pipelines
  • Distributed tracing across clusters
  • Unified dashboards

This eliminates:

  • Per-cluster monitoring silos
  • Inconsistent telemetry formats
  • Manual correlation during incidents

Fleet Networking (Multi-Cluster)

Fleet supports multi-cluster networking patterns:

  • Service discovery across clusters
  • Cross-cluster service mesh
  • Failover-aware routing
  • Traffic locality control

Often paired with:

  • Anthos Service Mesh (Istio-based)
  • Global Load Balancing

Fleet Configuration Management

Fleet allows declarative configuration at scale:

  • GitOps-style config sync
  • Fleet-wide baselines
  • Environment overlays
  • Drift detection

This enables:

  • Immutable infrastructure
  • Reproducible environments
  • Safe progressive rollouts

Fleet vs Single-Cluster GKE


Aspect

Single Cluster

GKE Fleet

Scope

Organization-wide

IAM

Per cluster

Centralized

Policies

Local

Global

Observability

Fragmented

Unified

Security

Reactive

Preventive

Scalability

Limited

Fleet and DevSecOps

GKE Fleet is DevSecOps-native.

CI/CD Integration

  • Policy checks before deploy
  • Fleet-aware rollouts
  • Environment promotion via Git
  • Multi-cluster canary deployments

Supply Chain Security

  • Image provenance enforcement
  • Binary Authorization
  • SBOM validation
  • Runtime policy enforcement

Common Use Cases

Enterprise Platforms

  • Multiple product teams
  • Shared security requirements
  • Strong compliance needs

SaaS at Scale

  • Regional isolation
  • High availability
  • Traffic locality

Hybrid / Edge

  • On-prem + cloud
  • Store/Factory/Edge clusters
  • Central governance with local execution

Common pitfalls

  • Treating Fleet as “just metadata”
  • No separation of fleet host project
  • Over-granting IAM permissions
  • Ignoring GitOps principles
  • Mixing cluster-level and fleet-level concerns

Design Principles for GKE Fleet

  1. Fleet-first thinking
  2. Policy over convention
  3. Identity before networking
  4. Declarative over imperative
  5. Security by default
  6. Observability as a baseline

Summary

GKE Fleet is:

  • A strategic control plane, not a feature
  • Essential for production-grade Kubernetes at scale
  • The foundation for secure, compliant, multi-cluster platforms
  • A key enabler of Zero Trust and DevSecOps

If you want to operate Kubernetes professionally, Fleet is non-negotiable.

GKE Hub

Definition and Purpose

GKE Hub is the central control plane component of GKE Fleet, responsible for:

  • Registering clusters
  • Maintaining cluster state and metadata
  • Enabling fleet-level services (security, policy, identity, observability)

It acts as a control-plane abstraction layer over distributed Kubernetes clusters, allowing Google Cloud to:

  • Treat multiple clusters as a single logical system
  • Apply centralized governance and security policies
  • Provide uniform APIs across heterogeneous environments
In simple terms:
GKE Hub = control plane for multi-cluster Kubernetes operations

Core Responsibilities

GKE Hub is responsible for:

Cluster Registration & Lifecycle

  • Onboarding clusters into a fleet
  • Maintaining cluster identity
  • Tracking health and connectivity

Metadata Management

  • Cluster labels, attributes, capabilities
  • Version, region, environment classification
  • Policy applicability context

Service Enablement Layer

GKE Hub enables:

  • Policy Controller
  • Config Sync
  • Service Mesh
  • Multi-cluster services
  • Observability integrations

Secure Communication Channel

  • Establishes trusted control channel between clusters and Google Cloud
  • Uses authenticated agents
  • Ensures encrypted communication

Architecture Overview

Logical Architecture

                 Google Cloud Control Plane
                         │
                ┌────────▼────────┐
                │     GKE Hub     │
                │ (Fleet Control) │
                └────────┬────────┘
                         │
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       │                 │                 │
┌──────▼──────┐  ┌───────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼──────┐
│  Cluster A  │  │  Cluster B   │  │  Cluster C  │
│ (GKE/EKS/…) │  │              │  │             │
└──────┬──────┘  └───────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘
       │                 │                 │
       ▼                 ▼                 ▼
  Connect Agent     Connect Agent     Connect Agent

Key Components

Connect Agent

The Connect Agent is a lightweight in-cluster component installed during registration.

Responsibilities:

  • Maintains connection to GKE Hub
  • Authenticates cluster identity
  • Streams metadata and health
  • Receives configuration and instructions

Security Properties:

  • Uses mutual TLS (mTLS)
  • Identity bound to Google IAM
  • Runs with minimal privileges (should be enforced)

Membership Resource

Each registered cluster is represented as a Membership resource in GKE Hub.

Contains:

  • Cluster identity
  • Endpoint metadata
  • Labels (env, region, team, etc.)
  • State (healthy, degraded, disconnected)

This is the source of truth for fleet topology.

Feature APIs

GKE Hub exposes Feature APIs, which enable fleet services:

Examples:

  • configmanagement.googleapis.com → Config Sync
  • policycontroller.googleapis.com → OPA/Gatekeeper
  • servicemesh.googleapis.com → Anthos Service Mesh
  • multiclusterservicediscovery.googleapis.com

Each feature:

  • Is enabled at fleet level
  • Is enforced at cluster level via agents

Cluster Registration Flow (Detailed)

Step-by-step

    • Cluster Preparation Enable required APIs
    • Configure IAM roles
    • Register Command Execution Using gcloud container fleet memberships register
    • Connect Agent Deployment Installed into cluster (usually gke-connect namespace)
    • Identity Binding Cluster associated with Google IAM service account
    • Secure Channel Establishment Agent connects to GKE Hub over mTLS
    • Membership Creation Cluster appears in Fleet
    • Feature Enablement Fleet services can now target the cluster

Identity and Authentication Model

GKE Hub integrates deeply with Google Cloud IAM.

Identity Layers

    • Cluster Identity Represented in GKE Hub
    • Bound to IAM service account
    • User Identity IAM users/groups
    • Federated identities
    • Workload Identity Kubernetes Service Accounts mapped to IAM

Security Model (Zero Trust Alignment)

  • No implicit trust between clusters

  • Every interaction is:

    • Authenticated
    • Authorized
    • Audited

This aligns with:

  • NIST Zero Trust Architecture
  • Google BeyondCorp principles

Communication Model

Outbound-Only Connectivity

Clusters initiate connection to GKE Hub:

  • No inbound firewall exposure required

  • Works in:

    • Private clusters
    • On-prem environments
    • Restricted networks

Transport Security

  • TLS encryption
  • Certificate-based authentication
  • Rotating credentials

GKE Hub Features

Policy Controller Integration

  • Hub pushes constraints to clusters
  • Enforcement happens locally
  • Violations reported centrally

Config Sync

  • GitOps engine
  • Hub coordinates repo sync targets
  • Cluster agents enforce state

Service Mesh Integration

  • Hub manages mesh topology
  • Certificates, identities, policies distributed centrally

Multi-Cluster Services

  • Hub maintains service registry
  • Enables cross-cluster discovery

DevSecOps Integration

CI/CD Pipeline Integration

Typical flow:

Git → CI Pipeline → Artifact Registry → Deploy
                     ↓
             Policy Validation (Hub)
                     ↓
           Multi-cluster rollout

Hub enables:

  • Pre-deployment policy validation
  • Consistent rollout across clusters
  • Environment segmentation (dev/staging/prod)

Security Considerations

Least Privilege

  • Restrict Connect Agent permissions

  • Limit IAM roles:

    • roles/gkehub.admin only for platform team
    • Avoid broad project-level roles

Network Security

  • Enforce egress controls
  • Monitor outbound connections
  • Use VPC Service Controls if applicable

Supply Chain Security

  • Ensure trusted images for:

    • Connect Agent
    • Fleet components

  • Use:

    • Binary Authorization
    • Image signing (SLSA, Cosign)

Audit and Monitoring

  • Enable:

    • Cloud Audit Logs
    • Security Command Center

  • Track:

    • Cluster registrations
    • Feature enablement
    • Policy violations

Common pitfalls

Operational

  • Treating Hub as optional (it becomes mandatory at scale)
  • Poor labeling strategy → no segmentation
  • Mixing environments without isolation

Security

  • Over-permissive IAM
  • Ignoring agent hardening
  • No audit logging

Architecture

  • Using Hub without GitOps
  • No policy enforcement baseline
  • Ignoring multi-cluster networking strategy

Best Practices

Architecture

  • Dedicated Fleet Host Project

  • Strong labeling strategy:

    • env=prod/dev
    • region=eu-west
    • team=payments

Security

  • Enforce OPA policies early
  • Use Workload Identity everywhere
  • Avoid static credentials

Operations

  • GitOps-first approach
  • Automate cluster registration
  • Standardize cluster baselines

Comparison with Alternatives

GKE Hub

DIY Multi-Cluster

Identity

Centralized

Fragmented

Policy

Unified

Per cluster

Observability

Integrated

Security

Summary

GKE Hub is the foundation of Fleet.

It provides:

  • Centralized control
  • Secure cluster connectivity
  • Unified identity and policy enforcement
  • Multi-cluster orchestration capabilities

Without GKE Hub:

  • Fleet does not exist
  • Multi-cluster becomes operationally expensive
  • Security posture degrades rapidly


Components


Policy Controller (OPA / Gatekeeper)

What it is?

Policy Controller is a managed policy enforcement service in GKE built on:

  • Open Policy Agent (OPA) – general-purpose policy engine
  • OPA Gatekeeper (Gatekeeper) – Kubernetes-native enforcement layer

It enables declarative, policy-as-code governance across clusters in a GKE Fleet.

Purpose

The core objective is:

Prevent insecure, non-compliant, or misconfigured resources from being deployed into Kubernetes clusters.

This is achieved via:

  • Admission control (real-time enforcement)
  • Continuous audit (drift detection)
  • Centralized policy distribution (via Fleet)

Importance

Without Policy Controller:

  • Security is reactive (detect after deployment)
  • Configuration drift is uncontrolled
  • Compliance is manual and error-prone

With Policy Controller:

  • Security becomes preventive
  • Compliance becomes automated
  • Policies become version-controlled artifacts

This aligns with:

  • NIST SP 800-53 (CM, AC controls)
  • CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
  • OWASP Kubernetes Top 10 (misconfiguration prevention)

Architecture

High-Level Flow

User → kubectl apply → Kubernetes API Server
                      ↓
              Admission Controller
                      ↓
              Gatekeeper Webhook
                      ↓
                 OPA Engine
                      ↓
         ALLOW / DENY / MUTATE (if enabled)

Key Components

Admission Webhook

  • Intercepts API requests
  • Validates resources before persistence
  • Enforces fail-fast security

OPA Engine

  • Evaluates policies written in Rego
  • Stateless, deterministic evaluation

ConstraintTemplates

  • Define reusable policy logic
  • Written in Rego
  • Equivalent to “policy classes”

Constraints

  • Instantiate templates with parameters
  • Define actual enforcement rules

Audit Controller

  • Scans existing resources
  • Detects violations post-deployment

Policy Lifecycle

Step-by-step

  1. Define policy logic → ConstraintTemplate
  2. Apply policy instance → Constraint
  3. Admission webhook enforces policy
  4. Audit controller scans existing resources
  5. Violations are reported centrally (Fleet)

Rego Language

Rego is a declarative policy language.

Key Concepts:

  • Input = Kubernetes resource
  • Output = allow/deny decision
  • Rules are evaluated as logic expressions

Example – Block privileged containers

package k8sblockprivileged

violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  input.review.object.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged == true
  msg := "Privileged containers are not allowed"
}

Example Policies (Practical)

Enforce Non-Root Containers

apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sPSPNonRootUser
metadata:
  name: require-non-root
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Pod"]

Require Resource Limits

violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
  not container.resources.limits.cpu
  msg := "CPU limits must be defined"
}

Restrict Image Registries

violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  image := input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image
  not startswith(image, "gcr.io/your-project/")
  msg := "Only approved registries are allowed"
}

Policy Controller in GKE Fleet

Centralized Policy Management

Policies are:

  • Defined once (Fleet level)
  • Propagated to all clusters
  • Enforced locally

Benefits:

  • No policy duplication
  • Consistent enforcement
  • Scalable governance

Modes of Operation

Enforce Mode

  • Blocks non-compliant resources
  • Used in production

Audit Mode

  • Reports violations
  • Does not block
  • Used during rollout/testing

DevSecOps Integration

CI/CD Pipeline Integration

Best practice: shift-left policy enforcement

Example Flow:

Developer → PR → CI
               ↓
      Policy Validation (OPA)
               ↓
          Merge allowed
               ↓
        Deploy to cluster
               ↓
     Admission Controller check

Tools:

  • OPA CLI
  • Conftest
  • Terraform OPA validation
  • GitOps (Config Sync)

Security Considerations

Policy Integrity

  • Store policies in Git
  • Enforce signed commits
  • Use protected branches

Bypass Risks

  • Direct API access (bypass CI)
  • Disable admission webhook (misconfiguration)
  • Incorrect scope matching

Mitigation:

  • Enforce:

    • RBAC restrictions
    • Admission controller fail-closed mode

Performance Impact

  • Policy evaluation adds latency
  • Poorly written Rego → performance degradation

Best practice:

  • Optimize rules
  • Avoid excessive iteration

Multi-Tenant Security

  • Use namespace scoping
  • Label-based targeting
  • Separate policies per environment

Common pitfalls

  • Writing overly complex Rego rules
  • Not versioning policies
  • Enforcing too early (breaking dev workflows)
  • Lack of testing environment
  • Ignoring audit violations

Best practices

Policy Design

  • Small, composable policies
  • Clear naming conventions
  • Parameterized constraints

Deployment Strategy

  1. Audit mode
  2. Monitor violations
  3. Gradual enforcement
  4. Full enforcement

Governance

  • Central policy repository
  • Code reviews for policies
  • Security team ownership

Compliance Mapping

Map policies to:

  • CIS controls
  • Internal standards
  • Regulatory requirements

Advanced Use Cases

Supply Chain Security

  • Enforce signed images (Cosign)
  • Require SBOM presence
  • Integrate with SLSA

Zero Trust Kubernetes

  • Enforce identity-based access
  • Restrict network policies
  • Validate service accounts

Platform Engineering

  • Enforce platform standards
  • Prevent “snowflake clusters”
  • Guarantee baseline configuration

Comparison


Feature

OPA/Gatekeeper

Kyverno

Language

Rego

YAML

Flexibility

Very high

Medium

Complexity

Higher

Lower

Enterprise usage

High

Growing

Summary

Policy Controller (OPA/Gatekeeper) is:

  • A critical security control plane for Kubernetes
  • A policy-as-code enforcement engine
  • A foundation of Zero Trust in container platforms

It transforms:

  • Security → from reactive to preventive
  • Compliance → from manual to automated
  • Governance → from fragmented to centralized


ConfigSync

What it is?

Config Sync is a GitOps-based configuration management system for Kubernetes, provided by GKE as part of Fleet (via GKE Hub).

It continuously:

  • Pulls configuration from a Git repository
  • Applies it to clusters
  • Ensures the cluster state matches the declared desired state

Core Purpose

Guarantee that Kubernetes clusters are always in a known, controlled, and compliant state.

Config Sync solves:

  • Configuration drift
  • Manual cluster changes
  • Inconsistent environments
  • Lack of auditability

GitOps Principle

Config Sync is built on GitOps:

Git is the single source of truth for cluster configuration.

Key principles:

  • Declarative configuration
  • Version-controlled infrastructure
  • Automated reconciliation
  • Immutable operations (no manual changes)

Architecture

High-Level Flow

Git Repository
      ↓
Config Sync (Operator)
      ↓
Cluster State (Kubernetes API)
      ↓
Continuous Reconciliation Loop

Components

Sync Controller

  • Runs inside the cluster
  • Watches Git repo
  • Applies manifests

Reconciler

  • Ensures actual state == desired state
  • Detects drift
  • Reverts unauthorized changes

GKE Hub Integration

  • Centralizes configuration across Fleet
  • Enables multi-cluster sync

Key Concepts

RootSync

  • Defines cluster-wide configuration source
  • One per cluster (usually)

  • Controls:

    • Repo URL
    • Branch
    • Directory
    • Auth method

RepoSync

  • Defines namespace-scoped configuration
  • Allows team-level autonomy
  • Enables multi-tenancy

Hierarchical Namespace Controller (HNC)

Optional but powerful:

  • Enables namespace inheritance

  • Useful for:

    • Policy propagation
    • Multi-tenant environments

Repository Structure

Recommended Structure

repo/
├── cluster/
│   ├── prod/
│   ├── staging/
│   └── dev/
├── namespaces/
│   ├── team-a/
│   ├── team-b/
├── policies/
├── platform/
└── apps/

Best Practices

  • Separate:

    • Platform config
    • Application config
    • Policies
  • Use environment overlays
  • Avoid monolithic repos

Reconciliation Model

Config Sync uses a continuous reconciliation loop:

  1. Pull latest Git state
  2. Compare with cluster state
  3. Apply changes
  4. Detect drift
  5. Reconcile automatically

Drift Handling

If someone runs:

kubectl edit deployment my-app

Config Sync:

  • Detects drift
  • Reverts change
  • Restores Git-defined state

Security Model

Git as Source of Truth

  • Enforce:

    • Signed commits
    • Protected branches
    • Code reviews

Authentication to Git

Supported methods:

  • SSH keys
  • HTTPS with token
  • Workload Identity (preferred)

Best practice:

  • Use short-lived credentials
  • Avoid static secrets

RBAC Enforcement

  • Restrict direct cluster access
  • Force changes through Git

  • Separate:

    • Platform team
    • Application teams

Integration with Policy Controller

Config Sync + Policy Controller:

  • Config Sync applies resources
  • Policy Controller validates them
This creates a closed-loop governance system

DevSecOps Integration

CI/CD Pipeline Integration

Developer → PR → CI Validation
               ↓
      Policy + Lint Checks
               ↓
          Merge to Git
               ↓
         Config Sync pulls
               ↓
     Deploy to cluster(s)

Validation Tools

  • OPA / Conftest
  • kubeval / kubeconform
  • Helm lint
  • Terraform validation (if used)

Multi-Cluster Management

Config Sync enables:

  • Same config → multiple clusters
  • Environment-specific overlays
  • Regional deployments

Example

cluster/prod/eu/
cluster/prod/us/
cluster/staging/

Benefits

  • Consistency
  • Scalability
  • Reduced operational overhead

Operational Modes

Continuous Sync

  • Default mode
  • Always reconciles

Manual Sync

  • Breaks GitOps model
  • Should be avoided

Common pitfalls

Architecture

  • Monolithic repo → hard to manage
  • No separation of concerns

Security

  • Hardcoded Git credentials
  • No branch protection

Operations

  • Allowing manual kubectl changes
  • No validation in CI

Best Practices

Repository Strategy

  • One repo per domain or environment
  • Clear ownership boundaries

Change Management

  • PR-based workflow only
  • Mandatory reviews
  • CI validation

Environment Separation

  • Use overlays or separate directories
  • Avoid mixing prod/dev configs

Secrets Management

  • Do NOT store secrets in Git

  • Use:

    • Secret Manager
    • External Secrets Operator
    • Sealed Secrets

Advanced Patterns

Multi-Tenant GitOps

  • RepoSync per namespace
  • Team isolation
  • Shared platform layer

Progressive Delivery

  • Canary deployments via Git branches
  • Gradual rollout per cluster

Platform Engineering

  • Define “golden templates”
  • Enforce via Config Sync
  • Combine with Policy Controller

Manual

Strong

Scenario:

You want:

  • Enforce namespace structure
  • Deploy base policies
  • Configure logging

Flow:

  1. Define YAML in Git
  2. Merge PR

  3. Config Sync applies to:

Compliance Alignment

Config Sync supports:

Config Sync is:

Cloud Service Mesh (CSM)

What it is?

Cloud Service Mesh (CSM) is Google Cloud’s fully managed service mesh offering, built on:

  • Istio (control plane concepts)
  • Envoy (data plane proxy)

It provides:

  • Secure service-to-service communication
  • Traffic management
  • Observability
  • Policy enforcement

across:

  • GKE clusters
  • Multi-cluster environments (via Fleet)
  • Hybrid and multi-cloud deployments

Core Purpose

Abstract and secure service-to-service communication in distributed systems without modifying application code.

Usage

In modern microservices:

  • Services communicate over the network
  • Security is inconsistent
  • Observability is fragmented
  • Traffic control is manual

Without mesh:

  • TLS is optional and inconsistent
  • Retry logic is duplicated in code
  • No uniform visibility
  • Hard to enforce Zero Trust

With mesh:

  • Security is default
  • Networking is policy-driven
  • Observability is automatic
  • Application code is simplified

Architecture

Data Plane

Each pod gets a sidecar proxy (Envoy):

[Service A Container] ↔ [Envoy Proxy]
                               ↓
                        Network (mTLS)
                               ↓
[Envoy Proxy] ↔ [Service B Container]

Responsibilities:

  • Traffic interception
  • Encryption (mTLS)
  • Routing
  • Metrics and logs

Control Plane

Manages:

  • Configuration distribution
  • Certificate issuance
  • Policy enforcement

Fleet Integration

With GKE Fleet:

  • Mesh spans multiple clusters
  • Central configuration via GKE Hub
  • Unified identity and trust domain

Core Capabilities

Zero Trust Security (Critical)

Mutual TLS (mTLS)

  • All service-to-service communication is encrypted
  • Identity is based on workload identity (not IP) 
Service A → Authenticated → Encrypted → Service B

Identity Model

  • Each workload has a cryptographic identity
  • Issued by mesh CA
  • Rotated automatically

Benefits

  • No plaintext traffic
  • Strong service authentication
  • Resistant to lateral movement

Traffic Management

Fine-grained traffic control without code changes.

Example: Canary Deployment

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
spec:
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: service
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: service
        subset: v2
      weight: 10

Capabilities

  • Canary releases
  • Blue/green deployments
  • Traffic splitting
  • A/B testing
  • Fault injection

Observability

Automatically provides:

  • Metrics (latency, error rates)
  • Distributed tracing
  • Access logs

Key Insight

Observability is infrastructure-level, not application-level

Resilience

Built-in reliability features:

  • Retries
  • Timeouts
  • Circuit breakers
  • Load balancing

Policy Enforcement

  • Authorization policies
  • Access control rules
  • Rate limiting
  • Request validation

DevSecOps Integration

CI/CD Integration

Service mesh enables:

  • Safe rollouts (canary)
  • Automated rollback
  • Policy validation

Example Pipeline

Build → Deploy → Mesh routing → Gradual rollout → Observe → Promote

Security Deep Dive

Threat Model (MITRE ATT&CK Alignment)


Threat

Mitigation

Lateral movement

mTLS + identity

Service impersonation

Strong identity

Data exfiltration

Encrypted traffic

MITM attacks

Certificate validation

Zero Trust Principles

  • No implicit trust
  • Identity-based communication
  • Continuous verification

Certificate Management

  • Automatic issuance
  • Rotation
  • Revocation

Multi-Cluster Mesh (Fleet Context)

Capabilities

  • Cross-cluster communication
  • Global service discovery
  • Failover routing

Example

Cluster A (EU) → fails → traffic routed → Cluster B (US)

Common pitfalls

Architecture

  • Deploying mesh without clear use case
  • Overcomplicating small systems

Security

  • Misconfigured mTLS (partial enforcement)
  • Weak authorization policies

Operations

  • Ignoring observability data
  • Not tuning retries/timeouts

Best Practices

Security

  • Enforce STRICT mTLS
  • Use fine-grained authorization policies
  • Integrate with workload identity

Architecture

  • Start with critical services only
  • Gradually expand mesh coverage

Observability

  • Define SLOs based on mesh metrics

  • Monitor:

    • latency
    • error rate
    • saturation

Performance

  • Monitor sidecar overhead
  • Optimize resource allocation

Comparison

Feature

Service Mesh

Traditional Networking

Security

mTLS default

Optional

Observability

Built-in

Manual

Traffic control

Dynamic

Static

Complexity

Higher

Lower

When NOT to Use Service Mesh

Avoid when:

  • Simple monolithic systems
  • Low traffic environments
  • No multi-service communication complexity

Real-World Use Cases

SaaS Platform

  • Multi-region deployment
  • Canary releases
  • Zero Trust communication

Financial Systems

  • Strict compliance
  • Full encryption
  • Auditability

IoT / Edge

  • Secure hub communication
  • Identity-based device interactions
  • Centralized control

Summary

Cloud Service Mesh is:

  • A networking + security abstraction layer
  • A core Zero Trust enabler
  • A critical component of production Kubernetes platforms

It provides:

  • Secure communication (mTLS)
  • Advanced traffic control
  • Deep observability
  • Policy enforcement



Logging and monitoring


Logging

Introduction

Google Cloud Logging (formerly Stackdriver Logging) is a fully managed, scalable, and highly integrated service that enables the collection, storage, analysis, monitoring, and alerting of log data across Google Cloud and custom applications. It is a foundational component of the Google Cloud Operations Suite (formerly Stackdriver) and is heavily used for troubleshooting, auditing, compliance, and observability.

Use cases

  • Troubleshooting and Diagnostics: Identify and resolve issues across workloads by searching and analyzing logs.
  • Operational Insights: Gain visibility into system behavior, application performance, and anomalies.
  • Security and Compliance: Track access and activity through audit logs and meet regulatory requirements.
  • Real-time Monitoring and Alerts: Generate alerts based on logs and integrate with other monitoring tools.

Architecture


Log Ingestion Layer – Log Collection

Cloud Logging collects log data from multiple sources, including:

  • Google Cloud-native services:

    • Compute Engine (VM logs, system logs)
    • App Engine (request logs, application logs)
    • Cloud Functions
    • Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) (container logs, node logs)
    • Cloud Run and Cloud Load Balancing

  • Custom applications:

    • Via the Cloud Logging API or Logging client libraries.

  • On-premises or multi-cloud environments:

    • Using Ops Agent or Fluentd-based agents to stream logs.

Logs are typically collected as structured JSON payloads, enhancing parsing and analysis.

Log Router – Filtering and Routing

Once logs are ingested, they pass through the Log Router, which processes and determines the destination for each log entry.


Key Features:

  • Inclusion filters: Define which logs to capture.
  • Exclusion filters: Reduce log volume and cost by discarding unneeded data.
  • Custom routing rules: Tailor log flows for different teams, services, or compliance zones.

Routing is policy-driven and can direct logs to various sinks.

Log Sinks – Storage and Export

A log sink defines a destination where logs are delivered and stored. There are several sink types:

Sink Type

Description

Log Buckets

Default and user-created storage in Cloud Logging. Support regionalization and retention policies.

BigQuery

Store and query logs using SQL for advanced analytics. Ideal for correlation with business data.

Cloud Storage

Store logs as JSON objects. Useful for long-term cold storage or archival.

Pub/Sub

Forward logs in real-time to external systems, SIEMs, or custom processors.


Each sink can have its own filters, and you can create multiple sinks per project, folder, or organization.

Log Analysis – Visibility and Insights

Cloud Logging includes powerful tools to explore and analyze logs:

Logs Explorer

  • Advanced UI for filtering, querying, and viewing logs.
  • Features: histogram view, log stream, resource tree, text and structured filtering.

Error Reporting

  • Detects and groups recurring application errors.
  • Supports automatic notifications and error tracking dashboards.

Logs-based Metrics

  • Convert logs into custom metrics for dashboards and alerting.
  • Examples: Count of errors per minute, response time anomalies.

Alerting

  • Define conditions on logs or metrics.
  • Integrate with Cloud Monitoring, email, SMS, Slack, or custom webhook notifications.

Log Analytics (Powered by BigQuery)

  • Perform ad hoc analysis with SQL on logs stored in BigQuery.
  • Enables correlation with other datasets and complex aggregations.

Logs categories

In Google Cloud Logging, logs are organized into categories based on their source and purpose. These categories help users understand where the logs originate, how they are collected, and what insights they provide. Understanding these categories is crucial for designing efficient observability, monitoring, and security strategies.

Platform logs

These logs are generated by Google Cloud services themselves.

  • Purpose: Provide operational visibility into the behavior of Google-managed infrastructure.

  • Examples:

    • VPC Flow Logs: Show network traffic information for VMs.
    • Cloud Load Balancing Logs: Record HTTP(S) traffic behavior.
    • Cloud NAT Logs: Show source-to-destination IP mappings.
    • Cloud Storage Access Logs: Show file access history.

These logs help users troubleshoot, optimize performance, and understand system activity without requiring custom instrumentation.

Component logs

Generated by Google-managed components running in your environments (e.g., GKE clusters or custom VMs).

  • Examples:

    • Kubernetes system logs (kubelet, kube-proxy, etc.)
    • Fluentd or Ops Agent system messages
    • GKE node-level metrics and daemon activity

These logs are particularly important in hybrid environments, where Google software runs outside of managed Google Cloud services.

Security logs

Logs specifically related to security, access control, and compliance.

  • Cloud Audit Logs:

    • Admin Activity Logs: Log administrative operations such as resource creation or deletion.
    • Data Access Logs: Show read/write access to user data.
    • System Event Logs: Log actions on behalf of the system.

  • Access Transparency Logs:

    • Logs any access by Google support or engineering staff to your data.

  • Firewall and IAM Deny Logs:

    • Show denied traffic or permission violations.

These logs answer the essential forensic question: “Who did what, where, and when?”

User-Written Logs

Custom logs generated by applications and services you build or manage.

  • Sources:

    • Web applications
    • Microservices
    • Background services and daemons

  • Ingestion methods:

    • Ops Agent / Fluent Bit / Fluentd
    • Cloud Logging API (entries.write)
    • Logging client libraries
    • gcloud CLI (gcloud logging write)

Applications can use standard logging libraries (e.g., winston, log4j, bunyan, etc.) and emit logs to stdout/stderr, which agents can collect and forward to Cloud Logging.

Multi-cloud and Hybrid-cloud Logs

Logs from non-Google environments:

  • Multi-cloud: Logs from AWS, Azure, etc.
  • Hybrid-cloud: Logs from on-premise systems and legacy infrastructure.

  • Collection methods:

    • Logging agents (installed on external systems)
    • API integration with third-party tools
    • Pub/Sub and custom exporters

These logs enable a centralized logging solution across your entire IT footprint.

Storing and routing

After logs are collected from various sources (services, applications, on-prem systems), they pass through a routing and storage pipeline within the Cloud Logging infrastructure. This architecture is highly flexible, supporting real-time streaming, advanced filtering, long-term retention, and integration with external systems.

Centralized logging API & Log Router

At the core of Cloud Logging is the centralized Logging API, which serves as the entry point for all log data. Every log entry passes through this unified API interface and is then handed off to the Log Router.

Log Router Key Roles:

  • Receives all ingested logs (from both Google Cloud and custom sources).
  • Applies filters to determine inclusion or exclusion.
  • Routes log entries to one or multiple destinations called sinks.
  • Buffers data efficiently and handles streaming at scale.

The Log Router ensures that logs are processed in real-time and delivered reliably to the appropriate destinations.

Log Routing via Sinks

Sinks are responsible for exporting logs to other Google Cloud services or external systems. You can define filters per sink to route only specific subsets of log data.

Sink Components:

  • Query filter: Determines which logs are included in the sink.
  • Destination: Where the logs should be stored or forwarded.

Sink Levels (Scopes):

  • Project-level sink: Routes logs from a single project.
  • Folder-level sink: Aggregates logs from all projects and folders inside a folder.
  • Organization-level sink: Centralized log export for the entire organization hierarchy.
  • Billing-account-level sink: Used for exporting logs related to billing activities.

Sinks run in parallel with default logging, meaning logs can go both to the standard logging buckets and any number of custom destinations.

Log Storage Options (Destinations)

Logs can be stored in various destinations based on retention, queryability, access needs, or integration requirements.

Cloud Logging Buckets

  • _Required bucket:

    • Stores Admin Activity, System Events, and Access Transparency logs.
    • Immutable: Cannot be modified or deleted.
    • Free of charge with 400-day retention.

  • _Default bucket:

    • Stores all other log entries by default.
    • Retained for 30 days by default (can be customized).
    • Standard Cloud Logging pricing applies.

You can also create custom buckets to segregate logs by workload, region, or retention policy.

BigQuery

  • Enables advanced, SQL-powered analytics over large-scale logs.
  • Supports integration with Looker Studio and BI tools.
  • Recommended for security analysis, anomaly detection, and long-term insights.

Use case: “Query all failed App Engine requests over the last month.”

Cloud Storage

  • Stores logs as JSON files in object format.
  • Ideal for archival, regulatory retention, or integration with external processors.
  • Supports auto-tiering, retention policies, and object lifecycle management.

Use case: Archive VPC Flow logs for 10 years using Nearline/Coldline tiers.

Pub/Sub

  • Streams log entries to real-time consumers.

  • Used for event-driven processing, such as:

    • Alert generation
    • Data enrichment
    • Sending logs to third-party services

Use case: Pub/Sub → Dataflow → BigQuery pipeline for real-time security alerts.

Splunk or SIEM Integration

  • Export logs via Pub/Sub to Splunk Dataflow connector.
  • Use Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud for ingestion.
  • Ensures centralized security event monitoring.

External Project

  • Logs can be routed to Cloud Storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub in a different Google Cloud project.
  • Useful for creating centralized logging environments with access control separation.

Filtering: Inclusion & Exclusion

To control which logs are routed or stored, the Log Router supports:

  • Inclusion filters: Define what should be captured.
  • Exclusion filters: Prevent unneeded logs from being routed or stored.

⚠️ Warning: Excluded logs are permanently discarded. Use carefully.

Access control and Compliance

Cloud Logging supports fine-grained IAM roles to manage access:

  • View logs at project, folder, or organization level.
  • Differentiate roles for viewers, editors, and admins.
  • Ensures audit logs (Admin Activity, Data Access, etc.) are secure and immutable.

Audit logs are automatically generated for most Google Cloud services and are essential for compliance tracking.

Integration and extensibility

Cloud Logging can be integrated with third-party platforms and tools:

  • SIEM tools via Pub/Sub.
  • Monitoring stacks like Prometheus or Grafana via exporters.
  • Custom dashboards and analytics pipelines using BigQuery or Data Studio.

You can also configure log-based alerts, structured payloads, or Log4j, Fluent Bit, OpenTelemetry, etc., for custom logging needs.

Conclusion

Google Cloud Logging offers a robust, scalable, and flexible architecture designed to meet the observability needs of modern cloud-native and hybrid systems. It acts as the nervous system of your infrastructure, ensuring that logs are not just stored, but transformed into actionable insights for reliability, security, and performance.

By combining powerful routing, analysis, and alerting capabilities with seamless integration across Google Cloud and external tools, Cloud Logging empowers teams to maintain control, ensure compliance, and rapidly respond to issues at any scale.


Terraform

Introduction

Terraform is a powerful Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool that integrates seamlessly with Google Cloud to manage and provision cloud resources efficiently.

  • Terraform enables the provisioning and management of Google Cloud resources through declarative configuration files.
  • It interacts with Google Cloud APIs to automate the deployment and management of infrastructure.

Tools and resources

Terraform Registry

A centralized hub for discovering and using Terraform modules and providers.

Features:

  • Plugins to manage Google Cloud resources via the Google provider.
  • Pre-built modules for common infrastructure setups.
  • Examples of best practices for writing Terraform configurations.

Usage:

  • Search for modules specific to Google Cloud.
  • Use verified modules developed by HashiCorp, Google, or third-party contributors.

Cloud Foundation Toolkit (CFT)

A collection of Terraform modules designed to reflect Google Cloud best practices. Known as Terraform blueprints.

Purpose: Build repeatable and consistent foundations in Google Cloud.

Features:

  • IAM management for multiple projects within a single module.
  • Modules for networking, compute, storage, and more.

Example Use Case:

  • Manage IAM bindings across multiple projects efficiently:
  module "iam_bindings" {
    source  = "terraform-google-modules/iam/google"
    version = "X.Y.Z"
  
    projects = ["project-one", "project-two"]
  
    bindings = {
      "roles/compute.networkUser" = [
        "user:network-user@example.com",
        "group:network-group@example.com"
      ]
      "roles/appengine.appAdmin" = [
        "user:app-admin@example.com",
        "group:app-group@example.com"
      ]
    }
  }

Cloud Foundation Fabric (CFF)

A repository of Terraform modules and end-to-end examples for Google Cloud.

Purpose: Used for fast prototyping or as modular components for production environments.

Features:

  • Comprehensive blueprints for networking, IAM, and application setups.
  • Modules and examples designed for diverse organizational needs.

Infrastructure Manager (Infra Manager)

A managed service for automating the deployment of Google Cloud infrastructure using Terraform.

Purpose: Define and deploy infrastructure via Terraform configurations.

Limitations:

  • Does not manage application deployment (use tools like Cloud Build or Cloud Deploy for applications).


Cheetsheet

Basics

Export region and location

export my_region=us-west1
export my_cluster=autopilot-cluster-1

Autocompletion

source <(kubectl completion bash)

List the active account name

gcloud auth list

List the project ID

gcloud config list project

Configure access to cluster

gcloud container clusters get-credentials $my_cluster --region $my_region

IAM

List roles (project type)

gcloud iam roles list --project $DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID

Describe role

gcloud iam roles describe app_viewer --project \
$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID

Create a role

gcloud iam roles create app_viewer --project \
$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID --file role.yaml

role.yaml

title: App Viewer
description: Custom role to view apps
stage: ALPHA
includedPermissions:
- compute.instances.get
- compute.instances.list
- appengine.versions.get
- appengine.versions.list

Update a role

gcloud iam roles update app_viewer --project \
$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID --file update-role.yaml

Disable a role

gcloud iam roles update app_viewer --project \
$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID --stage DISABLED

Delete a role

gcloud iam roles delete app_viewer --project \
$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID

List roles (show deleted)

gcloud iam roles list --project $DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID \
--show-deleted

Un-delete a role

gcloud iam roles undelete app_viewer --project \
$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID

Get the list of permissions available for your project

gcloud iam list-testable-permissions //cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID

View the role metadata

gcloud iam roles describe [ROLE_NAME]

List grantable roles from your project

gcloud iam list-grantable-roles //cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID

Service account

Create service account

gcloud iam service-accounts create my-sa-123 --display-name "my service account"

Grant access for service account

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID \
    --member serviceAccount:my-sa-123@$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role roles/editor

Network

Create network

gcloud compute networks create mynetwork --subnet-mode=auto

gcloud compute networks create privatenet --subnet-mode=custom

gcloud compute networks subnets create privatesubnet \
--network=privatenet --region=europe-west1 \
--range=10.0.0.0/24 --enable-private-ip-google-access

Add firewall rule

gcloud compute firewall-rules create \
mynetwork-ingress-allow-ssh-from-cs \
--network mynetwork --action ALLOW --direction INGRESS \
--rules tcp:22 --source-ranges $ip --target-tags=lab-ssh

Enable VPC flow logs

gcloud compute networks subnets update default \
--region us-central1 --enable-flow-logs \
--logging-metadata=include-all

Disable VPC flow logs

gcloud compute networks subnets update default \
--region europe-west1 --no-enable-flow-logs

Create subnet

gcloud compute networks subnets create cloud-ids-useast1 \
--range=192.168.10.0/24 \
--network=cloud-ids \
--region=us-east1

Configure private services access

gcloud compute addresses create cloud-ids-ips \
--global \
--purpose=VPC_PEERING \
--addresses=10.10.10.0 \
--prefix-length=24 \
--description="Cloud IDS Range" \
--network=cloud-ids

Create a private connection

gcloud services vpc-peerings connect \
--service=servicenetworking.googleapis.com \
--ranges=cloud-ids-ips \
--network=cloud-ids \
--project=$PROJECT_ID

Create the allow-http-icmp rule

gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-http-icmp \
--direction=INGRESS \
--priority=1000 \
--network=cloud-ids \
--action=ALLOW \
--rules=tcp:80,icmp \
--source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0 \
--target-tags=server

Create the allow-iap-proxy rule

gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-iap-proxy \
--direction=INGRESS \
--priority=1000 \
--network=cloud-ids \
--action=ALLOW \
--rules=tcp:22 \
--source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20

Create a Cloud Router

gcloud compute routers create cr-cloud-ids-useast1 \
--region=us-east1 \
--network=cloud-ids

Configure Cloud NAT

gcloud compute routers nats create nat-cloud-ids-useast1 \
--router=cr-cloud-ids-useast1 \
--router-region=us-east1 \
--auto-allocate-nat-external-ips \
--nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges

List packet mirrorings

gcloud compute packet-mirrorings list

Create packet mirroring policy

export FORWARDING_RULE=$(gcloud ids endpoints describe cloud-ids-east1 --zone=us-east1-b --format="value(endpointForwardingRule)")
echo $FORWARDING_RULE

gcloud compute packet-mirrorings create cloud-ids-packet-mirroring \
--region=us-east1 \
--collector-ilb=$FORWARDING_RULE \
--network=cloud-ids \
--mirrored-subnets=cloud-ids-useast1

VMs

Create VM

gcloud compute instances create default-vm-1 \
--machine-type e2-micro \
--zone=europe-west1-d --network=default

Add tags for VMs

gcloud compute instances add-tags mynet-vm-2 \
    --zone us-central1-f \
    --tags lab-ssh
gcloud compute instances add-tags mynet-vm-1 \
    --zone europe-west1-d \
    --tags lab-ssh

API Services

Enable Service Networking API

gcloud services enable servicenetworking.googleapis.com \
    --project=$PROJECT_ID

Enable Cloud IDS API

gcloud services enable ids.googleapis.com \
    --project=$PROJECT_ID

Enable Cloud Logging API

gcloud services enable logging.googleapis.com \
    --project=$PROJECT_ID

Cloud IDS

List of Cloud IDS endpoints

gcloud ids endpoints list --project=$PROJECT_ID

Create Cloud IDS endpoint

gcloud ids endpoints create cloud-ids-east1 \
--network=cloud-ids \
--zone=us-east1-b \
--severity=INFORMATIONAL \
--async

KMS

Create KeyRings

gcloud kms keyrings create $KEYRING_NAME --location asia-south1

Create CryptoKey

gcloud kms keys create $CRYPTOKEY_1_NAME --location asia-south1 \
--keyring $KEYRING_NAME --purpose encryption

Encrypt data using REST API

curl \
"https://cloudkms.googleapis.com/v1/projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID/locations/asia-south1/keyRings/$KEYRING_NAME/cryptoKeys/$CRYPTOKEY_1_NAME:encrypt" \
-d "{\"plaintext\":\"$PLAIN_TEXT\"}" \
-H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default \
print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json"

Descrypt data using REST API

curl -v \
"https://cloudkms.googleapis.com/v1/projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID/locations/asia-south1/keyRings/$KEYRING_NAME/cryptoKeys/$CRYPTOKEY_1_NAME:decrypt" \
-d "{\"ciphertext\":\"$(cat data1.encrypted)\"}" \
-H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default \
print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type:application/json" \
| jq .plaintext -r | base64 -d > data1.decrypted

Google Storage

Check storage encryption

gsutil kms encryption gs://$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID-kms

Allow service account to use 

gsutil kms authorize -p $DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID -k \
projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID/locations/asia-south1/keyRings\
/$KEYRING_NAME/cryptoKeys/$CRYPTOKEY_1_NAME
gsutil kms authorize -p $DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID -k \
projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID/locations/asia-south1/keyRings\
/$KEYRING_NAME/cryptoKeys/$CRYPTOKEY_2_NAME

Encrypt storage using key

gsutil kms encryption -k \
projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID/locations/asia-south1/keyRings\
/$KEYRING_NAME/cryptoKeys/$CRYPTOKEY_1_NAME \
gs://$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID-kms

Push object with specified key for encryption

gsutil -o \
"GSUtil:encryption_key=projects/$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID/locations/asia-south1/keyRings\
/$KEYRING_NAME/cryptoKeys/$CRYPTOKEY_2_NAME" \
cp file3.txt gs://$DEVSHELL_PROJECT_ID-kms
